Infra Handbook

Working notes on Linux, cloud and infrastructure. Written while learning each topic hands-on, and kept as the reference I come back to.

$ tree infra-handbook
infra-handbook
├── linux/        16 chapters
├── bash/         3 chapters
├── aws/          next

├── docker/       16 chapters

Revise one

docs.title: Bash Scripting
docs.text:
Writing scripts that are correct, readable and safe to run. Read in order.

  1. Bash Basics Arguments, command types, shebang, variables, expansion, arithmetic
  2. Conditionals, Loops & Functions Exit codes, && / ||, [[ ]], tests, loops, case, functions
  3. Script Safety set -euo pipefail, trap, mktemp, common pitfalls

docs.title: Bash Basics
docs.text: Hands-on notes, from the BashGuide

docs.title: Commands and arguments
docs.text:
• Bash splits a line on spaces → first word = command, rest = arguments
  • echo a b → 2 args → prints a b
  • echo "a b" → 1 arg → prints a b
  • Quotes decide how many arguments a command gets

docs.title: Types of commands
docs.text:
• Alias → text shortcut → ll = ls -alF
  • Function → named block of bash code
  • Builtin → inside bash itself → cd, echo, read
  • Keyword → bash syntax → if, for, while, [[
  • Executable → program file on disk → /usr/bin/ls
  • type cd / type -a ls → shows which kind
  • cd must be builtin → a separate program can't change your shell's directory
  • Same name → alias wins, then keyword, function, builtin, executable

docs.title: [ needs spaces
docs.text:
• [ is a command → [ $x = 5 ] → args: $x, =, 5, ]
  • [$x = 5] → bash looks for command named [5 → not found

docs.title: Scripts and the shebang
docs.text:
• Shebang → #!/usr/bin/env bash → tells Linux which program reads the file
  • Without it → may run under sh, bash features break
  • .sh extension means nothing to Linux → first line decides
  • /usr/bin/env bash → finds bash in PATH → more portable than /bin/bash
  • Runnable needs → chmod +x + shebang → run with ./script.sh
  • ./script.sh → ./ needed because current dir is not in PATH
  • bash script.sh → shebang ignored, bash already chosen

docs.title: Special characters
docs.text:
• "..." → expands $var, keeps spaces
  • '...' → everything literal, no expansion
  • \ → escape next char
  • $ → expansion → $var, $(cmd), $((1+2))
  • # → comment
  • ; → run commands one after another
  • && → run next only if previous succeeded | || → run next only if previous failed
  • > < | → redirect, input, pipe (see Redirection & Pipes)
  • { } → group in same shell | ( ) → group in subshell
  • ~ → home | * → any chars | ? → one char

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
• name="aditya" → no spaces around =
  • "$name" → always quote
  • "${name}_bak" → braces when text touches the name

docs.title: Special parameters
docs.text:
• $0 → script name
  • $1 $2 → arguments
  • $# → number of arguments
  • "$@" → all args, each kept separate → use this
  • "$*" → all args glued into one string → only for messages
  • $? → exit code of last command, 0 = success
  • $$ → PID of current shell

docs.title: Parameter expansion
docs.text:
• ${var:-default} → default if empty/unset → PORT=${PORT:-8080}
  • ${#var} → length
  • ${f%.gz} → remove from end → backup.tar.gz → backup.tar
  • ${f#backup.} → remove from start → backup.tar.gz → tar.gz

Quoting danger

  • file='no secret'; rm $file → runs rm no secret → deletes wrong file
  • rm "$file" → one argument → correct

docs.title: Arithmetic
docs.text:
• Variables are strings by default → a=5; a+=2 → 52 (string append)
  • a=$((a + 2)) → 7
  • let a+=2 → 7
  • declare -i a=5; a+=2 → 7 → integer attribute, every assignment is math
  • a=5+2 → "5+2" text | declare -i a=5+2 → 7
  • Prefer $(( )) and (( )) → a=$((a+2)), (( a++ ))

docs.title: Here documents
docs.text:
• cat > file <<'EOF' ... EOF → write many lines into a file at once
  • Quoted 'EOF' → no expansion inside → $vars written literally
cat > notes.txt <<'EOF'
line one
$HOME stays as text
EOF

Interview points

  • Shebang purpose → picks the interpreter → #!/usr/bin/env bash finds bash in PATH
  • $@ vs $* → "$@" keeps each arg separate, "$*" glues them into one string
  • Why is cd a builtin → a separate program can't change your shell's directory
  • a=5; a+=2 gives 52 → variables are strings → use $(( )) for math

docs.title: Conditionals, Loops & Functions
docs.text: Hands-on notes, from the BashGuide

docs.title: Exit status
docs.text:
• Every command returns 0–255 → 0 = success, else failure
  • echo $? → see last exit code
  • exit 1 in scripts when something goes wrong
  • Exit codes are 0–255 → ping: 0 reply, 1 no reply, 2 other error
  • >&2 → send message to stderr → all error messages go there
  • ! cmd → flips exit status → ! grep -q bad file
  • grep -q → no output, just exit code → used in conditions

docs.title: && and ||
docs.text:
• mkdir d && cd d → cd only if mkdir worked
  • cd "$dir" || { echo "no dir" >&2; exit 1; } → stop script if cd fails
  • { ...; } groups commands → needs ; before }
  • ; vs && → ; runs next always, && only on success
  • a && b && c || d → d runs if ANY earlier one failed → group: a && { b || d; }

docs.title: if
docs.text:
• if [[ cond ]]; then ... elif [[ cond ]]; then ... else ... fi
if [[ -f "$file" ]]; then
    echo "exists"
elif [[ -d "$file" ]]; then
    echo "is a dir"
else
    echo "missing"
fi

docs.title: [ vs [[
docs.text:
• [ → command, unquoted vars get split → breaks on spaces/empty
  • [[ → bash keyword, no splitting → safe, supports patterns + regex
  • In bash scripts always use [[ ]]
  • [ apple < banana ] → < is redirection → use [[ ]] or \<

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• Files → -e exists | -f file | -d dir | -r readable | -w writable | -x executable | -s not empty
  • -h file → true if symlink
  • f1 -nt f2 → f1 newer | -ot → older
  • [[ $var ]] → true if var not empty | [[ ! $var ]] → true if empty
  • Strings → -z empty | -n not empty | = != compare
  • Numbers → -eq -ne -lt -gt -le -ge → or (( n > 5 ))
  • Strings vs numbers → "314" < "9" as text, but 314 -gt 9 as numbers
  • [[ $f == *.log ]] → pattern
  • [[ $u =~ ^[a-z]+$ ]] → regex
  • [[ $x = $pat ]] unquoted right side → pattern match | "$pat" quoted → exact string

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
• for f in *.log; do ...; done → loop files → never $(ls)
  • for i in {1..5}; do ...; done
  • for (( i=0; i<5; i++ )) → C-style loop
  • while read -r line; do ...; done < file → read line by line
  • read -r → don't treat \ as escape → always use -r
  • until cmd → loop while cmd fails → same as while ! cmd
  • break → exit loop | continue → next iteration
  • select → simple menu → rarely used

docs.title: case
docs.text:
• case $1 in start) ... ;; stop) ... ;; *) usage ;; esac
  • ;& → fall through to next block
case $1 in
    start) echo "starting" ;;
    stop)  echo "stopping" ;;
    *)     echo "usage: $0 start|stop" ;;
esac

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
• name() { ...; }
  • Inside function → $1 $@ are the function's args
  • local var=x → variable stays inside function
  • return 0/1 → function exit code | exit → ends whole script

Interview points

  • [ vs [[ → [ is a command with word splitting, [[ is a keyword without it
  • a && b || c → c also runs if b fails → not a real if/else
  • return vs exit → return ends the function, exit ends the whole script
  • Why never for f in $(ls) → filenames with spaces split → use for f in *

docs.title: Script Safety
docs.text: Hands-on notes, from the BashGuide

docs.title: set -euo pipefail
docs.text:
• -e → stop when a command fails
  • -u → error on unset variable → stops $dirr typo becoming rm -rf /*
  • ${3:-} → empty if $3 missing → stops set -u from erroring on optional args
  • -o pipefail → pipe fails if any part fails, not just last
  • -e doesn't catch failures inside if or before && || → safety net, not guarantee

docs.title: trap
docs.text:
• trap 'cleanup' EXIT → runs when script ends, even on failure
  • Used to delete temp files / half-written archives

docs.title: mktemp
docs.text:
• mktemp → unique temp file | mktemp -d → temp dir
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

tmp=$(mktemp -d)
cleanup() { rm -rf "$tmp"; }
trap cleanup EXIT

tar -czf "$tmp/backup.tar.gz" "$HOME/notes"

docs.title: Pitfalls 1–5
docs.text:
• for f in $(ls) → use for f in *
  • cp $file $dst → cp -- "$file" "$dst"
  • Filenames starting with - → use -- or ./*
  • [ $foo = bar ] → quote or use [[ ]]
  • cd $dir → cd "$dir" || exit 1
  • All the same rule → quote vars, globs not ls, handle failures

Interview points

  • set -euo pipefail flag by flag → -e stop on failure, -u error on unset var, -o pipefail pipe fails if any part fails
  • Does set -e catch everything → no, not inside if or before && || → safety net, not guarantee
  • trap cleanup EXIT → cleanup runs even when the script fails
  • Common bash pitfalls → quote vars, globs not ls, handle failures

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Hands-on notes, written while learning Docker on my own Ubuntu machine

  1. Introduction Container vs VM, namespaces, cgroups, OverlayFS, core objects
  2. Architecture CLI, docker.sock, dockerd, containerd, shim, runc
  3. Install & Upgrade Install method, upgrading docker-ce, socket activation
  4. Containers Lifecycle, docker run flags, ps -aq, stop vs rm, --rm
  5. Images & Storage Layers, copy-on-write, tags vs digests, Dockerfile, volumes
  6. Networking Ports, docker0, drivers, custom networks, DNS, host mode
  7. Namespaces The 7 namespaces, nsenter, lsns, unshare
  8. Logs & Files on Disk /var/lib/docker, the -json.log file, docker logs
  9. Volumes & Bind Mounts -v vs --mount, named volumes, bind mounts, tmpfs, backup
  10. The Docker Socket docker.sock, mounting it, why it is root, Portainer
  11. Dockerfile FROM, RUN vs CMD, ARG vs ENV, building and running an image
  12. ENTRYPOINT & CMD fixed command vs default arguments, --entrypoint, exit codes, main process
  13. EXPOSE, COPY, WORKDIR & USER EXPOSE vs -p, COPY vs ADD, non-root USER, -f
  14. Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless AS build, COPY --from, distroless images, no shell, 750MB to 292MB
  15. Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup layers, build cache, image ID vs tag, docker history, prune, secrets
  16. Registries & Pushing Images full image names, Docker Hub, ECR, GCR, docker tag, docker push, build context

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Hands-on notes, Docker architecture

docs.title: Daemon
docs.text:
• Daemon → any program that runs in the background all the time, no window or terminal, waits for work
  • Names end in d by tradition → sshd, systemd, crond, dockerd, containerd
  • "The Docker daemon" = dockerd → same thing

docs.title: The components (top to bottom)
docs.text:
• docker CLI (/usr/bin/docker) → only a client / remote control, does no container work itself
  • CLI turns docker run nginx into an HTTP request (REST API) → sends it through /var/run/docker.sock
  • docker.sock → Unix socket = special file two programs on the same machine talk through
  • docker --version works even when the daemon is down → only the client is involved
  • Access to docker.sock = effectively root access
  • dockerd → the manager, runs as root → API, image builds (BuildKit), networks (creates docker0, iptables NAT, container IPs), volumes, pull/push, logs
  • dockerd does NOT run containers itself → delegates to containerd
  • containerd → container runtime manager → stores images, unpacks layers (snapshots), container lifecycle (create, start, stop, delete), starts a shim per container
  • containerd came out of Docker, now an independent CNCF project → package containerd.io
  • containerd-shim → one small process per container = its babysitter → stays as the container's parent, holds stdin/stdout (docker logs, docker attach), records exit code
  • Shim is the parent → dockerd/containerd can restart without killing containers (with live-restore)
  • runc → low-level tool that creates the container → namespaces → cgroups → root filesystem → starts the process → exits
  • runc does not stay running → after that the container is a normal process (ps aux | grep nginx shows it)
  • Linux kernel → where isolation actually happens (namespaces, cgroups, OverlayFS, iptables/nftables + veth)
  • Registry → online store of images (Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR) → dockerd pulls from and pushes to it
Component Job Lifetime dockerd Manager: requests, pulls, networks, volumes, logs Always running containerd Supervisor: images, start/stop containers Always running containerd-shim Babysitter for one container As long as its container runc Builder: creates the container Split second, then exits

docs.title: dockerd vs containerd
docs.text:
• dockerd → Docker-specific features: commands, Dockerfiles, -p syntax, docker0, volumes, logs
  • containerd → only runs containers, knows nothing about Dockerfiles, Compose or docker0
  • Why split → core "run containers" part separated so other tools can use it without the rest of Docker
  • Kubernetes uses containerd directly, no dockerd
  • dockerd is started with --containerd=/run/containerd/containerd.sock → that's how it finds containerd
  • Docker's containers live in containerd's moby namespace → sudo ctr -n moby containers list
Restaurant analogy docker CLI Customer placing an order docker.sock Order window dockerd Manager: takes orders, buys ingredients, arranges tables, keeps records containerd Head chef: only cooks shim + runc Kitchen helpers who plate each dish Kernel The kitchen itself Registry Supplier / warehouse

docs.title: What happens on docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx
docs.text:
1. CLI sends a POST request over docker.sock to dockerd
  2. dockerd checks for the image locally → missing → pulls the layers from Docker Hub
  3. dockerd sets up the network (veth pair, IP, iptables rule for 8080) and any volumes
  4. dockerd asks containerd over gRPC to create and start the container
  5. containerd prepares the filesystem snapshot (layers + fresh writable layer) and starts a shim
  6. Shim calls runc → creates namespaces and cgroups, sets the root filesystem
  7. runc starts nginx, then exits
  8. nginx runs as an isolated process, shim is its parent, collects its output

  9. CLI prints the container ID and gives the terminal back (-d)

  10. docker run = pull (if missing) + create + start + attach (unless -d)

docs.title: Lab: see the stack on my machine
docs.text:
ps -ef --forest | grep -E 'dockerd|containerd|shim' | grep -v grep
systemctl status docker --no-pager | head -5
systemctl status containerd --no-pager | head -5
docker info | grep -E 'Runtime|Storage Driver|Cgroup'
ls /var/lib/docker
sudo ctr -n moby containers list
  • Two separate services, two separate processes → docker and containerd

Interview points

  • What does the docker CLI do? → nothing by itself; it sends REST API requests to dockerd over /var/run/docker.sock
  • Why is access to docker.sock dangerous? → whoever can write to it controls dockerd, which runs as root, so it is effectively root access
  • dockerd vs containerd? → dockerd handles Docker features (API, builds, networks, volumes, logs); containerd only manages images and container lifecycle
  • What does runc do? → creates namespaces and cgroups, sets the root filesystem, starts the process, then exits
  • Why a shim per container? → it stays as the container's parent, keeps its logs and exit code, so dockerd/containerd can restart without killing containers
  • Does Kubernetes need Docker? → no, it talks to containerd directly
  • What is a daemon? → a background program that runs all the time waiting for work, usually named with a trailing d

docs.title: Containers
docs.text: Hands-on notes, running and cleaning up containers

docs.title: Processes and signals
docs.text:
• Process → a running program, has a PID | PID 1 on the host → systemd
  • A container is just a process → main process exits = container stops
  • Signals → SIGTERM (15) "shut down cleanly" | SIGKILL (9) "die now", can't be ignored | SIGINT (2) → what Ctrl+C sends
  • docker stop → SIGTERM, waits 10s, then SIGKILL | docker kill → SIGKILL immediately
  • nginx image sets its stop signal to SIGQUIT → finish current requests, then quit → Exited (0)

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
• created → running → paused → running → stopped (exited) → removed
State Meaning Created Set up, process not started Running Main process alive Paused Process frozen (cgroup freezer) Exited Main process ended, container still exists with its writable layer Removed Gone completely
  • Stopped container is NOT deleted → sits there until docker rm
  • docker run ubuntu exits instantly → default command bash, no terminal attached → bash exits
  • Exit codes → 0 success | 1 app error | 137 SIGKILL / out of memory | 143 SIGTERM
  • Restart policies → no (default) | on-failure | always | unless-stopped

docs.title: Foreground vs detached
docs.text:
• No -d → attached to terminal, shows the app's output, looks "stuck" → nginx is a server, meant to run forever
  • -d → runs in background, prints the container ID, terminal comes back
  • -it → -i keep input open + -t give it a terminal → for interactive shells

docs.title: docker run flags
docs.text:
Flag Meaning -d Detached (background) -it Interactive + terminal --name x Own name instead of a random one --rm Delete automatically when it stops -p H:C Publish container port C on host port H -v src:dst Volume or bind mount -e KEY=val Environment variable --network n Join a network --restart Restart policy -m / --cpus Memory / CPU limits (cgroups)
  • Flags go AFTER the subcommand → docker run --rm ... ✓ | docker --rm ... ✗ unknown flag
  • No --name → random adjective_scientist name (wizardly_boyd, stoic_wu)
  • --rm → container + writable layer deleted as soon as it stops → docker stop alone leaves nothing in ps -a
  • --rm does NOT let docker rm delete a running container → only cleans up after stop
  • --rm for throwaway/test containers → skip it when I need the logs or exit code afterwards

docs.title: Command shapes
docs.text:
• docker <object> <action> → container, image, volume, network, system
  • Old shortcuts → docker ps = docker container ls | docker run = docker container run | docker rmi = docker image rm
  • run → creates a NEW container | start → restarts an existing stopped one → running run again = second container
  • run → new container | exec → command inside an existing running one → docker exec -it web bash

docs.title: Listing and cleaning up
docs.text:
• docker ps → running only | docker ps -a → all, including stopped
  • -q → IDs only, no table → docker ps -aq = IDs of all containers
  • $( ... ) → runs the inner command and pastes its output in place
  • docker rm $(docker ps -aq) → remove every stopped container (running ones error out)
  • docker rm -f $(docker ps -aq) → force-remove everything, running too → careful
  • docker stop $(docker ps -q) → stop all running, don't delete
  • --filter ancestor=nginx → only containers made from that image
  • docker container prune → remove stopped containers only
  • docker stop + docker rm → clean | docker rm -f → SIGKILL + remove in one step, fine for tests, not for databases
  • docker rm removes containers | docker rmi removes images → image stays after rm, next run starts instantly

docs.title: Bash: multi-line commands
docs.text:
• Unfinished line + Enter → bash doesn't run it, shows > (continuation prompt PS2) and waits
  • for i in {1..10}; do → Enter → docker run -d nginx:latest → Enter → done → Enter → runs 10 containers
  • One line → for i in {1..10}; do docker run -d nginx:latest; done → ; replaces line breaks
  • Bash keeps waiting after → for/while ... do (needs done) | if ... then (needs fi) | line ending in \ | unclosed quote | line ending in a pipe or &&
  • Long docker commands → split with \ at the end of each line
  • Stuck at > → Ctrl+C

docs.title: Debugging toolkit
docs.text:
• docker ps -a → all containers | docker logs -f x → output live | docker inspect x → everything as JSON
  • docker exec -it x sh → get inside | docker stats → live CPU/RAM | docker system df → disk used

docs.title: Lab: first containers
docs.text:
docker run --name app1 nginx:latest
docker run --rm -d --name app1 nginx
for i in {1..10}; do docker run -d nginx:latest; done
docker ps -a
docker rm $(docker ps -aq)
Symptom Cause Fix Terminal stuck on nginx log lines Ran in foreground (no -d), nginx runs forever Ctrl+C, then use -d cannot remove container "app1": container is running docker rm refuses running containers docker stop app1 then docker rm app1, or docker rm -f app1 unknown flag: --rm Left out run, flags belong to the subcommand docker run --rm -d --name app1 nginx 10 containers Exited (0) still listed Stopped containers aren't deleted docker rm $(docker ps -aq) ps -a empty after docker stop Started with --rm Expected docker exect: unknown shorthand flag: 'i' Typo, exect isn't a command docker exec 'docker exec' requires at least 2 arguments Gave the command but no container docker exec -it app1 bash → container + command

Interview points

  • Why does a container exit immediately? → its main process ended; e.g. bash with no terminal exits at once
  • docker stop vs docker kill? → stop sends SIGTERM, waits 10s, then SIGKILL; kill sends SIGKILL immediately
  • Is a stopped container deleted? → no, it stays with its writable layer until docker rm
  • What does --rm do? → deletes the container automatically when it stops; it does not remove a running container
  • docker run vs docker start? → run creates a new container; start restarts an existing stopped one
  • docker run vs docker exec? → run makes a new container; exec runs a command inside an existing running one
  • docker ps -aq? → IDs of all containers, running and stopped, used with $( ) to feed other commands
  • docker rm vs docker rmi? → rm removes containers, rmi removes images
  • Exit code 143? → the process got SIGTERM

docs.title: The Docker Socket
docs.text: Hands-on notes, Docker internals and Portainer

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
• Docker has two parts → the docker CLI is only a client, dockerd (the daemon) does the real work
  • They talk over a REST API → the daemon listens on /var/run/docker.sock by default
  • Unix socket → same-machine communication exposed as a file, permissions decide who can use it, no network involved
  • ls -l /var/run/docker.sock → srw-rw---- root docker, so only root and the docker group
  • docker ps → the CLI sends GET /containers/json through the socket and prints the reply
  • Adding yourself to the docker group → avoids sudo, but see the warning below
curl --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock http://localhost/containers/json
curl --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock "http://localhost/containers/json?all=true"
  • [] → the call worked, nothing is running
  • all=true → include stopped containers

docs.title: Mounting the socket into a container
docs.text:
• A container is isolated → it has its own filesystem and cannot see /var/run/docker.sock on the host
  • Mounting the socket is a bind mount of one file, a volume cannot do this
  • Inside the container the CLI now reaches the host's daemon
docker run -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock ...
docker run --mount type=bind,source=/var/run/docker.sock,target=/var/run/docker.sock ...
  • docker images inside the container → lists the host's images, proof it is the host daemon
  • Used by → CI runners (Jenkins, GitLab runner), Portainer, Traefik, Watchtower
  • Called Docker-out-of-Docker → containers started this way are siblings on the host, not children
  • Docker-in-Docker → a separate daemon inside a privileged container, different thing
  • --network none → does not help, the socket is a file mount, not a network path

docs.title: Why it is root on the host
docs.text:
• The daemon runs as root and does whatever the API asks
  • Anyone who can reach the socket can start a container with the host's / mounted
# read-only demo, prints the host's hostname from inside a container
docker run --rm -v /:/host alpine cat /host/etc/hostname
  • Replace cat with a write or chroot /host sh → root shell on the host
  • docker group membership → same as root without sudo

Docker socket = root on the host

Only mount it into containers you would trust with root. A bug in a web app that has the socket mounted is a host takeover.

docs.title: Reducing the risk
docs.text:
• Don't mount it into untrusted or internet-facing containers
  • :ro on the socket → only stops writes to the socket file, the API still accepts every command, so it is weak
  • Socket proxy → tecnativa/docker-socket-proxy allows only chosen API calls, for example list containers
  • Rootless Docker or Podman → the daemon is not root, so a breakout is not root
  • Never expose the daemon on TCP 2375 (no TLS) → 2376 with TLS only, otherwise anyone on the network has root

docs.title: Lab: socket in a container
docs.text:
• Any image that ships the docker CLI works, for example docker:cli
  • Same image, one flag difference
# 1. no socket
docker run --rm -d --name app1 --network none docker:cli sleep 600
docker exec -it app1 docker ps
#    Cannot connect to the Docker daemon at unix:///var/run/docker.sock
docker stop app1

# 2. socket mounted
docker run --rm -d --name app1 -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock --network none docker:cli sleep 600
docker exec -it app1 docker ps        # works, lists the host's containers
docker exec -it app1 docker images    # the host's images
docker inspect app1 | grep IPAddress  # empty, no network, still full control
docker stop app1
  1. Without the mount → the CLI exists but there is no socket file to reach the daemon
  2. With the mount → same file as the host, so the request reaches the host's dockerd
  3. IPAddress is empty with --network none → the container still controls the host's Docker

docs.title: Lab: Portainer
docs.text:
• Portainer → web UI for Docker, runs as a container itself
  • Socket bind mount → how it sees and controls Docker
  • portainer_data volume → keeps the admin user and settings across container recreation
  • Port 9443 is HTTPS only → https://localhost:9443, accept the self-signed certificate warning
  • Setup token → printed in docker logs portainer, changes on every restart
  • Setup window → about 5 minutes to create the admin user, then the page locks
docker run -d -p 8000:8000 -p 9443:9443 --name portainer \
  --restart=always \
  -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
  -v portainer_data:/data \
  portainer/portainer-ce:lts

docs.title: Errors I hit
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Client sent an HTTP request to an HTTPS server. Opened http://localhost:9443 Use https://localhost:9443 Dashboard shows 0 containers, 0 images while the environment says Up Pinned Portainer 2.11.1 is too old for a Docker 29 daemon, logs show client version 1.37 is too old. Minimum supported API version is 1.40 Run portainer/portainer-ce:lts Your Portainer instance timed out for security purposes Admin user not created within about 5 minutes docker restart portainer, then create the user quickly Request failed with status code 403 on Create user Wrong or stale setup token Read the new token from docker logs portainer, hard-reload the page, paste it exactly

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
• Removing the container keeps the volume → admin and settings survive
  • --restart=always → it comes back after a reboot until the container is removed
docker rm -f portainer
docker volume rm portainer_data
docker rmi portainer/portainer-ce:lts

Quick revision

  • Socket → the phone line to dockerd, a file at /var/run/docker.sock
  • Mounting it → bind mount, gives the container the host's Docker
  • Socket access → root on the host

Interview points

  • What is the Docker socket? → /var/run/docker.sock, the Unix socket the daemon listens on. The CLI and tools like Portainer use the REST API through it
  • Why is mounting it dangerous? → the daemon runs as root, so a process with the socket can start a container with the host's / mounted. It is root on the host
  • Does --network none protect a container that has the socket? → no, the socket is a file mount, not a network path
  • Why do CI runners mount it? → to start sibling containers on the host's daemon (Docker-out-of-Docker). Docker-in-Docker runs its own daemon in a privileged container instead
  • How do you make socket access safer? → rootless Docker or Podman, a socket proxy that allows only certain API calls, no mount into untrusted containers
  • Why is docker group membership a security concern? → it can reach the socket, which is equivalent to root
  • Why is exposing the daemon on TCP 2375 bad? → no TLS or auth, anyone on the network gets root. If you need remote access use 2376 with TLS
  • Why did Portainer show 0 containers on a newer Docker? → the daemon raised its minimum API version and an old Portainer client was rejected, so upgrade Portainer
  • Which two mounts does a Portainer container need and why? → the socket (bind mount, to control Docker) and a volume on /data (to keep its settings)

docs.title: Dockerfile
docs.text: Hands-on notes, building images

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
• Dockerfile → a text file of instructions that tells Docker how to build an image
  • Image → the finished read-only package | container → a running instance of an image
  • docker build -t name:tag . → build from the Dockerfile in the current folder, the . is the build context
  • docker build only creates an image → nothing runs, docker ps -a stays empty until docker run

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
• FROM → base image to start from, always first → FROM ubuntu:24.04
  • LABEL → metadata only → LABEL name="aditya"
  • ENV → environment variable, present at build time and in every container, baked into the image
  • ARG → build-time variable only, set with --build-arg, gone when the container runs
  • RUN → run a command at build time, the result is saved as a layer → RUN apt update && apt install -y nginx
  • COPY → copy files from the build context into the image
  • ADD → like COPY but also extracts tarballs and fetches URLs, prefer COPY
  • WORKDIR → set the working directory, created if missing
  • EXPOSE → documents the port the app uses, does not publish it, -p does
  • USER → run the rest as a non-root user, see EXPOSE, COPY, WORKDIR & USER
  • CMD → default command when a container starts, only the last one counts, docker run image other-cmd overrides it
  • ENTRYPOINT → fixed command, CMD then becomes its default arguments, see ENTRYPOINT & CMD
  • .dockerignore → paths left out of the build context → .git, .venv, .env

docs.title: RUN vs CMD
docs.text:
• RUN → executes while the image is being built
  • CMD → only recorded during the build, executes when a container starts from the image
  • After docker build finishes nothing is running, the image is just a file on disk
  • Never start a long-running process in RUN → the build would hang
  • Each docker run starts CMD again, RUN happened once
FROM alpine
RUN echo "building"
CMD ["echo", "running"]

docker build -t t1 .          # prints "building" once
docker run --rm t1            # prints "running"
docker run --rm t1 echo hi    # overrides CMD, prints "hi"

docs.title: CMD forms and the foreground rule
docs.text:
• Exec form → CMD ["nginx","-g","daemon off;"] runs nginx directly as the main process, signals from docker stop reach it
  • Shell form → CMD nginx -g "daemon off;" wraps it in /bin/sh -c
  • A container lives only as long as its main process
  • nginx forks into the background by default → the first process exits and the container stops
  • -g "daemon off;" → global directive that keeps nginx in the foreground
  • The official nginx image already sets this → needed when you install nginx on ubuntu yourself
docker run --rm -d --name n1 nginx nginx -g "daemon off;"   # stays up
docker run --rm -d --name n2 nginx nginx                    # exits right away

docs.title: ARG vs ENV
docs.text:
• ARG → build time only | ENV → build time and run time
  • --build-arg belongs to docker build
  • -e belongs to docker run
  • Changing an ARG value changes the RUN layers that use it, so they rebuild
  • Versions that are downloaded during the build must be changed at build time, an env var at run time is too late
docker build -t aditya/custom:v2 --build-arg T_VERSION=1.5.0 --build-arg P_VERSION=1.4.0 .

docs.title: Lab: devops tools image
docs.text:
• Ubuntu base, installs jq, net-tools, curl, wget, unzip, nginx, iputils-ping
  • Downloads Terraform and Packer from HashiCorp with versions from ARG
  • Runs nginx in the foreground
FROM ubuntu:latest

LABEL name="aditya"

ENV AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX \
    AWS_SECRET_KEY_ID=XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX \
    AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=US-EAST-1A

ARG T_VERSION='1.6.6' \
    P_VERSION='1.8.0'

RUN apt update && apt install -y jq net-tools curl wget unzip \
    && apt install -y nginx iputils-ping

RUN wget https://releases.hashicorp.com/terraform/${T_VERSION}/terraform_${T_VERSION}_linux_amd64.zip \
    && wget https://releases.hashicorp.com/packer/${P_VERSION}/packer_${P_VERSION}_linux_amd64.zip \
    && unzip terraform_${T_VERSION}_linux_amd64.zip && unzip packer_${P_VERSION}_linux_amd64.zip \
    && chmod 777 terraform && chmod 777 packer \
    && ./terraform version && ./packer version

CMD ["nginx","-g","daemon off;"]

docker build .                                     # image with no name, ~143s the first time
docker ps -a                                       # empty, build creates no container
docker build -t aditya/custom:v1 .                 # 1.3s, every step CACHED, same image ID
docker run --rm -d --name app1 -p 8000:80 aditya/custom:v1
docker exec -it app1 bash                          # shell inside the running container
docker exec app1 packer version
docker stop app1
  • The two RUN steps showed up as [2/3] and [3/3] → only they and FROM are build steps with real work, ENV, ARG, LABEL, CMD add no data
  • ls / inside the container showed terraform, packer and both .zip files → no WORKDIR, so everything landed in /
  • Two containers from one image → -p 8000:80 and -p 8001:80, same port 80 inside, different host ports

docs.title: Errors I hit
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix unknown flag: --build-arg on docker run --build-arg is a build flag Rebuild with docker build --build-arg ... -t new-tag . docker ps and docker ps -a empty after docker build A build makes an image, not a container docker run it 233MB layer and .zip files still in / Downloads were never removed rm -f *.zip in the same RUN, or unzip -d /usr/local/bin SecretsUsedInArgOrEnv warning during build Keys set with ENV Remove them, pass at run time, see image layers and tags

docs.title: Things to fix in this Dockerfile
docs.text:
• Secrets in ENV → remove, use docker run -e or an IAM role
  • Variable name → AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, not AWS_SECRET_KEY_ID
  • Region → us-east-1, US-EAST-1A is an availability zone
  • chmod 777 → chmod +x is enough
  • ubuntu:latest → pin a version such as ubuntu:24.04
  • Install to /usr/local/bin and delete the zips in the same RUN
  • Clean the apt cache in the same RUN → rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

Quick revision

  • RUN → build time, CMD → container start
  • ARG → build only, ENV → build and run
  • --build-arg → docker build, -e → docker run
  • Main process in the foreground or the container exits

Interview points

  • Dockerfile vs image vs container? → the Dockerfile is the instructions, the image is what they build, a container is a running instance of the image
  • RUN vs CMD? → RUN executes at build time and saves a layer, CMD is stored in the image and executes each time a container starts
  • CMD vs ENTRYPOINT? → ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable, CMD supplies default arguments and is easy to override with docker run
  • ARG vs ENV? → ARG exists only during the build, ENV is also set in running containers
  • Why does docker run --build-arg fail? → --build-arg is a docker build option, ARG values are fixed once the image is built
  • Why does nginx need daemon off;? → a container stops when its main process exits, and nginx backgrounds itself by default
  • Exec form vs shell form of CMD? → exec form runs the program directly as the main process, shell form wraps it in /bin/sh -c
  • Does EXPOSE publish a port? → no, it only documents it, -p publishes it
  • COPY vs ADD? → ADD also extracts archives and downloads URLs, COPY is simpler and preferred
  • What does .dockerignore do? → keeps files like .git and .env out of the build context so they are not sent to the daemon or copied in

docs.title: ENTRYPOINT & CMD
docs.text: Hands-on notes, building images

docs.title: The two
docs.text:
• ENTRYPOINT → the fixed executable, always runs
  • CMD → the default command, or the default arguments when an ENTRYPOINT exists
  • docker run image something → something replaces CMD, with an ENTRYPOINT it is appended to it
  • docker run --entrypoint other image → the only way to replace the ENTRYPOINT
  • Only the last CMD and the last ENTRYPOINT in a Dockerfile count
  • ENTRYPOINT is the program, CMD is its default arguments
Dockerfile docker run img docker run img x CMD ["echo","hello"] echo hello x runs instead, so x must be a full command ENTRYPOINT ["echo"] echo echo x ENTRYPOINT ["python","app.py"] + CMD ["--port","8000"] python app.py --port 8000 python app.py x
  • Use exec form (["a","b"]) for both → shell form wraps the program in /bin/sh -c, it is not PID 1 and misses SIGTERM from docker stop
  • Shell-form ENTRYPOINT ignores CMD and the arguments from docker run
  • Kubernetes names → command replaces ENTRYPOINT, args replaces CMD
  • ENTRYPOINT for an image that is a tool (kubectl, a wrapper script that ends in exec "$@"), CMD for a default people swap out (bash), both for an app with default flags

docs.title: Lab: ping image
docs.text:
• ENTRYPOINT is ping, CMD is the default host
  • Only the host is passed at docker run, never the command
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/bin/ping","-c 4"]
CMD ["www.google.com"]

docker run app3                        # 4 pings to www.google.com, exits 0
docker run app3 www.youtube.com        # CMD replaced, pings youtube instead
docker run app3 ping www.youtube.com   # fails, exits 2
docker ps -a                           # COMMAND column: /usr/bin/ping '-c 4…
  • The failing run became /usr/bin/ping -c 4 ping www.youtube.com → ping was treated as a hostname → No address associated with hostname
  • Same extra ping on an image with only CMD ["ping", ...] worked and kept pinging until Ctrl+C → the whole CMD was replaced by ping www.youtube.com
  • "-c 4" as one string worked, but ["/usr/bin/ping","-c","4"] is the correct form → one argument per element
  • Exit codes → 0 success, 2 ping could not resolve or reach the host

docs.title: A container lives as long as its main process
docs.text:
• With the ping ENTRYPOINT, docker run --rm -d --name expose -p 80:80 app4 → ping ran 4 times and finished
  • docker ps and docker ps -a were both empty → the container exited and --rm removed it
  • Nothing listened on port 80 → nginx was installed but never started
  • Fix → drop the ping ENTRYPOINT and end the Dockerfile with CMD ["nginx","-g","daemon off;"]
  • docker inspect expose after the fix → Path is nginx, Args is -g, daemon off;, Config.Entrypoint is null
  • docker inspect also showed the ENV values in Config.Env → anything set with ENV is readable by anyone who can inspect or pull the image
docker run --rm -d --name expose -p 80:80 app5
docker inspect expose        # Path, Args, Entrypoint, Env, PortBindings
docker stop expose           # --rm removes it

docs.title: Errors I hit
docs.text:
Symptom Cause Fix unknown flag: --rm Typed docker --rm ..., --rm belongs to docker run docker run --rm ... docker run requires at least 1 argument Image name missing after -p 8005:80 Add the image at the end No address associated with hostname Extra word appended to the ENTRYPOINT became a hostname Pass only the host, not ping host docker ps -a empty after run --rm -d Main process finished, --rm removed the container Keep a foreground process, or drop --rm and read docker logs Weird ping output on CMD Markdown link pasted into CMD as [www.google.com](https://...) Plain "www.google.com"

Quick revision

  • ENTRYPOINT → what runs, CMD → its default arguments
  • docker run image args → replaces CMD, appended to ENTRYPOINT
  • --entrypoint → the only way to replace ENTRYPOINT
  • Main process ends → container ends

Interview points

  • CMD vs ENTRYPOINT? → ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable, CMD is the default command or arguments and is replaced by anything after the image name in docker run
  • Both in one Dockerfile? → CMD is passed as arguments to ENTRYPOINT, so the image behaves like a command with default flags
  • How do you override ENTRYPOINT? → docker run --entrypoint cmd image, in Kubernetes the command field
  • Why use exec form? → the program is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM from docker stop, shell form puts /bin/sh -c in front and the signal may never reach the app
  • A container starts and exits immediately, why? → its main process finished or ran in the background, keep it in the foreground, for nginx daemon off;
  • docker run app ping host fails on an image with ENTRYPOINT ["ping"], why? → the extra ping is appended as an argument and read as a hostname
  • Where are ENTRYPOINT and CMD visible? → docker inspect shows Path, Args, Config.Entrypoint and Config.Cmd

docs.title: EXPOSE, COPY, WORKDIR & USER
docs.text: Hands-on notes, building images

docs.title: EXPOSE
docs.text:
• EXPOSE 80 → documents the port the app listens on, nothing else
  • It does not publish the port → -p HOST:CONTAINER does that
  • docker run -P (capital) → publishes every EXPOSEd port to a random host port, the only place EXPOSE changes behaviour
  • -p 8080:80 works without EXPOSE, and EXPOSE without -p is not reachable from the host
  • -p always wins → EXPOSE 80 with -p 8000:8000 forwards host 8000 to container 8000, nothing checks it against EXPOSE
  • The container side of -p must be the port the app really binds → app on 80 needs -p 8000:80
  • The app must listen on 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1, or -p has nothing to reach
  • Containers on the same network reach any listening port, EXPOSE or not
  • docker inspect keeps the two apart → Config.ExposedPorts is the note, HostConfig.PortBindings is what -p created
docker run --rm -d --name expose -p 80:80 app5       # host 80 → container 80
docker run --rm -d --name appx   -p 8000:80 copy     # same image port 80, different host port
docker ps                                            # 0.0.0.0:8000->80/tcp, [::]:8000->80/tcp

docs.title: COPY vs ADD
docs.text:
• COPY src dest → copies from the build context into the image
  • ADD → same, plus it extracts local tarballs (.tar, .tar.gz, .tar.xz) and accepts URLs
  • A URL given to ADD is downloaded, not extracted → the .zip just sits in the image
  • Prefer COPY → ADD has hidden behaviour
  • For downloads use RUN wget ... && unzip ... && rm ... → download, extract and delete in one layer
  • The source must be inside the build context → COPY ../file . fails
  • COPY dir /dest copies the contents of dir, not the folder itself
  • A destination ending in / is a directory
  • COPY --chown=user:group → files are owned by root otherwise
  • Put what changes rarely first so the cache survives → COPY package.json and install, then COPY . .
COPY index.nginx-debian.html /var/www/html/
COPY scorekeeper.js /var/www/html/
COPY style.css /var/www/html/
  • ADD https://releases.hashicorp.com/terraform/1.9.0/terraform_1.9.0_linux_amd64.zip /var/www/html took 14.7s on the first build and was CACHED after → it only put a zip in the web root
  • Image sizes → copy image (with the ADD) 486MB, app5 459MB, cleaned dev image 357MB

docs.title: WORKDIR
docs.text:
• WORKDIR /app → working directory for every later RUN, COPY, ADD, CMD, ENTRYPOINT, and for docker exec
  • Created if missing, no RUN mkdir needed
  • Relative paths stack → WORKDIR /a then WORKDIR b is /a/b
  • RUN cd /app only lasts for that one line, WORKDIR stays
  • docker run -w /other overrides it
  • Default is /, which is why Terraform and Packer landed in / before WORKDIR was added
  • After WORKDIR /app the downloads ended up there → docker exec -it last bash opened in /app and ls showed packer terraform

docs.title: USER
docs.text:
• USER appuser → every later instruction and the running container use that user, default is root
  • Root-only steps (apt install) must come before USER
  • The user must exist first → RUN groupadd appuser && useradd -r -g appuser appuser
  • useradd -r makes a system user with a nologin shell → su -s /bin/bash appuser to switch into it
  • Can be a number → USER 1000, Kubernetes runAsNonRoot needs a numeric UID
  • docker run -u root or docker exec -u appuser override it
  • Why → a compromised process as root is root inside the container, with mounted volumes and escapes it does far more damage
  • Non-root cannot bind ports below 1024, cannot write /var/log/nginx, /run/nginx.pid or nginx's temp dirs → nginx on port 80 needs root, or listen on 8080 with a config that points those paths at writable folders

docs.title: Custom Dockerfile name
docs.text:
• Default lookup is Dockerfile, lowercase dockerfile is also accepted on Linux
  • docker build -f dockerfile.dev -t dev . → any file name, the extension does not matter
  • . is the build context, separate from the Dockerfile location
  • Editors only highlight Dockerfile, Dockerfile.dev and dev.Dockerfile
  • Compose → build: { context: ., dockerfile: dockerfile.dev }

docs.title: Lab: running as a non-root user
docs.text:
• First attempt had USER appuser above the apt step, so the build failed
docker build -t dev -f dockerfile.dev .

Error: List directory /var/lib/apt/lists/partial is missing. - Acquire (13: Permission denied)
ERROR: failed to build: ... exit code: 100
  • Fix → install as root first, create the user and set WORKDIR after, drop USER for nginx on port 80
  • Build then took 72s, nothing cached, image 357MB
  • Testing the user from inside the running container:
docker run --rm -d --name last -p 8005:80 dev:latest
docker exec -it last bash          # opens as root in /app
su -s /bin/bash appuser
touch /app/test                    # Permission denied
exit
docker stop last
  • Other ways to see it without editing the Dockerfile → docker run --rm -u appuser dev whoami, docker exec -u appuser last bash
  • Running nginx itself as appuser shows the next errors → /var/log/nginx/error.log and /run/nginx.pid permission denied, then port 80 bind() denied

docs.title: Errors I hit
docs.text:
Symptom Cause Fix apt Permission denied, exit code 100 USER appuser placed before RUN apt install Root steps first, USER last su appuser gives no shell useradd -r sets a nologin shell su -s /bin/bash appuser touch: cannot touch '/app/test' as appuser /app was created by root COPY --chown, or chown it before USER docker exec requires at least 2 arguments No command after the container name docker exec -it last bash Own index.html replaced by the default page COPY ran before apt install nginx, the package ships its own file at that path Install first, COPY the site after SecretsUsedInArgOrEnv warning AWS keys in ENV Remove, pass with docker run -e, see image layers and tags

Quick revision

  • EXPOSE → note, -p → real, -P → all EXPOSEd to random ports
  • COPY by default, ADD only for local tarballs
  • WORKDIR → persists, RUN cd does not
  • USER goes after the root steps, nginx on 80 needs root

Interview points

  • Does EXPOSE publish a port? → no, it documents it, -p publishes, -P publishes all EXPOSEd ports to random host ports
  • EXPOSE 80 and -p 8000:8000, what happens? → -p wins, host 8000 goes to container 8000, if the app listens on 80 the connection fails with no warning
  • COPY vs ADD? → ADD also extracts local tarballs and downloads URLs, a downloaded archive is not extracted, use COPY and RUN curl instead
  • Why WORKDIR instead of RUN cd? → cd lasts one RUN, WORKDIR applies to every later instruction and to the running container
  • Why run as non-root? → a breakout or a bug then gives an unprivileged user, not root
  • Build fails with Permission denied in apt, why? → USER was set before the install, root-only steps must run first
  • Can a non-root user run nginx on port 80? → not by default, ports below 1024 need root or a capability, use 8080
  • How do you build with a differently named Dockerfile? → docker build -f name -t tag ., the . stays the context
  • Why are secrets in ENV bad? → they are baked into the image layers and show up in docker inspect and docker history

docs.title: Image Layers, Tags & Cleanup
docs.text: Hands-on notes, Docker images

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
• An image is a stack of read-only layers → one per instruction that changes files
  • RUN, COPY, ADD → add data | ENV, ARG, LABEL, CMD, EXPOSE → 0B, metadata only
  • A container is the image layers plus one thin writable layer on top → why data is lost on docker rm, see volumes
  • Layers are shared between images and containers → a second container from the same image copies nothing
  • Deleting a file in a later layer does not shrink the image → remove it in the same RUN that created it, or leave the build tools behind with a multi-stage build
  • docker history aditya/custom:v1 → layers newest first with size and the instruction that made them
  • <missing> in the IMAGE column → normal, those layers have no local image ID of their own
  • docker history --no-trunc → full instructions, including ENV values
CMD ["nginx" "-g" "daemon off;"]            0B
RUN |2 T_VERSION=1.5.0 P_VERSION=1.4.0 ...  233MB   ← terraform and packer downloads
RUN |2 T_VERSION=1.5.0 P_VERSION=1.4.0 ...  67.3MB  ← apt install
ARG T_VERSION=1.5.0 P_VERSION=1.4.0         0B
ENV AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=...                   0B
LABEL name=Aditya                           0B
(Ubuntu base)                               102MB

docs.title: Build cache
docs.text:
• Docker reuses a layer when its instruction and everything above it are unchanged
  • A change breaks the cache from that line downward
  • Put what changes rarely first (apt install, dependencies) and what changes often last (your code)
  • --no-cache → ignore the cache and rebuild everything
  • Used ARG values are part of the cache key → a new version rebuilds the RUN that uses it
Build Time Why First docker build . 143.5s Nothing cached, base image pulled docker build -t aditya/custom:v1 . 1.3s Every step CACHED, same image ID After changing LABEL and --build-arg 158.9s Change sits above the RUNs, they rebuilt

docs.title: Image ID vs tag
docs.text:
• ID (ec7d7ab8c135) → the identity of the image, a content hash
  • Tag (aditya/custom:v1) → a movable name that points at an ID
  • docker build -t on a fully cached build → adds a name to the same ID, no second image is created
  • Rebuilding with a change under the same tag → new ID, the tag moves, the old image loses its name
  • One image can have several names → docker tag aditya/custom:v1 aditya/custom:latest
  • docker rmi <tag> → removes that name only, the image stays while other names or containers use it
  • latest is just a default tag name, not "newest" → pin versions
docker images
docker tag aditya/custom:v1 aditya/custom:v2
docker rmi aditya/custom:v2
docker images --no-trunc

docs.title: Dangling images and cleanup
docs.text:
• Dangling image → untagged, shown as <none> or <untagged>, usually the old version after a rebuild
  • docker images -f dangling=true → list them
  • docker image prune → delete dangling images only
  • docker system prune → stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images and unused build cache, asks y/N
  • Add -a to also remove every image no container uses, check first
  • docker system df → what is using disk
  • docker rmi nginx:latest → remove a specific image, fails while a container still uses it

Check before pruning

My dangling list held two images, the old aditya/custom build and an untagged kindest/node (974MB). docker image prune deleted both, 974.2MB reclaimed. The second was not mine to lose from this build, it just had lost its tag to a newer one. Read the list first.

docs.title: Secrets in images
docs.text:
• ENV and ARG values are stored in the image metadata, not just the running container
  • docker history --no-trunc image and docker inspect image show them
  • docker exec app1 env listed the baked-in keys in every container started from the image
  • docker run -e AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=hidden → overrides the value in that container, but the original is still inside the image, and other baked values like AWS_DEFAULT_REGION remain
  • BuildKit warns with SecretsUsedInArgOrEnv → this is exactly why
  • Pass secrets at run time → -e NAME (copies from your shell), --env-file, or an IAM role on AWS
  • Secrets needed during a build → BuildKit RUN --mount=type=secret
  • A key that was baked into an image that left your machine → rotate it
  • Never commit real keys in Dockerfiles or notes in a public repo

Quick revision

  • Image ID = identity, tag = a name for it
  • Cache breaks from the first changed line down
  • docker image prune = dangling only, read the list first
  • Secrets: runtime, never ENV

Interview points

  • What is an image layer? → a read-only filesystem diff made by an instruction like RUN or COPY, stacked to form the image and shared between images
  • Which instructions make the image bigger? → RUN, COPY, ADD. ENV, ARG, LABEL, CMD are 0B metadata
  • How does the build cache work? → a layer is reused if its instruction and all earlier layers are unchanged. The first change invalidates everything below it
  • How do you order a Dockerfile for fast rebuilds? → rarely changing steps first (base, packages, dependencies), frequently changing steps (your code) last
  • Does deleting a file in a later layer reduce image size? → no, the earlier layer still holds it. Delete in the same RUN
  • Image ID vs tag? → the ID identifies the image content, a tag is a movable name. Rebuilding under the same tag moves the tag to a new ID
  • What is a dangling image and how do you remove it? → an untagged image left behind when a tag moves. docker image prune
  • What does docker system prune remove? → stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images and unused build cache
  • Why are secrets in ENV bad, and what do you do instead? → they are stored in the image and visible via docker history and docker inspect. Pass them at run time or use an IAM role, and rotate any key that was baked in
  • What does <missing> mean in docker history? → those layers have no local image ID, which is normal for layers from a base image or BuildKit

docs.title: Images & Storage
docs.text: Hands-on notes, image layers and where container data lives

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
• Image → stack of read-only layers
  • Each filesystem-changing Dockerfile instruction (RUN, COPY, ADD) → one new layer holding only what changed
  • Layers are shared → 10 images on ubuntu:24.04 store that layer once
  • Layer ID → hash of its contents (sha256) → same content = same hash
Layer 4: COPY app.py              (my 5 KB file)
Layer 3: RUN pip install flask    (flask files)
Layer 2: RUN apt install python3  (python files)
Layer 1: FROM ubuntu:24.04        (base OS files)

docs.title: Writable layer and copy-on-write
docs.text:
• Running a container → Docker adds one thin writable layer on top
  • OverlayFS merges all layers into the one / the container sees → top-most file wins
  • Reading → found in whichever layer has it
  • Changing a file from a lower layer → copied up into the writable layer first, then modified → copy-on-write → image untouched
  • Deleting → "whiteout" marker hides it → still exists in the lower layer, image doesn't shrink
  • Delete the container → writable layer gone with all its data → databases need volumes

docs.title: Names, tags and digests
docs.text:
• Full name → registry/namespace/repository:tag
  • nginx → short for docker.io/library/nginx:latest
  • latest → just a default tag name, NOT "newest" → don't rely on it for real work
  • Tag → mutable, can be moved to another image
  • Digest → nginx@sha256:... → immutable, always the exact same image

docs.title: Dockerfile instructions
docs.text:
Instruction What it does Layer? FROM Base image Starts the stack RUN Command at build time (install packages) Yes COPY Files from my machine into the image Yes ADD COPY + URL/tar extraction (prefer COPY) Yes WORKDIR Current directory Metadata ENV Environment variables Metadata EXPOSE Documents a port, does NOT open it Metadata USER User the app runs as Metadata CMD Default command when the container starts Metadata ENTRYPOINT Fixed main executable, CMD becomes its arguments Metadata
  • RUN → once, while building | CMD → every time a container starts
  • Only CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"] → docker run img bash replaces it
  • ENTRYPOINT ["ping"] + CMD ["google.com"] → docker run img 8.8.8.8 runs ping 8.8.8.8 → only CMD replaced
  • nginx image → ENTRYPOINT /docker-entrypoint.sh runs setup scripts, then starts nginx

docs.title: Build cache, context, multi-stage
docs.text:
• Each layer is cached → unchanged instruction + inputs → reused instantly
  • One layer changes → every layer after it rebuilds → rarely-changing things (dependencies) first, code last
  • docker build . → . = build context, folder sent to the builder → COPY only sees files inside it
  • .dockerignore → exclude node_modules, .git → faster builds, no leaked secrets
  • Multi-stage → build in one stage with compilers, copy only the final binary into a small second stage

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Type Where data lives Use for Example Volume /var/lib/docker/volumes/<name>/, managed by Docker Databases, anything persistent -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data Bind mount Any host folder I choose Dev: edit on host, container sees it live -v $(pwd):/app tmpfs RAM only, gone on stop Secrets, scratch --tmpfs /tmp
  • -v left side starts with / or ./ → bind mount | just a name → volume
  • Mounting over a folder hides what the image had there
  • Volume survives docker rm | writable layer doesn't

docs.title: Lab: first pull
docs.text:
docker run --name app1 nginx:latest
docker images
docker system df
  • Unable to find image 'nginx:latest' locally → dockerd checked local storage
  • Pulling from library/nginx → went to Docker Hub
  • 7 × Pull complete → 7 image layers downloaded
  • Digest: sha256:... → the exact image latest pointed to at that moment
  • Only the first pull is slow (~64 MB here) → layers cached → next run starts in about a second
Symptom Cause Fix Same layers downloading again minutes later Image deleted, or that terminal talks to a different daemon/context Compare docker context ls, docker info, docker images in both terminals Pull feels slow Cloudflare WARP tunnel (MTU 1300, extra hop) time docker pull with and without warp-cli disconnect pull access denied ... repository does not exist or may require 'docker login' Typo in the repo/username (Docker Hub gives the same message for missing and private repos) Check the exact name on Docker Hub manifest for ...:latest not found: manifest unknown Repo exists but has no latest tag; no tag means Docker assumes :latest Use a tag that exists, e.g. :v1

Interview points

  • What is an image layer? → a read-only slice of the filesystem created by RUN, COPY or ADD, identified by a content hash
  • What is copy-on-write? → changing a file from a lower layer copies it up into the container's writable layer first; the image is never modified
  • Why doesn't deleting a file in a later layer shrink the image? → it only adds a whiteout marker; the file still exists in the earlier layer
  • Does latest mean newest? → no, it is just a default tag name that can point anywhere
  • docker pull says manifest unknown for :latest? → the repo has no latest tag; pass an existing tag explicitly
  • Tag vs digest? → tag is mutable, digest (sha256) always points to the exact same image
  • RUN vs CMD? → RUN executes at build time; CMD is the default command each time a container starts
  • CMD vs ENTRYPOINT? → ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable; CMD supplies default arguments that docker run can replace
  • Does EXPOSE publish a port? → no, it only documents it; only -p publishes
  • Why order Dockerfile instructions carefully? → a changed layer invalidates the cache for every layer after it
  • Volume vs bind mount? → volume is managed by Docker under /var/lib/docker/volumes; bind mount maps a host path I choose
  • Where does container data go when the container is removed? → the writable layer is deleted; only volumes and bind mounts survive

docs.title: Install & Upgrade
docs.text: Hands-on notes, upgrading Docker on Ubuntu 24.04

docs.title: Find how Docker was installed
docs.text:
docker --version
dpkg -l | grep -E 'docker|containerd' | awk '{print $2, $3}'
snap list 2>/dev/null | grep docker
  • docker-ce → Docker's official apt repo → upgrade with apt
  • docker.io → Ubuntu's own package, usually behind → remove it, switch to the official repo
  • Shows in snap list → snap install → sudo snap refresh docker, has sandbox quirks with paths/permissions
  • Mine → docker-ce 5:29.9.2 + containerd.io, docker-buildx-plugin, docker-compose-plugin, docker-ce-rootless-extras, Ubuntu 24.04 (noble)

docs.title: Upgrade (official repo)
docs.text:
sudo apt update
apt list --upgradable 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'docker|containerd'
sudo apt install --only-upgrade docker-ce docker-ce-cli docker-ce-rootless-extras containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin
sudo systemctl restart docker
docker version
docker compose version
  • apt list --upgradable empty → already on the latest version in the repo
  • Restart → running containers stop → restart: always / unless-stopped come back on their own
  • Specific version → apt-cache madison docker-ce then sudo apt install docker-ce=<VERSION> docker-ce-cli=<VERSION>

docs.title: Switching from docker.io
docs.text:
• sudo apt remove docker.io docker-doc docker-compose docker-compose-v2 podman-docker containerd runc → removes packages, keeps data in /var/lib/docker (no --purge)
  • Then add Docker's GPG key + apt repo → install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin
  • Removing snap Docker → DOES delete its images and volumes
  • Compose v2 → docker compose (space, plugin) | old docker-compose (hyphen) → deprecated
  • Run docker without sudo → sudo usermod -aG docker $USER, log out and in → docker group = root-equivalent

docs.title: systemd and socket activation
docs.text:
• systemctl status docker → Loaded: ...; disabled + TriggeredBy: docker.socket
  • disabled → dockerd does not start at boot
  • Socket activation → systemd listens on docker.socket, starts dockerd only when something connects to it
  • sudo systemctl enable --now docker → start at boot + start now
  • Drop-in → /etc/systemd/system/docker.service.d/override.conf → local customisation of the service (mine adds --exec-opt native.cgroupdriver=systemd)

docs.title: Lab: docker0 missing
docs.text:
Symptom Cause Fix ifconfig showed no docker0 dockerd wasn't running: service disabled, only socket-activated, nothing had touched the socket yet sudo systemctl enable --now docker docker --version worked anyway Only the CLI runs for that, it never talks to the daemon docker version shows both client and server docker0 shows state DOWN, NO-CARRIER Normal: no containers plugged into the bridge Run a container → it goes UP
  • ifconfig → deprecated, hides down interfaces → use ip a / ip -br a
  • docker0 only exists while dockerd runs → dockerd creates it at startup → see Networking

Interview points

  • How do you check how Docker was installed on Ubuntu? → dpkg -l for docker-ce vs docker.io, and snap list
  • docker.io vs docker-ce? → docker.io is Ubuntu's package and lags behind; docker-ce comes from Docker's official repo
  • Service shows disabled but Docker works? → socket activation: systemd starts dockerd when something connects to docker.socket
  • Why is docker0 missing? → dockerd isn't running (or bridge is disabled in daemon.json); dockerd creates docker0 at startup
  • enable vs start? → start runs it now, enable starts it at boot; enable --now does both
  • Does removing docker.io delete my images? → no, apt remove without --purge keeps /var/lib/docker

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Hands-on notes, Docker basics

docs.title: The problem Docker solves
docs.text:
• "Works on my machine" → app works on laptop, breaks on server → different runtime version, missing library, different OS or config
  • Docker's answer → ship the app together with everything it needs (code + runtime + libraries + config) as one sealed package
  • Image → that sealed package | Container → a running copy of it
  • Analogy → shipping containers: every ship, crane and truck handles the same standard box, doesn't care what's inside

docs.title: Container vs VM
docs.text:
Virtual machine Container Inside Full OS with its own kernel Only the app and its libraries Kernel Separate kernel per VM Shares the host kernel Startup Tens of seconds to minutes Milliseconds to seconds Size GBs MBs Isolation Very strong (hardware level) Good, but weaker (shared kernel) Runs Any OS Linux containers need a Linux kernel
  • Analogy → VM = separate house (own foundation, plumbing) | container = flat in one building (shared foundation = kernel, own walls and door)
  • Docker Desktop on Mac/Windows → secretly runs a small Linux VM and puts containers inside it
  • Native Ubuntu → containers run directly on my kernel, no VM in between

docs.title: Kernel vs user space
docs.text:
• Kernel → core of the OS, talks to hardware, decides who gets CPU/RAM/disk/network → only one kernel runs on the machine
  • User space → every program (bash, nginx, dockerd) → can't touch hardware, asks the kernel through system calls
  • Every container on the machine shares the one host kernel → main difference from a VM
  • Proof → nginx inside a container logs OS: Linux 6.14.0-37-generic = my host kernel

docs.title: What a container actually is
docs.text:
• Container = normal Linux process + namespaces + cgroups + layered filesystem
  • Namespaces → what the process can see (own process list, network, files, hostname) → see Namespaces
  • cgroups → what the process can use (CPU, RAM, disk I/O, process count) → --memory=512m is enforced here
  • Over the memory limit → kernel OOM killer kills it → exit code 137
  • OverlayFS → stacks read-only image layers + one writable layer into one / → see Images & Storage
  • Container lives only as long as its main process (PID 1) → main process exits = container stops

docs.title: Core objects
docs.text:
Object What it is Analogy Image Read-only template: files + config + default command Recipe / class Container Running (or stopped) instance of an image Dish cooked from the recipe / object Layer One slice of an image's filesystem One page of the recipe Dockerfile Text file with instructions to build an image Recipe written down Registry Server that stores images App store / library Repository + tag nginx:1.27 → repo nginx, tag 1.27 Book title + edition Volume Storage that outlives the container External hard drive Network Virtual network containers join Virtual switch
  • One image → many containers (same recipe, many dishes)

Interview points

  • Container vs VM? → VM has its own kernel and full OS; container is a process sharing the host kernel, so it is smaller and starts in milliseconds but isolation is weaker
  • What is a container, technically? → a normal Linux process with namespaces (what it sees), cgroups (what it uses) and a layered filesystem
  • Why does a container stop when its app exits? → the container lives only as long as its main process (PID 1)
  • Exit code 137? → process got SIGKILL, often the OOM killer after hitting the memory limit
  • Can a Linux container run on a Windows kernel natively? → no, containers share the host kernel; Docker Desktop runs a Linux VM for this
  • Image vs container? → image is the read-only template, container is a running instance of it with its own writable layer

docs.title: Logs & Files on Disk
docs.text: Hands-on notes, what Docker keeps on disk for each container

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text: Path What /usr/bin/docker The CLI /usr/bin/dockerd The daemon /var/run/docker.sock The API socket /etc/docker/daemon.json Daemon config (may not exist yet) /var/lib/docker/ All of Docker's data /var/lib/docker/overlay2/ Image and container layers /var/lib/docker/volumes/ Named volumes /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/ One folder per container /etc/systemd/system/docker.service.d/override.conf Custom service override ~/.docker/config.json Registry logins

docs.title: A container's folder
docs.text:
File What it is <id>-json.log Everything the container printed (stdout/stderr) → docker logs reads this config.v2.json Container config: image, command, env vars, name, state hostconfig.json Host-side settings: -p mappings, restart policy, memory limits, mounts hostname Container's hostname (short ID by default) → mounted as /etc/hostname → UTS namespace hosts Becomes the container's /etc/hosts resolv.conf Becomes the container's /etc/resolv.conf → which DNS server it uses mounts/ Extra mounts like secrets checkpoints/ Saving container state (rare), empty
  • Container removed (docker rm / --rm) → whole folder deleted, logs included

docs.title: The -json.log file
docs.text:
• One JSON object per line → {"log": "text", "stream": "stdout or stderr", "time": "..."}
  • App writes output → shim catches it → dockerd saves it here (json-file log driver)
  • stream → where it came from → nginx entrypoint wrote to stdout, nginx [notice] lines go to stderr by design
  • time ends in Z → UTC → 13:15 in the log = 18:45 IST
  • cat <id>-json.log | jq → pretty-prints each JSON object

docs.title: docker logs
docs.text:
• docker logs app1 → nice reader for that file, strips the JSON, shows only the text
  • docker logs -f app1 → follow live, Ctrl+C stops watching, container keeps running
  • docker logs -t app1 → with timestamps from the time field
  • docker inspect -f '{{.LogPath}}' app1 → exact path of the log file

docs.title: Log growth
docs.text:
• Log file grows forever by default → chatty container can fill the disk
  • Cap it in /etc/docker/daemon.json → "log-driver": "json-file", "log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"} → max 3 files of 10 MB per container (not applied yet)

docs.title: Lab: reading a container's files
docs.text:
sudo ls /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>
sudo cat /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/<id>-json.log | jq
Symptom Cause Fix cat: ...: Is a directory + No such file or directory Space instead of / between folder and file → cat got two arguments Join with / → <folder>/<file> cd 56: No such file or directory Linux needs the full name, doesn't guess Type cd 56 + Tab → bash completes it
  • sudo su - → full root shell, mistakes get costly → prefer sudo ls / sudo cat for one-off reads

Interview points

  • Where does docker logs get its data? → from /var/lib/docker/containers//-json.log, written by the json-file log driver
  • How do you find a container's log file path? → docker inspect -f '{{.LogPath}}'
  • Why do nginx notices appear as stderr? → nginx writes its own logs to stderr by design; it does not mean an error
  • What happens to logs when a container is removed? → the whole container folder, logs included, is deleted
  • How do you stop container logs filling the disk? → set log-opts max-size and max-file in /etc/docker/daemon.json
  • Where does a container's /etc/hostname, /etc/hosts and /etc/resolv.conf come from? → files in its folder under /var/lib/docker/containers, mounted in at start

docs.title: Multi-Stage Builds & Distroless
docs.text: Hands-on notes, Spring PetClinic image

docs.title: Distroless
docs.text:
• Distroless image → only your app and its runtime, no OS userland → no shell, no package manager, no ls, curl, apt
  • Maintained by Google → gcr.io/distroless/...
  • A normal ubuntu or debian base ships hundreds of tools the app never uses
  • Fewer packages → fewer CVEs for scanners, smaller image, and an attacker who gets code execution has no shell or curl to work with
  • gcr.io/distroless/static → static binaries (Go, Rust), static-debian13 pulled at 2.37MB
  • gcr.io/distroless/base → adds glibc
  • gcr.io/distroless/java17-debian12, python3, nodejs22 → language runtimes
  • Tags → :nonroot runs as UID 65532, :debug adds a busybox shell for troubleshooting only
  • scratch → completely empty image, static binaries only | alpine → small but has a shell and apk, uses musl instead of glibc
  • Cost → no docker exec -it c bash, no RUN apt install in the final stage, exec-form CMD and ENTRYPOINT only because shell form needs /bin/sh
  • Debugging → :debug tag in dev, kubectl debug with an ephemeral container in Kubernetes

docs.title: Why some apps need a build stage
docs.text:
• Compiled languages (Go, Java, C/C++, Rust) → source turned into machine code or bytecode before running → needs a build stage with compilers and tools → fast at runtime, the binary is tied to one CPU architecture / OS
  • Interpreted languages (Python, JavaScript/Node.js, PHP) → source run directly by an interpreter at runtime → no separate build step usually → slower, but runs anywhere the interpreter exists
  • Build stage → compilers, build tools, dependencies (e.g. build-essential, Maven, JDK) → needed to make the app
  • Runtime stage → only what is needed to run it (e.g. the JRE, Flask)
  • Analogy → making a pizza needs a measuring cup, an oven and raw ingredients, but only the baked pizza is served
  • Separating them → smaller image, faster push/pull, fewer vulnerabilities

docs.title: Multi-stage build
docs.text:
• Several FROM lines in one Dockerfile → each starts a new stage
  • FROM image AS build → names a stage
  • COPY --from=build /app/app.jar app.jar → copies a file out of an earlier stage
  • Only the last stage becomes the image → the JDK, Maven, source and caches of earlier stages are left behind
  • Pattern → fat stage with the toolchain builds, slim stage only runs
  • docker build --target build -t pc-build . → stop at one stage, useful to inspect what the build produced
  • Layers of the build stage still sit in the local cache → rebuilds stay fast, they just do not ship
# Stage 1: build
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN ./mvnw package -DskipTests && cp target/*.jar app.jar

# Stage 2: runtime (distroless, no shell, non-root)
FROM gcr.io/distroless/java17-debian12:nonroot
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/app.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
  • cp target/*.jar app.jar runs inside RUN, which has a shell, so the * expands and the jar gets a fixed name
  • The final stage then uses that name → no glob in exec form
  • ENTRYPOINT rather than CMD → the image only ever runs this one thing, see ENTRYPOINT & CMD
  • Runtime Java must be the same or newer than the build Java → a jar built on 17 does not run on 11

docs.title: Lab: Spring PetClinic
docs.text:
• Cloned spring-projects/spring-petclinic, wrote a single-stage Dockerfile first, then the multi-stage one
git clone https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-petclinic.git
cd spring-petclinic
docker build -t petclinic .
docker run --rm -d --name petclinic -p 8080:8080 petclinic
docker logs -f petclinic
Image Base Size Build petclinic single-stage eclipse-temurin:17-jdk 750MB 296s, 105s of it pulling the base new-distro multi-stage gcr.io/distroless/java17-debian12:nonroot 292MB 211s, mvnw package 207s distroless/static-debian13 alone none 2.37MB pulled only
  • About 60% smaller → the single-stage image carries the JDK, the source and the Maven cache, the final stage only the JRE and one jar
  • Log of the running distroless container → PID 1, started by nonroot in /app, Java 17.0.18, Spring Boot 4.1.0, Tomcat on 8080, Started PetClinicApplication in 6.53 seconds
  • Non-root works here because the app listens on 8080, a port above 1024
  • RUN ./mvnw package ran again on every rebuild (172s to 207s) → most likely because COPY . . copies the whole folder, Dockerfiles included, so any edit there breaks the cache from that line down

docs.title: Proof that distroless has no shell
docs.text:
• Used static-debian13 as the base of the earlier tools image and kept RUN apt update && apt install ...
runc run failed: unable to start container process: error during container init:
exec: "/bin/sh": stat /bin/sh: no such file or directory
  • RUN needs /bin/sh → with no shell in the image, even the build step cannot start
  • Fix → do all RUN work in a build stage and COPY --from the result

docs.title: Errors I hit
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix docker build requires 1 argument Typed docker build -t petclinic Dockerfile ., two paths docker build -t petclinic ., or -f Dockerfile . unknown shorthand flag: 'r' -r does not exist, the flag is -f docker build -f dockerfile.new -t x . openjdk:17-jdk-slim: not found The openjdk image was removed from Docker Hub eclipse-temurin:17-jdk open dockerfil.new: no such file or directory Typo in the -f name Tab completion docker ps empty after run -d --rm The app crashed at start and --rm removed it Run in the foreground without -d and --rm Error: Unable to access jarfile target/*.jar Exec-form CMD does not expand * cp target/*.jar app.jar in a RUN, ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","app.jar"] exec: "/bin/sh": stat /bin/sh: no such file RUN in a distroless stage Move the RUN to a build stage

docs.title: Things to improve
docs.text:
• Copy pom.xml and the Maven wrapper first, run ./mvnw dependency:go-offline, then COPY src → dependencies stay cached when only code changes
  • Add a .dockerignore with target/, .git, *.md, the extra Dockerfiles → smaller context, fewer cache busts
  • Pin tags more tightly or by digest → latest-style moves break builds
  • Use a JRE-only build stage image if the project allows it, and Java 21 if the Spring Boot version asks for it

Quick revision

  • Multi-stage → many FROM, last one ships, COPY --from=name pulls files across
  • Distroless → no shell, no package manager, small and low-CVE
  • RUN needs /bin/sh → do it in the build stage
  • :nonroot for the user, :debug for a shell while troubleshooting

Interview points

  • What is a multi-stage build? → several FROM stages in one Dockerfile, a heavy stage compiles the app and the last, slim stage copies only the artifact with COPY --from
  • Why use it? → the final image has no compiler, source or build cache, so it is smaller and has a smaller attack surface
  • What is a distroless image? → a base with the app runtime only, no shell, no package manager, no OS tools
  • Benefits of distroless? → fewer CVEs, smaller image, an attacker who gets in has no shell or curl to use
  • Downsides? → no docker exec shell, no RUN apt install in the final stage, only exec-form CMD and ENTRYPOINT, debugging needs the :debug tag or an ephemeral container
  • Why did RUN apt update fail on a distroless base? → RUN starts /bin/sh -c and the image has no /bin/sh
  • How do you debug a distroless container in Kubernetes? → kubectl debug with an ephemeral container that shares the pod's namespaces
  • distroless vs scratch vs alpine? → scratch is empty and only fits static binaries, distroless adds CA certs, timezone data and a non-root user, alpine is small but has a shell and uses musl
