  • How do you harden an image? → multi-stage build, minimal or distroless base, non-root USER, pinned versions, no secrets in ENV
  • What does docker build --target do? → builds only up to the named stage and tags that

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text: Hands-on notes, plus Red Hat's "The 7 most used Linux namespaces" article

docs.title: What a namespace is
docs.text:
• Kernel feature that partitions resources → different sets of processes see different resources
  • Article's analogy → flats in one building complex: shared structure, separate addresses, names and utilities
  • Namespaces → what a container can see | cgroups → what it can use

docs.title: The 7 namespaces
docs.text:
Namespace Isolates In Docker PID Process list nginx is PID 1 inside, some other PID on the host NET Interfaces, IPs, ports, routing Own eth0 (veth into docker0), 10 containers can all use port 80 MNT Filesystem view Sees the OverlayFS image as /, not the host's files (compare chroot) UTS Hostname docker run --hostname web1 IPC Shared memory, message queues, semaphores Containers can't touch each other's shared memory USER UID mapping Root inside can map to an unprivileged user outside CGROUP View of /sys/fs/cgroup Sees only its own cgroup tree
  • nginx log 1#1 → nginx is PID 1 inside its PID namespace

docs.title: Corrections to the article
docs.text:
• USER namespace → real point is security: container root ≠ host root
  • Docker doesn't enable it by default → container root = real root unless "userns-remap" in daemon.json or rootless Docker (docker-ce-rootless-extras)
  • There are 8 now → TIME namespace (kernel 5.6+) came after the article, Docker doesn't use it by default

docs.title: Lab: see namespaces
docs.text:
docker run -d --name ns-test nginx
PID=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' ns-test)
echo $PID
sudo ls -l /proc/$PID/ns
sudo ls -l /proc/self/ns
sudo nsenter -t $PID -n ip a
sudo nsenter -t $PID -p -m ps aux
sudo lsns -p $PID
docker rm -f ns-test
  • docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' → the container's PID on the host
  • /proc/$PID/ns vs /proc/self/ns → different namespace IDs = separate namespaces from my shell
  • nsenter -n ip a → inside the container's network namespace → only lo and eth0
  • nsenter -p -m ps aux → container's own process list, nginx is PID 1
  • lsns -p → every namespace the process belongs to

docs.title: Lab: a "container" without Docker
docs.text:
sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc --uts bash
hostname fake-container
ps aux
exit
  • bash is PID 1, hostname change doesn't touch the real host → core of what runc does, minus cgroups and the image filesystem

Interview points

  • What is a Linux namespace? → a kernel feature that gives a set of processes its own view of a resource (processes, network, mounts, hostname...)
  • Namespaces vs cgroups? → namespaces limit what a process can see; cgroups limit what it can use
  • Name the 7 namespaces → PID, NET, MNT, UTS, IPC, USER, CGROUP (plus TIME on newer kernels)
  • Is container root the same as host root? → by default yes; user namespace remapping or rootless Docker changes that
  • How do you get a shell in a container's network namespace from the host? → nsenter -t -n
  • Why can 10 containers all listen on port 80? → each has its own network namespace

docs.title: Networking
docs.text: Hands-on notes, how containers reach each other and the outside world

docs.title: Basics first
docs.text:
• IP address → which building | localhost / 127.0.0.1 → my own machine
  • Port → which door of that building (0–65535) → web server 80, SSH 22, Postgres 5432
  • "Listening on port 80" → the program stands behind door 80, waiting for a knock
  • IP + port → one specific service → localhost:8000 = my machine, door 8000
  • Private ranges → 10.x, 172.16–31.x, 192.168.x → not reachable from the internet directly → Docker uses 172.17.x.x
  • Network interface → real or virtual network card → wlo1 Wi-Fi | lo loopback | docker0 Docker's switch | CloudflareWARP VPN
  • NAT → rewrites addresses on packets → how a home router shares one public IP
  • iptables/nftables → kernel firewall and packet-rewriting rules → Docker writes rules here automatically
  • DNS → names to IPs

docs.title: docker0
docs.text:
• docker0 → virtual network switch made of software → a Linux bridge
  • Created by dockerd at startup → stays with zero containers (DOWN, NO-CARRIER = nothing plugged in)
  • Has IP 172.17.0.1 → the gateway for containers
  • Containers get IPs from the same range → 172.17.0.2, 172.17.0.3 ...
  • Container doesn't know the way to google.com → sends to its gateway docker0 → host sends it out via Wi-Fi
  • Only for the default network → docker network create mynet → another bridge (br-...), another range (e.g. 172.18.0.x)

docs.title: veth pairs
docs.text:
• veth pair → virtual cable with two ends
  • One end inside the container's network namespace → renamed eth0
  • Other end on the host (veth3a9f1b2) → plugged into docker0
  • Each container = own network namespace = own IP, own ports, own routing → two containers can both use port 80
   Internet
       │
    wlo1 (192.168.1.x)         ← my real Wi-Fi
       │   NAT (iptables)
    docker0 (172.17.0.1)       ← virtual switch
     │          │
  vethA       vethB            ← host ends of virtual cables
     │          │
  [eth0]      [eth0]
 container1  container2
 172.17.0.2  172.17.0.3

docs.title: Three packet journeys
docs.text:
• Container A → container B → A's eth0 → veth → docker0 → veth → B's eth0 → never leaves the laptop
  • Container → internet → docker0 → iptables MASQUERADE swaps 172.17.0.2 for the host IP → out through wlo1 → reply translated back
  • Outside → container (-p 8080:80) → arrives at host:8080 → iptables DNAT rewrites to 172.17.0.2:80 → docker0 → nginx

docs.title: Port forwarding (-p)
docs.text:
• Container's doors are not the host's doors → host door 80 and container door 80 are different doors
  • No -p → localhost:8000 = connection refused → nobody behind the host's door
  • -p 8000:80 → pipe from host door 8000 to container door 80 → HOST:CONTAINER, outside:inside
  • Left → what I type in the browser | right → where the app is actually waiting
  • nginx never sees port 8000, only 80
  • -p 8000:80 → all interfaces, other Wi-Fi devices can reach it
  • -p 127.0.0.1:8000:80 → only my own machine
  • Two containers can both use container port 80 → each has its own namespace
  • Two containers can't both use host port 8000 → host has only one door 8000
  • EXPOSE 80 / PORTS 80/tcp in docker ps → documentation only, nothing published
  • Published → PORTS 0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp
  • Published ports bypass UFW → Docker's iptables rules run before UFW's
  • PORTS example → 8888/tcp, 0.0.0.0:8001->80/tcp, [::]:8001->80/tcp
  • 8888/tcp → EXPOSE only | 0.0.0.0:8001->80/tcp → -p on every IPv4 address | [::]:8001->80/tcp → same for IPv6

docs.title: Network drivers
docs.text:
• Driver → the type of network → how Docker wires the container
Driver How it wires the container Container gets When bridge veth cable into a software switch on this host (default) Own IP from the bridge's range Most single-host use host Nothing, uses the host's network namespace Host's IPs and ports Max performance, host-level tools, port conflicts possible null (none) Nothing Only lo Fully isolated jobs overlay Bridge spanning multiple hosts, tunnels between machines IP valid across hosts Swarm / multi-host macvlan / ipvlan Straight onto the physical LAN IP from the router, like a real device Container must look like a real device
  • docker network ls → mine shows bridge (= docker0), host, none, kind (bridge made by kind, Kubernetes-in-Docker)
  • host and none → built-in modes, always exist, can't be deleted
  • docker network → connect, create, disconnect, inspect, ls, prune, rm

docs.title: User-defined bridge networks
docs.text:
• docker network create custom --driver bridge → new, separate switch → host interface br-<network id> (e.g. br-d0340428...)
  • Subnet → Docker picks the next free range → 172.17 = docker0, 172.18 = kind, so custom got 172.19.0.0/16
  • Gateway → 172.19.0.1 → the bridge's own IP, same role as docker0's 172.17.0.1
  • IPs handed out in order → first container .2, then .3...
  • --network custom on docker run → join that network instead of the default
  • docker network inspect custom → subnet, gateway, attached containers with IP and MAC
  • IPsInUse: 6 → 3 containers + 3 reserved (.0 network address, .1 gateway, .255.255 broadcast)
  • DynamicIPsAvailable: 65530 → /16 = 65,536 addresses − 6
  • docker network rm custom → only works when no container is attached

docs.title: DNS by name
docs.text:
• Default docker0 → no DNS → containers reach each other only by IP
  • User-defined network → built-in DNS server at 127.0.0.11 inside each container → every container's name registered → reach each other by name (postgres:5432)
  • ping app4 → resolves to app4.custom → <name>.<network>
  • Container IPs change on every restart, names don't → always use a user-defined network for apps that talk to each other
  • Compose creates such a network automatically → services find each other by service name

docs.title: Isolation and multiple networks
docs.text:
• Networks are isolated from each other → container on custom can't reach one on docker0, by IP or name → Docker's iptables rules block traffic between bridges
  • docker network connect custom app1 → plugs a second cable into a running container
  • app1 then has two network cards → eth0 172.17.0.2 on docker0 + eth1 172.19.0.4 on custom → check with docker exec app1 ip -br a
  • Only way across two networks → a container connected to both
  • docker network disconnect custom app1 → unplug it again

docs.title: Host network mode
docs.text:
• docker run --rm -d --name nodeexporter --network host prom/node-exporter
  • No own network namespace → no docker0, no veth, no -p → listens on the host's port 9100 directly → PORTS empty
  • Why for Node Exporter → it reports the host's metrics, including real interfaces (wlo1, docker0) → in bridge mode it would see only its own eth0
  • Trade-off → no network isolation, port 9100 taken on the host itself → two can't run at once
  • Fuller recommended run → --network host --pid host -v /:/host:ro,rslave prom/node-exporter --path.rootfs=/host → also reads host processes and disks
docker inspect field Value Meaning NetworkMode host No own network namespace IPAddress "" No container IP, uses the host's SandboxKey /var/run/docker/netns/default The host's network namespace Ports / PortBindings {} Nothing to forward ExposedPorts 9100/tcp EXPOSE, documentation only Hostname host's hostname Shared with the host too AutoRemove true --rm User nobody Runs unprivileged Entrypoint /bin/node_exporter No CMD, ENTRYPOINT is the whole command GraphDriver LowerDir, UpperDir, MergedDir Read-only image layers, writable layer, the merged / → see Images & Storage

docs.title: My machine
docs.text:
• virbr0 (192.168.122.x) → libvirt/KVM bridge, separate, no conflict with Docker
  • Cloudflare WARP → takes over routes, MTU 1300 → first suspect if containers can't reach the internet or pulls are slow

docs.title: Lab: ports and docker0
docs.text:
docker run --rm -d --name test1 nginx
curl http://localhost:8000
docker inspect -f '{{.NetworkSettings.IPAddress}}' test1
curl http://172.17.0.2
docker stop test1

docker run --rm -d --name test2 -p 8000:80 nginx
curl http://localhost:8000
docker stop test2

docker run --rm -d --name web1 -p 8001:80 nginx
docker run --rm -d --name web2 -p 8002:80 nginx
sudo iptables -t nat -L DOCKER -n
docker stop web1 web2

ip -br addr show docker0
bridge link
  • No -p → localhost:8000 refused, but the container IP answers → nginx was there, just behind the container's door
  • With -p 8000:80 → localhost:8000 returns HTML
  • iptables -t nat -L DOCKER → dpt:8001 to:172.17.0.x:80 → the DNAT rule Docker wrote
  • bridge link → one veth... per running container plugged into docker0 → gone after stop
Symptom Cause Fix PORTS shows only 80/tcp, browser can't reach nginx No -p, 80/tcp is just EXPOSE docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx localhost:8000 connection refused Nothing published on host port 8000 Add -p 8000:80

docs.title: Lab: default bridge vs custom network
docs.text:
docker network ls
docker run --rm -d --name app1 -p 8000:80 kiran2361993/troubleshootingtools:v1
docker run --rm -d --name app2 -p 8001:80 kiran2361993/troubleshootingtools:v1
docker inspect app1 | grep -i IPAddress
docker inspect app2 | grep -i IPAddress
docker exec -it app1 bash
ping 172.17.0.3
exit

docker network create custom --driver bridge
docker run --rm -d --name app3 -p 8003:80 --network custom kiran2361993/troubleshootingtools:v1
docker run --rm -d --name app4 -p 8004:80 --network custom kiran2361993/troubleshootingtools:v1
docker inspect app3 | grep -i IPAddress
docker exec -it app3 bash
ping 172.19.0.3
exit

docker network connect custom app1
docker network inspect custom
docker exec -it app1 bash
ping app4
ping app3
ping app2
exit
docker stop $(docker ps -aq)
  • app1 172.17.0.2 → app2 172.17.0.3 by IP → works, ~0.1 ms → app1 eth0 → veth → docker0 → veth → app2
  • ttl=64 unchanged → no router in between, same switch
  • app3 172.19.0.2 → app4 172.19.0.3 → works on custom
  • After network connect → app1 gets 172.19.0.4 on custom as well
From app1 Result Why ping 172.19.0.3 Works app1 now has a cable on custom ping app4 Works, app4.custom Built-in DNS on the user-defined network ping app3 Works Same ping app2 Name or service not known app2 only on the default bridge → no DNS there (ping 172.17.0.3 still works)

docs.title: Lab: Node Exporter on the host network
docs.text:
docker run --rm -d --name nodeexporter --network host prom/node-exporter
docker ps
docker inspect nodeexporter
curl -s localhost:9100/metrics | head
curl -s localhost:9100/metrics | grep node_network_receive_bytes_total
docker stop nodeexporter
docker network rm custom
docker network ls
  • docker ps → PORTS empty → no forwarding in host mode
  • node_network_receive_bytes_total → lists my real interfaces (wlo1, docker0, CloudflareWARP) → it sees the host's network
Symptom Cause Fix ping app2: Name or service not known app2 is on the default bridge, which has no DNS Put both on a user-defined network, or use the IP unknown flag: --netwrok Typo --network host docker network rm fails Containers still attached Stop or disconnect them first

Interview points

  • What is docker0? → a Linux bridge (software switch) created by dockerd; containers plug into it via veth pairs and use 172.17.0.1 as their gateway
  • What is a veth pair? → a virtual cable; one end is eth0 inside the container, the other is plugged into the bridge on the host
  • What does -p 8080:80 mean? → host port 8080 forwards to container port 80 (HOST:CONTAINER) via an iptables DNAT rule
  • Why can't I reach a container without -p? → its IP is private to the host; nothing listens on the host port
  • Does EXPOSE publish a port? → no, it only documents it
  • How does a container reach the internet? → through docker0, then iptables MASQUERADE rewrites its source IP to the host's
  • Why can two containers use port 80 but not the same host port? → each has its own network namespace, but the host has only one of each port
  • Default bridge vs user-defined network? → user-defined networks have built-in DNS so containers reach each other by name
  • Why does a published port ignore UFW? → Docker's iptables rules are evaluated before UFW's
  • What is a network driver? → the type of network, i.e. how Docker wires the container: bridge, host, none, overlay, macvlan/ipvlan
  • Can a container on one user-defined network reach a container on another? → no, bridges are isolated by iptables; connect the container to both networks to cross
  • How do you add a running container to another network? → docker network connect ; it gets a second interface (eth1)
  • Which DNS server do containers on a user-defined network use? → Docker's embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11
  • Why use names instead of container IPs? → IPs change when containers restart, names stay the same
  • When would you use --network host? → when the container must see or serve on the host's network directly, e.g. Node Exporter; you lose isolation and can get port conflicts
  • Why does docker ps show no ports in host mode? → nothing is forwarded; the app listens on the host's port directly
  • Why does a /16 network show 65530 available IPs with 3 containers? → 65,536 minus the network address, gateway, broadcast and the 3 containers

docs.title: What a registry is
docs.text:
• Registry → server that stores and serves images → like an app store for images
  • Repository → one image's collection of versions inside a registry → nginx, myuser/my-app
  • Tag → one version inside a repository → 1.27, v1.0, latest
  • Public → Docker Hub (docker.io), GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io), Quay (quay.io)
  • Cloud / private → AWS ECR, Google Artifact Registry / GCR, Azure ACR, JFrog Artifactory, Nexus, self-hosted Harbor
  • Flow → build image locally → push to a registry → servers and Kubernetes nodes pull from it

docs.title: Anatomy of a full image name
docs.text:
docker.io / library / ubuntu : latest
registry    namespace  repo    tag
  • docker pull ubuntu → Docker fills in the rest → docker.io/library/ubuntu:latest
  • No registry given → Docker Hub (docker.io)
  • No namespace on Docker Hub → library = official images
  • No tag → latest → just a default tag name, not "newest" → pin real tags in production
  • Digest (@sha256:...) → exact, unchangeable content | tags can be moved to a new image
Registry Name format Example Docker Hub docker.io/<user>/<repo>:<tag> docker.io/myuser/my-app:v1.0 AWS ECR <account-id>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com/<repo>:<tag> 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-app:v1.0 Google GCR gcr.io/<project-id>/<image>:<tag> gcr.io/my-gcp-project/my-app:v1.0 Google Artifact Registry <region>-docker.pkg.dev/<project>/<repo>/<image>:<tag> us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/my-app:v1.0 GitHub ghcr.io/<user>/<image>:<tag> ghcr.io/myuser/my-app:v1.0
  • docker pull works the same everywhere → only the full name changes
  • Private registries → log in first

docs.title: Logging in
docs.text:
docker login                                  # Docker Hub, asks for username + access token
docker login ghcr.io
aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 \
  | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
docker logout
  • Use an access token, not the account password
  • Credentials saved in ~/.docker/config.json → base64 only unless a credential helper is configured → treat it like a password file

docs.title: Build, tag, push
docs.text:
FROM ubuntu:latest
CMD echo "Hello, Docker!"

docker build -t my-first-image .                          # . = build context
docker run my-first-image                                 # Hello, Docker!
docker tag my-first-image <username>/my-first-image:v1.0  # new name for the same image
docker images                                             # both names, same IMAGE ID
docker push <username>/my-first-image:v1.0                # really docker.io/<username>/my-first-image:v1.0
docker pull <username>/my-first-image:v1.0                # from any machine
  • docker tag → does not copy anything → adds another name pointing to the same image ID
  • Push needs the name to include my namespace → docker push my-first-image fails, Docker Hub's library/ is only for official images
  • Push sends only layers the registry doesn't already have → shared base layers are skipped ("Layer already exists")
  • Tag with a real version (v1.0, git SHA) → latest can't be rolled back to

docs.title: Custom Dockerfile name and build context
docs.text:
docker build -t my-app -f Dockerfile.prod .
docker build -t entry-image -f /path/to/custom-dockerfile /path/to/build-context
  • -f → which Dockerfile to use (e.g. Dockerfile.dev, Dockerfile.prod)
  • Last argument → build context → the folder sent to the daemon → COPY/ADD can only see files inside it
  • .dockerignore → keep .git, node_modules, secrets out of the context

docs.title: Everyday commands
docs.text:
Command Does docker images List local images docker ps -a All containers, including stopped docker inspect <id> Full metadata of a container or image docker top <container> Processes inside a running container docker stop $(docker ps -q) Stop all running containers docker container prune Delete all stopped containers docker rmi <image> Delete an image docker image prune -a Delete all images not used by a container

Interview points

  • Registry vs repository vs tag? → a registry is the server, a repository is one image's set of versions, a tag is one version
  • What does docker pull ubuntu actually pull? → docker.io/library/ubuntu:latest
  • Does latest mean the newest version? → no, it is just the default tag name; pin explicit tags or digests in production
  • Tag vs digest? → a tag is a movable label; a digest is the sha256 of the content and never changes
  • Why does docker push my-first-image fail on Docker Hub? → the image name needs your namespace, e.g. username/my-first-image
  • What does docker tag do? → adds another name to the same image ID, nothing is copied
  • How do you push to ECR? → get a token with aws ecr get-login-password, docker login to the account's registry URL, tag with the full ECR name, push
  • What is the build context? → the folder sent to the daemon during docker build; COPY and ADD only see files inside it, and .dockerignore trims it

docs.title: Volumes & Bind Mounts
docs.text: Hands-on notes, Docker storage

docs.title: Why containers need them
docs.text:
• Container filesystem → a writable layer that lives and dies with the container, docker rm deletes it
  • Two problems → data is lost when the container goes, and the container cannot see host files
  • Fix → mount something into the container: a volume, a bind mount, or tmpfs

docs.title: The three mount types
docs.text:
• Volume → storage created and managed by Docker, referred to by name → pgdata
  • Bind mount → a host path you choose, mapped into the container, same real files on both sides → /home/ganesh/site
  • tmpfs → memory only, never written to disk, gone when the container stops (Linux only) → --tmpfs /tmp

docs.title: -v versus --mount
docs.text:
• -v SOURCE:TARGET → short form, Docker guesses the type from SOURCE
  • Source starts with / or ./ → bind mount | just a name → named volume
  • --mount type=...,source=...,target=... → long form, explicit, no guessing
  • -v with a wrong host path → silently creates an empty root-owned directory
  • --mount type=bind with a wrong host path → fails with an error, which is what you want
# named volume
docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres
docker run --mount type=volume,source=pgdata,target=/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres

# bind mount
docker run -v /home/ganesh/site:/usr/share/nginx/html nginx
docker run --mount type=bind,source=/home/ganesh/site,target=/usr/share/nginx/html nginx

docs.title: When to use which
docs.text:
• Volume → data the app owns and must keep: databases, uploads
  • Bind mount → files you edit or inspect from the host: source code in development, a single config file
  • Bind mount → host resources only a path can reach: logs, /proc, the Docker socket
  • Avoid bind mounts for production data → they tie the container to one host's folder layout and let the container change host files
  • Read-only mount → add :ro (-v /home/ganesh/site:/usr/share/nginx/html:ro) when the container only needs to read
  • Mount the narrowest path possible → one file or subfolder, not a parent directory

docs.title: Volume commands
docs.text:
• docker volume create pgdata → create a named volume (also auto-created on first use)
  • docker volume ls → list volumes
  • docker volume inspect pgdata → shows Mountpoint, the real path on the host
  • docker volume rm pgdata → delete it, fails if a container still uses it
  • docker volume prune → delete every volume no container uses, check first, this is permanent
  • docker system df → disk used by images, containers and volumes

docs.title: Where volumes live on the host
docs.text:
• Path → /var/lib/docker/volumes/<name>/_data, the contents are in _data
  • Owned by root → cd /var/lib/docker/volumes as a normal user gives Permission denied, use sudo
  • Docker Desktop (Mac/Windows) → the path is inside a hidden VM, not browsable
  • Don't edit files there while a container is using the volume
  • Change the base location → data-root in /etc/docker/daemon.json, but that moves all Docker data

docs.title: Back up and restore a volume
docs.text:
• Idea → throwaway container mounts the volume and a host folder, then runs tar
  • This uses a named volume and a bind mount together
# backup
docker run --rm -v mongodb:/data -v "$PWD":/backup alpine \
  tar czf /backup/mongodb.tar.gz -C /data .

# restore into a volume
docker run --rm -v mongodb:/data -v "$PWD":/backup alpine \
  tar xzf /backup/mongodb.tar.gz -C /data

docs.title: Lab: Mongo with and without a volume
docs.text:
• No volume → data lives in the container's writable layer
  • --rm → removes the container on stop
  • Named volume → survives --rm, only docker volume rm deletes it
  • Mongo keeps its data in /data/db
# 1. no volume
docker run --rm -d --name mongodb -p 27017:27017 mongo:latest
docker exec -it mongodb mongosh
#    test> db.helo.insertMany([...])   → show dbs lists "test"
docker stop mongodb
docker run --rm -d --name mongodb -p 27017:27017 mongo:latest
#    show dbs → "test" is gone, the data went with the container

# 2. with a named volume
docker volume create mongodb
docker run --rm -d --name mongodb -v mongodb:/data/db -p 27017:27017 mongo:latest
#    insert the same documents, then:
docker stop mongodb
docker run --rm -d --name mongodb -v mongodb:/data/db -p 27017:27017 mongo:latest
#    db.helo.find() → all documents are back

# 3. look at the files on the host
sudo ls /var/lib/docker/volumes/mongodb/_data
#    collection-*.wt  index-*.wt  journal  WiredTiger*  mongod.lock ...

Publishing Mongo

-p 27017:27017 binds to every interface and this Mongo had no authentication. Fine behind home NAT, an open database on a cloud VM. Bind to localhost instead: -p 127.0.0.1:27017:27017.

docs.title: Errors I hit
docs.text:
Symptom Cause Fix Data gone after recreating the container No volume, data was in the container layer Mount a named volume on the data path (/data/db for Mongo) Permission denied on /var/lib/docker/volumes Directory is root-only sudo ls ... or sudo su - Files from a bind mount are owned by root on the host Container process runs as root Run with --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" or chown afterwards Empty root-owned folder appears at a typo path -v creates missing host paths Use --mount type=bind, it errors instead

Quick revision

  • Volume → Docker-managed, by name, for persistence
  • Bind mount → your host path, for dev files and host resources
  • --rm removes the container, never a named volume

Interview points

  • Volume vs bind mount? → a volume is managed by Docker and referenced by name, a bind mount maps a host path you choose. Volumes for persistent app data, bind mounts for dev code and config
  • Container was deleted and the data is gone, why? → the data was in the container's writable layer. Mount a volume on the data path
  • Does --rm delete a named volume? → no, only the container (and anonymous volumes). Named volumes stay until docker volume rm
  • How do you tell -v volume from bind mount? → source starting with / or ./ is a bind mount, a plain name is a volume
  • Why prefer --mount over -v? → it is explicit, and it errors on a missing bind source instead of creating an empty directory
  • Files written by a container show up root-owned on the host? → the container runs as root. Use --user with the host UID and GID
  • Where are named volumes stored on Linux? → /var/lib/docker/volumes/<name>/_data, readable only by root
  • How would you back up a volume? → run a throwaway container that mounts the volume and a host folder, and tar the data
  • When would you use tmpfs? → temporary or sensitive data you don't want written to disk

docs.title: Go
docs.text:
Notes on Go, starting with what Go is and why it exists, then how Go is laid out on a machine before any language syntax: where it is installed, where it keeps downloads and caches, and how modules, packages and files fit together. Knowing these layers makes setup and build errors much easier to debug. Language chapters follow.

  1. What is Go History, why it was built, compiled vs interpreted, single binary, goroutines, comparison with other languages, where it is used
  2. Installation & GOROOT Where Go lives, PATH, the toolchain behind go, go.env, duplicate installs
  3. GOPATH, Caches & go env ~/go/bin, module cache, build cache, settings priority, cleaning caches
  4. Modules & Packages go mod init, go.mod, folders as packages, package main, exported names
  5. Go Files, Running & Testing Parts of a .go file, go run / go build, reading compile errors, first test, linting
  6. Functions & Printing Println vs Printf verbs, parameters, multiple results, (value, error), named returns
  7. Variables, Types & Constants var and :=, zero values, type inference, basic types, conversions, const
  8. Loops & Conditionals for in all its forms, if with short statements, else, switch, evaluation order, square-root exercise
  9. Defer Delayed calls for cleanup, arguments evaluated immediately, LIFO stacking

docs.title: What defer does
docs.text:
func main() {
    defer fmt.Println("world")
    fmt.Println("hello")
}
// hello
// world
  • defer → don't run this now, run it right before the surrounding function returns
  • Written first, runs last → the call is saved on a list, executed when the function ends
  • Runs however the function exits → reaching }, any return, or a panic

docs.title: Why it exists → cleanup
docs.text:
func readConfig(path string) error {
    f, err := os.Open(path)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer f.Close()   // written right next to Open → can't be forgotten

    // … read the file, maybe return early in several places …
    return nil
}   // f.Close() runs here, on every exit path
  • Without defer → Close() must be repeated before every return → miss one and the file leaks
  • With defer → write it once, right after acquiring the resource
  • Typical uses → closing files, HTTP response bodies, DB connections, unlocking a mutex, removing temp files
  • Bash equivalent → trap 'rm -f /tmp/lockfile' EXIT

docs.title: Arguments are evaluated immediately
docs.text:
x := 1
defer fmt.Println("deferred x =", x)   // x is captured as 1 here
x = 100
fmt.Println("current x =", x)
// current x = 100
// deferred x = 1
  • The values are fixed when the defer line runs → only the call is delayed
  • Like a photo → snapshot taken at the defer line, printed at the end
  • Changing the variable later doesn't change what was saved

docs.title: Stacking defers
docs.text:
fmt.Println("counting")
for i := 0; i < 10; i++ {
    defer fmt.Println(i)
}
fmt.Println("done")
// counting
// done
// 9
// 8
// …
// 0
  • Deferred calls go onto a stack → run in LIFO order → last in, first out
  • Pile of plates → 0 goes in first, 9 lands on top → 9 comes off first
  • Each defer fmt.Println(i) captured the i of its own round → 0…9, not ten 10s
  • Reverse order matches cleanup → release things in the opposite order you acquired them:
db := connectDB()
defer db.Close()     // deferred 1st → runs last

f := openFile()
defer f.Close()      // deferred 2nd → runs first

defer fmt.Println("A")
defer fmt.Println("B")
fmt.Println("C")
defer fmt.Println("D")
// C
// D
// B
// A
Symptom Cause Fix Deferred call prints an old value arguments captured when defer ran defer after the value is final, or defer a closure that reads it at the end Deferred calls run in the "wrong" order defers are LIFO order the defer lines in reverse of the order you want them to run Files or connections pile up in a long loop defer inside a loop only runs when the function returns move the loop body into its own function, or close explicitly each round defer f.Close() panics on a nil f deferred before checking err check err first, then defer

Quick revision

  • defer f() → runs f just before the surrounding function returns
  • Arguments evaluated at the defer line, call delayed
  • Several defers → LIFO → last deferred runs first
  • Put defer x.Close() right after a successful open
  • defer in a loop waits for the function, not the loop round

Interview points

  • When does a deferred call run? → just before the surrounding function returns, on every exit path including panics
  • When are a deferred call's arguments evaluated? → immediately, when the defer statement executes; only the call is delayed
  • In what order do multiple defers run? → last in, first out, like a stack
  • Why is LIFO the right order for defers? → resources are released in reverse of how they were acquired
  • What is the classic use of defer? → cleanup such as closing files and response bodies or unlocking mutexes
  • Why is defer inside a long loop risky? → deferred calls pile up until the function returns, holding resources open
  • Why check err before deferring Close? → if the open failed the value may be nil and the deferred Close would fail or panic

docs.title: Parts of a .go file
docs.text:
• Every file has the same three parts, always in this order:
// 1. package → which folder-group this file belongs to
package main

// 2. imports → other packages this file uses
import (
    "fmt"
    "demo/greet"
)

// 3. code → functions, constants, variables, types
func main() {
    fmt.Println(greet.Hello())
}
  • package → first line (comments above it allowed), exactly one per file
  • import → single import "fmt" or grouped import ( ... ) → gofmt keeps the group sorted
  • Top level of a file holds only declarations → func, const, var, type
  • Statements (printing, loops, if) live inside functions → fmt.Println("hi") at top level is an error
  • Comments → // one line | /* many lines */

docs.title: Compiler rules that catch beginners
docs.text:
• Unused import → compile error, not a warning:
"os" imported and not used
  • Unused local variable → compile error
  • Unused function → allowed → defining a function doesn't run it, something must call it

docs.title: go run vs go build
docs.text:
go run hello.go      # compile + run one file, no binary left behind
go run .             # same for the whole package in this folder (preferred)
go build             # binary named after the module (module go-tour → ./go-tour)
go build -o hello .  # binary named hello
./hello
  • -o = name of the output binary → go build -o hello.go tries to write the binary over the source file:
build output "hello.go" already exists and is not an object file
  • . = the package in the current folder → prefer go run . / go build . over file names → keeps working once a package has several files
  • Binary is static (~2 MB for hello world) → Go runtime bundled in, no dependencies → copy to any Linux amd64 machine and run, Go not needed there
  • Why DevOps tooling is written in Go → kubectl, Terraform, Docker, Prometheus ship as single binaries
  • Keep binaries out of Git → add the binary name to .gitignore
file hello       # ELF 64-bit LSB executable
ls -lh hello

docs.title: Reading compile errors
docs.text:
./hello.go:5:12: syntax error: unexpected name string, expected (
  • ./hello.go → file | 5 → line | 12 → column | then the message
  • Example cause → func Hello string { → functions always need (), even with no inputs → func Hello() string {
  • One mistake often causes follow-up errors on later lines → fix the first error, re-run

docs.title: First test
docs.text:
// hello.go
package main

func Hello() string {
    return "Hello, world"
}

// hello_test.go
package main

import "testing"

func TestHello(t *testing.T) {
    got := Hello()
    want := "Hello, world"

    if got != want {
        t.Errorf("got %q want %q", got, want)
    }
}

go test
  • Test = code that checks other code → Go compares results instead of you reading output
  • File name must end in _test.go → only compiled by go test
  • Same package as the code under test → can call Hello() directly
  • Function name must start with Test and take t *testing.T → t reports failures (* = pointer, covered later)
  • got := Hello() → := creates a variable and assigns it
  • != → not equal | t.Errorf → marks the test failed with a message
  • %q → placeholder replaced by the value in double quotes → got "Hello there" want "Hello, world"
  • Loop → write test → watch it fail → fix code → watch it pass
  • Libraries have no main → tests are how their code gets run and checked

docs.title: Formatting and linting
docs.text:
• gofmt -w . / go fmt ./... → one standard format, no style debates → editors run it on save
  • go vet ./... → built-in checks for suspicious code (wrong Printf verbs, copied locks)
  • golangci-lint → runs go vet plus many more linters in one command → standard in CI for serious Go repos
curl -sSfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/golangci/golangci-lint/HEAD/install.sh | sh -s -- -b $(go env GOPATH)/bin
golangci-lint --version
golangci-lint run          # lint current module → "0 issues."
golangci-lint linters      # enabled / disabled linters
  • Catches what the compiler doesn't, e.g. an ignored error:
f, err := os.Open("file.txt")
f.Close()   // err never checked → crash if the open failed
Linter Catches errcheck errors that are ignored govet suspicious code staticcheck bugs, dead code, deprecated calls unused unused functions, variables, types ineffassign values assigned and never read

docs.title: Editor (VS Code + Go extension)
docs.text:
• Extension installs gopls (language server) and other tools into ~/go/bin
  • Format on save is on by default
  • F12 → go to definition | Shift+F12 → find usages | F2 → rename across files | Ctrl+Shift+R → refactor menu | hover → signature and docs
Symptom Cause Fix build output "x.go" already exists and is not an object file -o given a source file name -o takes the binary name → go build -o hello . imported and not used import never used remove it or use it syntax error: unexpected ..., expected ( function declared without () func Name() type non-declaration statement outside function body statement at top level move it inside a function Program output didn't change after adding a function function never called call it from main go test → no test files test file not named *_test.go rename it

Quick revision

  • File = package → import → declarations
  • Unused import/variable = error, unused function = fine
  • go run . to run, go build -o name . to build a static binary
  • Tests: *_test.go, func TestXxx(t *testing.T), go test

Interview points

  • What are the parts of a Go source file? → package clause, imports, then top-level declarations (func, const, var, type)
  • Why does Go fail on unused imports and variables? → to keep code clean and builds fast; unused code is treated as a likely mistake
  • go run vs go build? → go run compiles to a temporary binary and runs it; go build writes the binary to disk
  • Why is Go popular for DevOps tools? → it builds single static binaries with no runtime dependencies, easy to ship and cross-compile
  • How do you read a Go compile error location? → file:line:column, and fix the first error since later ones are often knock-on
  • What are the rules for a Go test? → file ends in _test.go, function starts with Test and takes *testing.T, run with go test
  • What does t.Errorf do? → reports a failure with a formatted message and lets the test continue
  • gofmt vs go vet vs golangci-lint? → gofmt formats, go vet runs built-in correctness checks, golangci-lint runs many linters including vet in one pass
  • What does errcheck catch? → returned errors that the code ignores

docs.title: Printing with fmt
docs.text:
fmt.Println("My favorite number is", rand.Intn(10))
fmt.Printf("Now you have %g problems.\n", math.Sqrt(7))
  • fmt.Println(a, b) → prints values, adds a space between them and a newline at the end
  • fmt.Printf("format", a, b) → you write the line with placeholders (verbs) → nothing is added for you → end with \n
  • rand.Intn(10) → random int from 0 to 9 (10 excluded)
Verb Prints Example %v any value, default format 42, true, hello %d integer 42 %s string hello %q string in double quotes → makes empty strings and spaces visible "hello", "" %g float, compact (no trailing zeros) 2.6457513110645907 %.2f float, 2 decimal places 2.65 %T the type of the value float64
  • %T is the quickest way to check what type Go picked for a variable

docs.title: Standard library packages used here
docs.text:
• fmt → printing and formatting
  • math → math.Sqrt, math.Pow, math.Pi
  • math/rand → random numbers → used as rand.Intn, not math.rand
  • math/rand is a separate package that lives in a subfolder of math/ → importing "math" does not give you rand
  • Name used in code = last element of the import path → "net/http" → http, "encoding/json" → json
  • Full list → pkg.go.dev/std

docs.title: Declaring a function
docs.text:
func add(x int, y int) int {
    return x + y
}
  • func → keyword | add → name | (x int, y int) → parameters | int after ) → return type
  • Type comes after the name → x int reads "x is an int" (C/Java write int x)
  • Declared return type → every path must return a value of that type, or it doesn't compile
  • Wrong argument type or count → compile error → add(10) → not enough arguments in call to add
  • Short functions can sit on one line → func needInt(x int) int { return x*10 + 1 }

docs.title: Shared parameter types
docs.text:
func add(x, y int) int           // x and y are both int
func h(a, b int, s string)       // a, b int → s string
func k(a int, s string, b int)   // a and b not consecutive → each needs its type
  • A type covers every name to its left back to the previous type
  • func add(x, y) int → error undefined: x → without a type Go reads x and y as type names → each group needs a type

docs.title: Multiple return values
docs.text:
func swap(x, y string) (string, string) {
    return y, x
}

a, b := swap("hello", "world")   // a = "world", b = "hello"
  • More than one return type → wrap them in ( )
  • Values are received by position
  • Unwanted value → blank identifier _ → a, _ := swap("hello", "world") → needed because unused variables are errors

docs.title: The (value, error) pattern
docs.text:
f, err := os.Open("config.yaml")
if err != nil {
    fmt.Println("failed:", err)
    return
}
  • Go has no exceptions → functions that can fail return the result plus an error
  • err is nil when nothing went wrong → check it right after the call
  • Same shape everywhere → strconv.Atoi, os.ReadFile, HTTP calls, Kubernetes client calls

docs.title: Named return values
docs.text:
func split(sum int) (x, y int) {
    x = sum * 4 / 9   // 17*4/9 = 68/9 = 7 (integer division drops .55)
    y = sum - x       // 10
    return            // naked return → sends back x, y
}
  • Named results are created at the start of the function with their zero values (0, "", false)
  • Assign with =, not := → they already exist
  • Bare return (naked return) → returns the current values of the named results
  • Same as writing (int, int) + x := ... + return x, y → just shorter
  • Use naked return only in short functions → in long ones the reader can't see what's returned
  • Names also document the result → (prefix string) says what comes back
func greetingPrefix(language string) (prefix string) {
    switch language {
    case "French":
        prefix = "Bonjour, "
    default:
        prefix = "Hello, "
    }
    return
}
Symptom Cause Fix not enough arguments in call to add fewer arguments than parameters pass every parameter cannot use "13" (untyped string constant) as int value argument of the wrong type pass the declared type, or convert it missing return a path through the function returns nothing return a value on every path undefined: x on a function's own parameter line func add(x, y) int → no type, so Go reads x and y as type names give the group a type → x, y int declared and not used: b received a return value you don't use replace it with _ assignment mismatch: 1 variable but swap returns 2 values caught only one of several results receive all of them, _ for the unwanted ones Printf output runs into the next line Printf adds no newline end the format with \n

Quick revision

  • func name(a, b int) (int, error) { ... } → type after name, shared types, results in ( )
  • Println = spaces + newline | Printf = verbs, add \n yourself
  • %v any | %d int | %s string | %q quoted | %T type
  • _ throws away a value | err != nil → something failed
  • Named results start at zero values, naked return only in short functions

Interview points

  • How does Go handle errors without exceptions? → functions return an error as their last value and the caller checks if err != nil
  • What is the blank identifier? → _ , used to discard a value you must receive but don't need
  • What are named return values? → result parameters declared with names; they start at zero values and a bare return sends them back
  • When should you avoid naked returns? → in long functions, because the reader can't tell what is being returned
  • Println vs Printf? → Println prints values separated by spaces with a newline; Printf uses a format string with verbs and adds nothing
  • Why use %q in test failure messages? → it quotes strings, so empty strings and stray spaces become visible
  • How do you find a value's type at runtime while debugging? → fmt.Printf("%T", v)
  • Is math/rand part of the math package? → no, it is a separate package stored under the math/ directory

docs.title: GOROOT vs GOPATH
docs.text:
• GOROOT → Go's own files (the install)
  • GOPATH → Go's storage for you → tools you install + libraries it downloads → default ~/go, created on first use
  • Your own code → not in GOPATH → any folder works (~/learn-go, ~/projects/...)
/usr/local/go   → Go itself                    (GOROOT)
~/go            → installed tools + downloads   (GOPATH)
~/anywhere      → your code

docs.title: Inside ~/go
docs.text:
~/go/
├── bin/                     ← binaries from `go install`
└── pkg/
    └── mod/                 ← module cache: every downloaded library
        ├── github.com/...
        ├── golang.org/...
        └── cache/download/  ← raw zip files they came from
  • ~/go/bin → e.g. golangci-lint, gopls (VS Code's language server), staticcheck, kind → each a single self-contained binary
  • ~/go/pkg/mod → folders named by URL → a module's name is where its code lives → that's how go get knows where to download from
  • Version is part of the folder name → kind@v0.33.0 → several versions of one library sit side by side
  • Files are read-only → can't accidentally edit a library
  • Tools installed with go install pull in their dependencies → module cache fills up even if you never downloaded anything yourself

docs.title: Build cache
docs.text:
• ~/.cache/go-build → GOCACHE → compiled results of every package built
  • Second build is fast → unchanged packages aren't recompiled
  • Also caches test results → go test prints (cached) when nothing changed
  • Safe to delete → builds just get slower once

docs.title: Variables at a glance
docs.text:
Variable Default Used for GOROOT /usr/local/go compiler + stdlib GOPATH ~/go root for the next two GOBIN empty → $GOPATH/bin where go install puts binaries GOMODCACHE $GOPATH/pkg/mod downloaded libraries GOCACHE ~/.cache/go-build build and test cache GOENV ~/.config/go/env your saved settings (go env -w) 
go env                                       # every setting
go env GOPATH GOBIN GOMODCACHE GOCACHE GOENV # specific ones
du -sh ~/.cache/go-build                     # build cache size

docs.title: Where a setting comes from
docs.text:
• Priority, lowest to highest:
    1. $GOROOT/go.env → Go's defaults
    2. ~/.config/go/env → written by go env -w KEY=value
    3. environment variables (export GOBIN=...) → win over everything
  • go env KEY shows the final value, not where it came from
  • Value set but not in ~/.config/go/env → it's an environment variable → echo $KEY, then grep the shell startup files
go env -w GOBIN=$HOME/go/bin   # save a setting
go env -u GOBIN                # remove a saved setting
cat $(go env GOENV)            # saved settings

docs.title: Why GOPATH still exists
docs.text:
• Before Go 1.11 (2018) → all code had to live in ~/go/src → imports resolved only from there
  • Modules (default since Go 1.16) removed that rule → project root is wherever go.mod is
  • Today ~/go only holds installed tools and downloads → creating ~/go/src by hand is not needed

docs.title: Cleaning
docs.text:
go clean -cache        # wipe build cache (GOCACHE)
go clean -testcache    # forget cached test results
go clean -modcache     # wipe module cache, re-downloaded on next build
Symptom Cause Fix Tool installed with go install → command not found ~/go/bin not in PATH add $HOME/go/bin to PATH Stale or odd build behaviour corrupted build cache go clean -cache A downloaded library looks broken corrupted module cache go clean -modcache go test prints (cached) and didn't re-run nothing changed since last run go test -count=1 or go clean -testcache "Why is Go using this value?" env var overrides saved settings and defaults go env KEY, echo $KEY, cat $(go env GOENV)

Quick revision

  • GOROOT = Go itself | GOPATH (~/go) = tools + downloads, not your code
  • ~/go/bin = installed tools | ~/go/pkg/mod = libraries, named by URL@version
  • ~/.cache/go-build = build cache
  • defaults < go env -w < environment variables

Interview points

  • GOROOT vs GOPATH? → GOROOT is where Go is installed; GOPATH (default ~/go) holds installed binaries and the module cache
  • Does your code need to live in GOPATH? → no, since modules your project can be anywhere; go.mod marks the project root
  • Where does go install put binaries? → GOBIN, which defaults to $GOPATH/bin
  • What is the module cache? → $GOPATH/pkg/mod, read-only copies of downloaded modules stored by path and version
  • What is GOCACHE? → the build cache of compiled packages and test results that makes rebuilds fast
  • Setting precedence in Go? → environment variables override go env -w settings, which override the go.env defaults
  • How do you force tests to re-run? → go test -count=1 or go clean -testcache
  • Why are module names URLs? → the path tells Go where to fetch the code from

docs.title: What an install gives you
docs.text:
• Installing Go = one folder on disk → everything Go needs is inside it
  • That folder = GOROOT ("Go's root") → standard location on Linux → /usr/local/go
  • Inside it, three things that matter:
    • the go command → one program that builds, runs, tests, formats and downloads
    • the compiler and other tools that go calls internally
    • the standard library source code → fmt, os, net/http … as plain .go files
go version            # go version go1.27.4 linux/amd64 → version + OS/arch
go env GOROOT         # /usr/local/go
ls $(go env GOROOT)

docs.title: What's inside GOROOT
docs.text: Path Purpose bin/ go and gofmt → the only two commands called directly src/ standard library source (src/fmt, src/os, …) pkg/tool/<os>_<arch>/ internal tools go runs for you go.env Go's default settings VERSION version string api/, doc/, lib/, misc/, test/ Go's own internals, ignore

docs.title: The toolchain behind go
docs.text:
ls $(go env GOROOT)/pkg/tool/linux_amd64
# asm  cgo  compile  cover  fix  link  preprofile  vet
Tool Does compile turns .go files of one package into object code link joins all compiled packages into one binary asm assembles the few .s assembly files in the stdlib cgo lets Go call C code vet what go vet runs → finds suspicious code cover test coverage → go test -cover fix rewrites old code to newer APIs preprofile helper for profile-guided optimization
  • Never called directly → go build = compile each package, then link

docs.title: The standard library is just folders
docs.text:
ls $(go env GOROOT)/src/fmt
head -20 $(go env GOROOT)/src/fmt/print.go
  • src/fmt = a folder of .go files, every one starting with package fmt
  • Split across files only for organization → print.go, scan.go, format.go, errors.go
  • *_test.go → test files, run by go test, left out of normal builds
  • doc.go → holds only the package's documentation comment (common convention)
  • fmt itself imports io, os, strconv … → stdlib = packages built from other packages
  • fmt.Println works because Println starts with a capital letter → exported | lowercase names like commaSpaceString stay private to fmt

docs.title: How the shell finds go
docs.text:
• Typing go → shell checks folders listed in PATH, left to right, runs the first go found
  • Go's bin not in PATH → go: command not found even though Go is installed
  • Add to ~/.bashrc (tarball install):
export PATH=$PATH:/usr/local/go/bin:$HOME/go/bin

which go                       # which go actually runs
echo $PATH | tr ':' '\n'       # PATH one folder per line

docs.title: ~/.profile vs ~/.bashrc
docs.text:
• ~/.profile → runs once at login → everything opened afterwards inherits that PATH
  • ~/.bashrc → runs every time a terminal opens → appends on top of the inherited PATH
  • Same folder added in both, or added twice → duplicates in PATH → harmless (first match wins) but confusing
  • Changed ~/.profile → log out and back in to see it | changed ~/.bashrc → new terminal or source ~/.bashrc

docs.title: go.env: default settings
docs.text:
cat $(go env GOROOT)/go.env
  • GOPROXY=https://proxy.golang.org,direct → libraries are downloaded from Google's module mirror first, straight from the source repo (e.g. GitHub) if that fails
  • GOSUMDB=sum.golang.org → every downloaded library is checked against a public checksum database → tampered code is rejected
  • GOTOOLCHAIN=auto → if a project's go.mod asks for a newer Go than installed, Go downloads that version and uses it → build may use a different version than go version shows

docs.title: Duplicate installs
docs.text:
• Two Go installs on one machine (e.g. snap + /usr/local/go) → classic trap → editor, script or CI may pick the other one → different version, different stdlib, confusing errors
  • Keep exactly one install
  • Snap installs → auto-update in the background, GOROOT path changes on every update (/snap/go/<revision>)
  • Tarball in /usr/local/go → official method, matches docs, CI images and Dockerfiles
which go
ls /usr/local/go                     # exists? → second install
/usr/local/go/bin/go version
snap list go                         # installed via snap?
sudo snap remove go                  # remove the snap copy
hash -r                              # forget cached command locations
Symptom Cause Fix go: command not found after install Go's bin not in PATH add /usr/local/go/bin to PATH in ~/.bashrc go version shows an unexpected version another install earlier in PATH, or a snap auto-update which go, keep one install No such file or directory for a binary that was moved or removed bash cached the old location hash -r or open a new terminal Build uses a newer Go than go version GOTOOLCHAIN=auto + go.mod asking for newer expected; check the go line in go.mod

Quick revision

  • GOROOT = where Go is installed → tools + stdlib source
  • PATH decides which go runs → first match wins
  • go build = compile + link
  • One Go install per machine

Interview points

  • What is GOROOT? → the directory where Go itself is installed, holding the go command, compiler and linker, and the standard library source
  • What does go build actually run? → the compile tool for each package, then the link tool to produce one binary
  • How does the shell decide which go binary runs? → it searches the PATH directories in order and runs the first match; which go shows it
  • What is GOPROXY? → where Go downloads modules from; default is the proxy.golang.org mirror with direct as fallback
  • What does GOSUMDB do? → verifies downloaded modules against a public checksum database so tampered code is rejected
  • What does GOTOOLCHAIN=auto do? → downloads and uses a newer Go toolchain when a module's go.mod requires one
  • Why is having two Go installs a problem? → different tools can pick different versions, giving inconsistent builds and confusing errors
  • Why run hash -r? → bash caches command locations; after moving or removing a binary it clears that cache

docs.title: The for loop
docs.text:
• Go has one loop keyword → for → no while, no do-while
  • Every loop does three jobs → start once, check before each round, update after each round
sum := 0
for i := 0; i < 10; i++ {
    sum += i
}
fmt.Println(sum)   // 45 → 0+1+…+9
Part Go name Here Runs start init statement i := 0 once, before the first round check condition i < 10 before every round → false stops the loop update post statement i++ at the end of every round
  • No ( ) around the header → for (i := 0; i < 10; i++) is a syntax error
  • Braces { } are always required, even for one line
  • i declared in the init exists only inside the loop → using it after } → undefined: i
  • i++ is a statement, not an expression → x := i++ is an error, ++i doesn't exist

docs.title: Init and post are optional
docs.text:
sum := 1                // start → done before the loop
for ; sum < 1000; {     // only the check is left in the header
    sum += sum          // update → done inside the body
}
fmt.Println(sum)        // 1024
  • The jobs still happen, just outside the header → the ; mark the empty slots
  • The check runs before each round → the value can overshoot (1024, not 1000)
  • Nothing updates the checked variable → infinite loop

docs.title: for as while
docs.text:
sum := 1
for sum < 1000 {        // no semicolons → Go's "while"
    sum += sum
}
  • Only a condition left → drop the ; → gofmt does this for you
  • C/Java while (x < 5) = Bash while [ $x -lt 5 ] = Go for x < 5

docs.title: Forever
docs.text:
for {
    // runs until break, return or the program is killed
}
  • No condition → loops forever → the Go playground kills it with timeout running program, locally stop it with Ctrl+C
  • Used by programs meant to keep running → servers, agents polling every N seconds, Kubernetes controllers' reconcile loops (Bash → while true; do … done)
  • Exit from inside with break (leave the loop) or return (leave the function)
count := 0
for {
    count++
    if count == 3 {
        break
    }
}

docs.title: All forms side by side
docs.text:
for i := 0; i < 5; i++ { }   // start + check + update
for ; i < 5; { }             // check only, gofmt removes the ;
for i < 5 { }                // while
for { }                      // forever

docs.title: if
docs.text:
func sqrt(x float64) string {
    if x < 0 {
        return sqrt(-x) + "i"
    }
    return fmt.Sprint(math.Sqrt(x))
}

fmt.Println(sqrt(2), sqrt(-4))   // 1.4142135623730951 2i
  • Same rules as for → no ( ) around the condition, braces required
  • return inside the block leaves the function → the lines below don't run
  • sqrt calling itself → recursion → safe here because -x is positive, so it stops after one extra call
  • fmt.Sprint(v) → like Println but returns the text instead of printing it

docs.title: if with a short statement
docs.text:
func pow(x, n, lim float64) float64 {
    if v := math.Pow(x, n); v < lim {
        return v
    }
    return lim
}

fmt.Println(pow(3, 2, 10), pow(3, 3, 20))   // 9 20
  • v := math.Pow(x, n) runs once before the check → same idea as the init in for
  • v exists only inside the if (and its else) → return v on the last line → undefined: v
  • Declaring it on its own line also works → then v lives until the end of the function:
v := math.Pow(x, n)
if v < lim {
    return v
}
return v   // fine, v is still in scope
Declare the variable… when on its own line you need it after the if in the short statement you only need it for the check and inside the block → can't be misused later, name can be reused
  • The most common real use → error checks that keep err scoped to one if:
if err := step1(); err != nil { return err }
if err := step2(); err != nil { return err }   // a fresh err each time

docs.title: if and else
docs.text:
func pow(x, n, lim float64) float64 {
    if v := math.Pow(x, n); v < lim {
        return v
    } else {
        fmt.Printf("%g >= %g\n", v, lim)
    }
    // v doesn't exist here
    return lim
}

fmt.Println(pow(3, 2, 10), pow(3, 3, 20))
// 27 >= 20
// 9 20
  • Only one of the two blocks runs
  • Short-statement variables are visible in if and else, gone after the final }
  • } else { must be on one line → else on its own line is a syntax error
  • Output order → arguments are computed before the call starts → both pow calls finish (the second one prints 27 >= 20) before Println prints 9 20
  • %g → float in its shortest form → 27, not 27.000000

docs.title: switch
docs.text:
switch os := runtime.GOOS; os {
case "darwin":
    fmt.Println("macOS.")
case "linux":
    fmt.Println("Linux.")
default:
    fmt.Printf("%s.\n", os)
}
  • Shorter way to write a chain of if / else if on the same value
  • runtime.GOOS → the OS the program runs on → "linux", "darwin" (macOS), "windows"
  • Optional short statement before the value, same scope rule as if → os lives only inside the switch
  • default → runs when no case matches → like the final else (Bash → *))
  • Runs only the matching case → no break needed, no accidental fall-through like C/Java
  • Want fall-through on purpose → fallthrough keyword (rare)
  • Cases don't have to be constants or integers → strings, variables, function calls all work

docs.title: Evaluation order
docs.text:
func f() int {
    fmt.Println("f was called!")
    return 1
}

switch i {
case 0:
    fmt.Println("matched 0")
case f():
    fmt.Println("matched f")
}
  • Cases are checked top to bottom, the first match wins, the rest are never evaluated
  • To check case f(): Go must call f to know its value
i Output Why 0 matched 0 first case matches → f never called 1 f was called! → matched f f called to get 1 → 1 == 1 2 f was called! f called → 2 != 1 → nothing matches
  • Cases can be calculations, and the switch value can be a constant:
today := time.Now().Weekday()   // Sunday = 0 … Saturday = 6
switch time.Saturday {
case today + 0:
    fmt.Println("Today.")
case today + 1:
    fmt.Println("Tomorrow.")
case today + 2:
    fmt.Println("In two days.")
default:
    fmt.Println("Too far away.")
}
  • The Go playground's clock is fixed at 2009-11-10 23:00:00 UTC → Go's public release date → a Tuesday → prints Too far away.

docs.title: switch with no condition
docs.text:
t := time.Now()
switch {
case t.Hour() < 12:
    fmt.Println("Good morning!")
case t.Hour() < 17:
    fmt.Println("Good afternoon.")
default:
    fmt.Println("Good evening.")
}
  • Nothing after switch = switch true → each case is its own true/false check → first true case runs
  • Clean replacement for long if / else if / else chains
  • Order matters → at 9 AM both < 12 and < 17 are true → first one wins → most specific check goes first
  • < 17 doesn't need "and ≥ 12" → earlier cases already caught smaller values

docs.title: Exercise: square root with a loop
docs.text:
• Find √x without math.Sqrt → guess, measure how wrong, improve, repeat
  • Improve step (Newton's method) → z -= (z*z - x) / (2*z)
    • z*z - x → how far the guess is from the target
    • / (2*z) → scales the correction to how fast z*z changes
  • Same thing in plain terms → z = (z + x/z) / 2 → if z is too big, x/z is too small → the answer is between them → take the average
Round z x / z New z (x = 25) 1 1 25 13 2 13 1.92 7.46 3 7.46 3.35 5.41 4 5.41 4.62 5.015 5 5.015 4.985 5.00002 
func Sqrt(x float64) float64 {
    z := 1.0                     // 1.0, not 1 → z must be float64
    for i := 0; i < 10; i++ {
        z -= (z*z - x) / (2 * z)
        fmt.Println(z)
    }
    return z
}
  • Stop when the guess stops changing instead of a fixed 10 rounds:
func Sqrt(x float64) float64 {
    z := 1.0
    for {
        next := z - (z*z-x)/(2*z)
        if math.Abs(next-z) < 1e-10 {
            return next
        }
        z = next
    }
}
  • math.Abs → distance without the sign | 1e-10 → 0.0000000001
  • Converges in a handful of rounds → result matches math.Sqrt to many decimal places
  • Pattern worth knowing → loop that improves a value until it's good enough → same shape as retry loops and reconcile loops
Symptom Cause Fix syntax error: unexpected :=, expected ) C-style header for (i := 0; …) remove the ( ) syntax error: unexpected name fmt, expected { if x < 2 fmt.Println() → missing braces always use { } undefined: i after a loop i lives only inside the for declare it before the loop if needed after undefined: v after an if short-statement variable is scoped to if/else declare it on its own line syntax error: unexpected keyword else, expected } else on a new line after } write } else { timeout running program / program never ends condition never becomes false, or for { } without break make sure the body changes what the check reads missing return a path through the function returns nothing return on every path Wrong switch case runs a broader case sits above a narrower one put the most specific case first Side effect in a case runs unexpectedly Go evaluated that case while searching earlier cases didn't match → it had to be checked Printf output runs into the next line no \n end the format with \n

Quick revision

  • for is the only loop → full form, for cond {} (while), for {} (forever)
  • No ( ) around for/if/switch headers, { } always required
  • Short statement if v := f(); v < x {} → v lives in if + else only
  • } else { on one line
  • switch runs only the matching case, no break needed, cases can be any expression
  • Cases checked top to bottom, stops at first match, later cases never evaluated
  • switch {} with no value → each case is a condition → cleaner if-else chain

Interview points

  • How many loop keywords does Go have? → one, for; while and infinite loops are written with for
  • How do you write a while loop in Go? → for condition { }
  • Where is a variable declared in a for init statement visible? → only inside that for statement
  • What is an if short statement? → a statement before the condition, like if v := f(); v < 10, whose variables exist only in the if and its else
  • Why use the if short statement for err? → it keeps err scoped to one check so it can't leak or clash with later errors
  • How does Go's switch differ from C's? → only the matching case runs with no break needed, and cases need not be constants or integers
  • What does fallthrough do? → forces execution to continue into the next case
  • In what order are switch cases evaluated? → top to bottom, stopping at the first match; later cases are not evaluated
  • What is a switch with no condition? → the same as switch true; each case is a boolean expression, used to replace long if-else chains
  • Are function arguments evaluated before the call? → yes, all arguments are fully computed before the function body runs

docs.title: The two levels
docs.text:
• Module = one project → marked by a go.mod file at its root
  • Package = one folder of .go files inside that project
  • One module, many packages
demo/                  ← module (the project)
├── go.mod             ← once, at the top
├── main.go            ← package main
└── wow/
    └── nice/
        ├── nice.go    ← package nice
        └── extra.go   ← package nice (same folder → same package)

docs.title: Module: go mod init
docs.text:
mkdir demo && cd demo
go mod init demo
cat go.mod

module demo

go 1.27
  • go mod init only creates one text file, go.mod
  • module demo → the project's name, also the prefix for importing its packages
  • go 1.27 → Go version the code is written for → the toolchain uses it to pick language behaviour (e.g. Go 1.22 changed how for loop variables work), not just a label
  • Without go.mod → go build, go test, go run . refuse:
go: go.mod file not found in current directory or any parent directory
  • Analogy → git init marks a folder as a repo | go mod init marks a folder as a Go project | npm init → package.json
  • Later, libraries you use get listed in go.mod with exact versions, plus a go.sum file with their checksums → same versions for everyone who clones the repo

docs.title: Naming the module
docs.text:
• Practice → any short name (hello, demo)
  • Real project → the repo URL → go mod init github.com/<user>/<repo> → others can go get it

docs.title: One go.mod covers every subfolder
docs.text:
• Go looks upward from the current folder until it finds go.mod → nested folders belong to that module automatically
  • Don't run go mod init in subfolders of a project
  • Don't nest one project inside another (module inside module) → editor tooling (gopls) gets confused → keep separate projects side by side:
~/learn-go/
├── hello-world/   ← own go.mod
├── integers/      ← own go.mod
└── iteration/     ← own go.mod

docs.title: Package: one folder
docs.text:
• Every .go file starts with package <name> → says which group it belongs to
  • Every file in one folder → same package name, otherwise compile error:
found packages nice (nice.go) and other (extra.go)
  • Convention → package name = folder name (math/rand/ → package rand)
  • Files in the same package see each other's code directly, no import needed, even lowercase names → Go treats the folder as one combined unit

docs.title: package main vs library
docs.text:
package main + func main() any other name (package greet) What it is runnable program library go run . runs package demo/greet is not a main package How it's used it is the program imported by main, or checked with go test
  • Program starts at func main() inside package main → both must be named exactly main
  • A library runs only when something imports and calls it

docs.title: One main per folder
docs.text:
• All files in a folder = one package → two func main() in one folder:
main redeclared in this block
  • More than one program → more than one folder, usually under cmd/:
demo/
├── go.mod
├── cmd/
│   ├── server/main.go   ← program 1
│   └── cli/main.go      ← program 2
└── greet/greet.go       ← shared library

go run ./cmd/server
go run ./cmd/cli
  • Same layout as Kubernetes → cmd/kubectl, cmd/kubelet … each package main, real logic in library packages

docs.title: Importing your own package
docs.text:
// greet/greet.go
package greet

func Hello() string {
    return "hello from greet"
}

// main.go
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "demo/greet"
)

func main() {
    fmt.Println(greet.Hello())
}
  • Import path = module name (from go.mod) + folder path → "demo/greet"
  • Call as <package name>.<Name> → greet.Hello()
  • Standard library → short paths ("fmt", "os") | your own or downloaded → full path

docs.title: Exported names
docs.text:
• Capital first letter → exported, usable from other packages → Hello, fmt.Println, math.Pi
  • Lowercase → private to its own package → greet.hello() from main is an error
  • No public / private keywords → capitalization is the whole system
Symptom Cause Fix go.mod file not found not inside a module go mod init <name> at the project root is not a main package go run on a library folder run the folder with package main, or test it with go test found packages a and b files in one folder declare different packages same package line in every file of a folder main redeclared in this block two func main() in one folder one program per folder, use cmd/<name>/ undefined: greet.hello / not exported lowercase name used from another package capitalize it → Hello Strange editor errors in nested projects module inside another module keep projects side by side

Quick revision

  • 1 project = 1 go.mod at the top
  • 1 folder = 1 package, every file says the same package name
  • 1 runnable folder = package main + 1 func main()
  • Import path = module name + folder | Capital = exported

Interview points

  • Module vs package in Go? → a module is a versioned project defined by go.mod; a package is one directory of .go files inside it
  • What does go mod init do? → creates go.mod with the module path and the Go version, marking the directory as a module root
  • What is go.sum for? → it records checksums of dependency versions so builds verify they get exactly the same code
  • How does Go find the module for a nested folder? → it walks up the directory tree to the nearest go.mod
  • What makes a Go program executable? → a package named main with a func main, the entry point
  • Can one directory hold two main functions? → no, a directory is one package; separate programs go in separate directories such as cmd/
  • How is an import path for your own package formed? → module path from go.mod plus the package's directory path
  • How does Go control visibility? → identifiers starting with a capital letter are exported, lowercase ones are package-private
  • Why do real module paths look like URLs? → so go get can locate and download the code, e.g. github.com/user/repo

docs.title: Declaring variables with var
docs.text:
var c, python, java bool   // package level → visible to every function in the package

func main() {
    var i int              // function level → only inside main
    fmt.Println(i, c, python, java)   // 0 false false false
}
  • var name type → type after the name, one type covers the whole list
  • Group several declarations in a block, like grouped imports:
var (
    ToBe   bool   = false
    MaxInt uint64 = 1<<64 - 1
)
  • Unused local variable → compile error declared and not used: z
  • Unused package-level variable → allowed

docs.title: Zero values
docs.text:
• A variable declared without a value gets its type's zero value → never garbage, never "undefined"
Type Zero value int, float64 0 bool false string "" → a string with no characters pointers, slices, maps, errors nil → "points to nothing" 
var s string
fmt.Println(len(s))          // 0
fmt.Printf("%q\n", s)        // ""
fmt.Println(1, s, s, s)      // "1   " → empty strings print as nothing, only the spaces remain
  • Empty strings are invisible with Println / %v → use %q to see them
  • if err != nil works because an error that was never set is nil

docs.title: Initializers and type inference
docs.text:
var i, j int = 1, 2                           // type given → values must match it
var c, python, java = true, 4.359, "no!"      // no type → Go infers bool, float64, string
  • Values are matched by position → count must match the names
  • Need at least a type or a value → var x alone is a syntax error
  • When the type is left out, Go takes it from the right side:
    • another variable → same type as that variable → var i int; j := i → j is int
    • a literal → from how it looks
Literal Inferred type 42 int 42.0, 3.142 float64 → the dot alone makes it a float "42" string → quotes make it text, even if it's digits true bool 0.5i complex128

docs.title: Short declaration :=
docs.text:
k := 3                                    // same as var k = 3
c, python, java := true, false, "no!"
got := Hello()                            // the line from the first test
  • := → create + assign + infer the type, in one step
  • Only inside functions → at package level it's syntax error: non-declaration statement outside function body → use var
  • := creates, = changes:
k := 3     // create
k = 5      // change an existing variable
k := 7     // ❌ no new variables on left side of :=
  • With several names, at least one must be new → b, err := g() after a, err := f() reuses err
  • Style → := inside functions by default | var x int when you mean "start at the zero value"

docs.title: Basic types
docs.text:
Use for Type whole numbers int → default choice decimals float64 → default choice text string true/false bool one raw byte (files, network data) byte = alias for uint8 one character (Unicode code point) rune = alias for int32
  • Sized variants exist for when a size is required (file formats, protocols): int8…int64, uint, uint8…uint64, uintptr, float32, complex64, complex128
  • Number = bits → int64 holds 64 bits | u = unsigned → no negatives
  • 1<<64 - 1 → 2⁶⁴ − 1 = 18446744073709551615 → the largest uint64
  • int, uint, uintptr → 64 bits on 64-bit systems, 32 bits on 32-bit systems
  • Strings are UTF-8 → "世界" works as-is

docs.title: Integer division
docs.text:
17 * 4 / 9   // 7, not 7.55
42 / 5       // 8, not 8.4
  • int ÷ int → int → the decimal part is dropped (truncated toward zero, not rounded)
  • Need decimals → make one side a float → 42.0 / 5 → 8.4

docs.title: Type conversions
docs.text:
• Go never converts types automatically → you write Type(value)
var x, y int = 3, 4
var f float64 = math.Sqrt(float64(x*x + y*y))   // Sqrt only accepts float64
var z uint = uint(f)
fmt.Println(x, y, z)                            // 3 4 5
  • Read nested calls inside-out → x*x + y*y = 25 (int) → float64(25) → Sqrt → 5
  • Conversion makes a new value of the new type → the original variable keeps its type
  • Mixing types in maths is an error → a + b with int and float64 → float64(a) + b
  • float variable → int truncates toward zero → f := 7.9 → int(f) = 7, int(-f) = -7
  • float constant → int that loses the fraction is a compile error → int(7.9) → cannot convert 7.9 (untyped float constant) to type int
  • Number → text is not string(n) → string(rune(65)) is "A" (a character code) → use strconv:
strconv.Itoa(65)       // "65"
n, err := strconv.Atoi("65")   // 65, nil → returns (value, error)
  • Env vars and flags always arrive as strings → strconv.Atoi for ports, replica counts, timeouts

docs.title: Constants
docs.text:
const Pi = 3.14

func main() {
    const World = "世界"
    const Truth = true
    fmt.Println("Hello", World)   // Hello 世界
}
  • const → value fixed at compile time, can never change → Pi = 3.15 → cannot assign to Pi
  • Allowed kinds → character, string, boolean, numeric
  • Package or function level, like var
  • No := → const Pi := 3.14 → syntax error: unexpected :=, expected =
  • Use for values that must not change → prefixes, default ports, fixed messages → a named constant reads better than a bare literal:
const englishHelloPrefix = "Hello, "

func Hello(name string) string {
    return englishHelloPrefix + name
}

docs.title: Untyped numeric constants
docs.text:
const (
    Big   = 1 << 100   // 1 followed by 100 binary zeros (~1.27e30)
    Small = Big >> 99  // 2
)

func needInt(x int) int           { return x*10 + 1 }
func needFloat(x float64) float64 { return x * 0.1 }

fmt.Println(needInt(Small))    // 21
fmt.Println(needFloat(Small))  // 0.2
fmt.Println(needFloat(Big))    // 1.2676506002282295e+29
fmt.Println(needInt(Big))      // ❌ overflows int
  • A constant without a type has no fixed type yet → it takes the type its context needs
  • Same Small goes into an int function and a float64 function with no conversion → a typed variable couldn't do that
  • Constants are kept at high precision → only checked when used
  • Value doesn't fit the type it's used as → compile error instead of a silently wrong number
  • e+29 → scientific notation → ×10²⁹
