Symptom Cause Fix declared and not used: z local variable never used use it, delete it, or assign to _ no new variables on left side of := := on a name that already exists use = to change it syntax error: non-declaration statement outside function body := at package level var k = 3 syntax error: unexpected semicolon, expected type var x with no type and no value give a type or a value cannot use x (variable of type int) as float64 value in argument to math.Sqrt no automatic conversion math.Sqrt(float64(x)) invalid operation: a + b (mismatched types int and float64) maths across types convert one side cannot convert 7.9 (untyped float constant) to type int constant would lose its fraction convert a variable, or use math.Floor / math.Round first cannot assign to Pi changing a constant use var if it must change syntax error: unexpected :=, expected = const x := ... const x = ... cannot use Big (untyped int constant ...) as int value ... (overflows) constant too large for the type use a bigger type such as float64 Output shows nothing where a string should be empty string "" print with %q string(65) gives "A" converts a code point, not digits strconv.Itoa(65) Division result is missing its decimals int / int make one operand a float

Quick revision

  • var x int → zero value | var x = 5 → inferred | x := 5 → inside functions only
  • Zero values: 0, false, "", nil
  • := creates, = changes
  • Default types: int, float64, string, bool
  • No automatic conversion → float64(x) | text ↔ number → strconv
  • int / int drops the decimals
  • const never changes, no := | untyped constants adapt to their context

Interview points

  • What is a zero value in Go? → the value a variable gets when declared without one: 0, false, "" or nil depending on the type
  • Why does Go have zero values instead of undefined? → every variable always holds a valid, predictable value, so there is no uninitialized memory to read
  • var vs := ? → := declares and infers inside functions only; var works everywhere and can declare without a value
  • When does := fail on an existing name? → when no variable on the left side is new
  • How does type inference work for literals? → 42 becomes int, 4.2 float64, "x" string, true bool
  • Does Go convert int to float64 automatically? → no, conversions are always explicit with T(v)
  • What happens when converting a float variable to int? → the fraction is truncated toward zero
  • Why is string(65) not "65"? → it converts the number to the character with that code point; use strconv.Itoa for decimal text
  • What is an untyped constant? → a constant with no fixed type that takes the type required where it is used, kept at high precision until then
  • Can a constant be declared with := ? → no, constants use const name = value
  • What are byte and rune? → aliases for uint8 and int32, used for raw bytes and Unicode characters

docs.title: In one line
docs.text:
• Go → an open-source, compiled, statically typed, garbage-collected language built at Google for large networked server software
  • Goals → fast to compile, fast to run, simple to read, easy concurrency
  • Name → Go | "golang" → search-friendly name, from the old site golang.org (now go.dev) | mascot → the gopher

docs.title: The problem it was built to solve
docs.text:
In 2007 Google's engineers were hitting the same walls every day:

Problem What it looked like Go's answer Slow builds large C++ programs took a very long time to compile → engineers waiting on builds compiles in seconds → simple dependency model, no header files, unused imports are errors Complex languages C++ and Java had grown huge → many ways to do one thing → hard to read someone else's code small language → 25 keywords, one loop, one official format (gofmt) Many cores, everything networked threads in older languages were heavy and error-prone goroutines and channels built into the language Huge teams, huge codebases code had to be readable by thousands of engineers explicit code, no hidden magic, strict tooling Dependency hell in deployment programs needed the right runtime and libraries on every server one self-contained binary
  • Core idea → keep the speed and safety of a compiled language with the ease of a scripting language

docs.title: History
docs.text: When Event Sep 2007 Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike and Ken Thompson start sketching Go at Google Nov 10, 2009 Go is announced publicly and open-sourced → the Go playground's clock is frozen at 2009-11-10 23:00 UTC for this reason Mar 2012 Go 1.0 → comes with the Go 1 compatibility promise → code written for Go 1 keeps compiling on later Go 1.x releases 2013 Docker is released, written in Go 2014 Kubernetes is released, written in Go → Go becomes the language of cloud infrastructure 2015 Go 1.5 → the compiler is rewritten in Go itself (no more C) → GC pauses drastically reduced 2018 Go 1.11 → modules (go.mod) introduced → replaces the old GOPATH-only workflow 2021 Go 1.16 → modules on by default Mar 2022 Go 1.18 → generics added → the biggest language change since 1.0 Ongoing A new release every ~6 months (February and August)

docs.title: The designers
docs.text:
• Ken Thompson → co-created Unix and the B language (C's predecessor) → co-designed UTF-8
  • Rob Pike → Unix team at Bell Labs, Plan 9 → co-designed UTF-8 with Ken Thompson
  • Robert Griesemer → worked on Google's V8 JavaScript engine and Java's HotSpot VM
  • This is why Go feels like "C, cleaned up" → familiar syntax, minus the dangerous and complicated parts

docs.title: What kind of language Go is
docs.text: Property Meaning Why it matters Compiled go build turns source into native machine code no interpreter at runtime → fast startup, fast execution Statically typed every value has a type fixed at compile time type mistakes are caught by the compiler, not in production Garbage collected the runtime frees unused memory automatically no manual malloc/free → no use-after-free or double-free bugs like C Memory safe (mostly) bounds-checked arrays and slices, no pointer arithmetic out-of-range access stops the program instead of corrupting memory Single binary the Go runtime is bundled into the program copy one file to a server and run it → no Go, no runtime, no pip install Cross-compiling GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go build build for any OS/CPU from your laptop Concurrency built in go f() starts a goroutine thousands of concurrent tasks are cheap Opinionated tooling go fmt, go vet, go test, go mod ship with Go every Go project is formatted, built and tested the same way Batteries-included stdlib HTTP, JSON, crypto, TLS, files, testing a production web server needs zero third-party packages

docs.title: Compiled vs interpreted
docs.text:
Python:  source.py ──► python interpreter reads it line by line at runtime
Go:      main.go  ──► go build ──► ./app (machine code) ──► CPU runs it directly
  • Interpreted → needs the interpreter installed everywhere, slower, errors only show when that line runs
  • Compiled → one build step up front → runs anywhere with the same OS/CPU, errors caught before running

docs.title: The single static binary
docs.text:
go build -o app .
ls -lh app          # one file, a few MB
scp app server:/usr/local/bin/
ssh server app      # runs, Go not installed on the server
  • Pure Go programs are linked statically → no external .so libraries needed
  • CGO_ENABLED=0 go build → guarantees no C dependencies → the usual setting for container images
  • Result → tiny Docker images → FROM scratch or distroless + one binary

docs.title: Concurrency in one look
docs.text:
go fetch("https://a.com")   // runs at the same time
go fetch("https://b.com")   // runs at the same time
  • Goroutine → a function running concurrently, managed by the Go runtime → starts with a stack of a few KB → you can run thousands
  • Channel → a pipe for goroutines to send data to each other safely
  • Motto → "Don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating."
  • OS threads cost far more memory and setup → the Go scheduler multiplexes many goroutines onto a few OS threads

docs.title: Go compared with other languages
docs.text:
Python Java C / C++ Go Execution interpreted bytecode on JVM native native Speed slow fast (after JVM warm-up) fastest fast Typing dynamic → checked at runtime static static static Memory GC GC manual GC Startup time medium slow (JVM) instant instant Deploy needs Python + packages a JVM binary + shared libs one binary Compile time none medium slow very fast Concurrency limited by the GIL threads threads goroutines + channels Language size small large very large small
  • vs Python → Go is much faster, typed, ships as one file → Python is quicker for small scripts and data work
  • vs Java → no JVM, no classes, far less boilerplate, instant startup
  • vs C/C++ → memory safe, garbage collected, much simpler, faster to compile → slightly slower, less low-level control
  • vs Rust → Go is simpler and faster to learn, uses a GC → Rust has no GC and stricter safety guarantees, but a much steeper learning curve

docs.title: What Go deliberately leaves out
docs.text:
Missing What Go uses instead Classes and inheritance structs + methods + interfaces (composition) Exceptions (try/catch) functions return an error → if err != nil { … } while, do-while for in all its forms Ternary x ? a : b a normal if / else Function overloading different function names Implicit type conversion explicit float64(x) Unused imports/variables compile error → keeps code clean Many code styles one style enforced by gofmt
  • Trade-off → more lines in places, but any Go code is readable by any Go developer
  • Go proverb → "Clear is better than clever."

docs.title: The 25 keywords
docs.text:
break     default      func    interface  select
case      defer        go      map        struct
chan      else         goto    package    switch
const     fallthrough  if      range      type
continue  for          import  return     var
  • Java has 50+ and C++ 90+ → the whole language fits in your head

docs.title: Where Go is used
docs.text: Area Written in Go Containers Docker, containerd, runc, Podman, Buildah Kubernetes kube-apiserver, kubelet, kube-scheduler, kubectl, etcd, CoreDNS, Helm, kind, k3s Infrastructure as Code Terraform and its providers, Pulumi's engine, OpenTofu Observability Prometheus, Grafana backend, Loki, Tempo, Jaeger, Thanos Service mesh & networking Istio control plane, Linkerd control plane, Traefik, Caddy, Cilium (control plane) Security & secrets Vault, Consul, Trivy, cosign CI/CD & GitOps Argo CD, Flux, Drone, Tekton CLIs & dev tools GitHub CLI (gh), Hugo, k9s, lazygit Companies Google, Uber, Cloudflare, Twitch, Dropbox, Monzo

docs.title: Why Go won cloud infrastructure
docs.text:
• Infra tools must run on thousands of machines → single binary = no install headaches
  • They talk over the network all day → stdlib HTTP/gRPC + goroutines
  • They must be fast and use little memory → compiled, small footprint
  • Many contributors across companies → simple, uniform code is easy to review
  • Kubernetes chose Go → the whole cloud-native ecosystem (operators, controllers, CRDs, client libraries) followed

docs.title: Why Go matters for DevOps / SRE
docs.text:
• Read the source of Kubernetes, Docker or Terraform when the docs don't explain a behaviour
  • Write Kubernetes operators and controllers → client-go, controller-runtime, Kubebuilder
  • Write Terraform providers and Prometheus exporters
  • Build internal CLI tools → ship one binary to the whole team
  • Replace fragile long Bash scripts with typed, tested programs

docs.title: Where Go is not the best fit
docs.text:
• Quick one-off scripts and text munging → Bash or Python are faster to write
  • Data science and ML → Python's ecosystem dominates
  • Hard real-time or kernel-level code → C or Rust (no GC pauses)
  • Desktop GUIs and mobile apps → other languages have far better tooling
Myth Reality "Go is Google's internal language" open source, governed in the open, used everywhere "GC makes Go slow" GC pauses are typically well under a millisecond → fine for servers "No generics" generics since Go 1.18 (2022) "Go is only for web servers" CLIs, infra tools, networking, databases (CockroachDB), operators "Go and golang are different" same language → "golang" is just the searchable name

Quick revision

  • Go → compiled, statically typed, garbage collected, built at Google (2007), public 2009, Go 1.0 in 2012
  • Created by Griesemer, Pike, Thompson → to fix slow builds, complexity and poor concurrency
  • Ships as one static binary → no runtime needed on the server
  • Goroutines + channels → cheap built-in concurrency
  • 25 keywords, no classes, no exceptions, no while → errors are values
  • Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, Prometheus, etcd, Helm are all written in Go

Interview points

  • Who created Go and when? → Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike and Ken Thompson at Google, started in 2007, open-sourced in 2009, Go 1.0 in 2012
  • Why was Go created? → slow C++ builds, overly complex languages, and the need for easy concurrency on multicore networked servers at Google scale
  • Is Go compiled or interpreted? → compiled to native machine code
  • Why is Go popular for DevOps and cloud tools? → single static binaries, fast startup, low memory use, strong networking stdlib and built-in concurrency
  • Why does a Go binary run on a server without Go installed? → the runtime and dependencies are linked into the binary
  • What is a goroutine? → a lightweight function running concurrently, managed by the Go runtime rather than the OS, with a small growable stack
  • What is the Go 1 compatibility promise? → programs written for Go 1 continue to compile and run on later Go 1.x releases
  • How does Go handle errors without exceptions? → functions return an error value that the caller checks with if err != nil
  • Does Go support object-oriented programming? → partly: structs with methods and interfaces, but no classes or inheritance; it favours composition
  • When were generics added to Go? → Go 1.18, in 2022
  • Name tools written in Go → Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, Prometheus, etcd, Helm, Vault
  • Go vs Python for infra tooling? → Go is faster, typed and ships as one binary; Python is quicker for small scripts and data work

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text:
Notes on Kubernetes, written while working through the CKA course on a local kind cluster. They start with why Kubernetes exists and how a cluster is built, then the YAML and objects everything is written in, how a real app is split into tiers and microservices, and how Services connect them (and how to debug them when they don't), the imperative commands used to generate manifests and test from inside the cluster, how namespaces split one cluster, and how Pods are placed on nodes (manual scheduling, static Pods, taints and tolerations), then go one layer deeper each chapter: what really happens on kubectl apply, how a Pod becomes a Linux process, how etcd stays consistent, and how access control and extensions work.

  1. Why Kubernetes Docker's limits, desired state and reconciliation, Kubernetes vs Swarm, Compose, ECS
  2. Architecture Control plane, worker nodes, API server, scheduler, controllers, kubelet, CRI/CNI/CSI
  3. YAML, Manifests & Objects Imperative vs declarative, YAML types, spec vs status, apiVersion and API groups
  4. Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments Nodes vs Pods, selectors, RC vs RS, rolling updates, change-cause, rollbacks
  5. kind, kubeconfig & Contexts Local clusters, pinned node images, ~/.kube/config, use-context vs set-context
  6. Three-Tier & Microservices Monolith vs three-tier vs microservices, middleware, where databases run, StatefulSets
  7. Services ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, ExternalName, port vs targetPort vs nodePort, DNS and iptables step by step
  8. Debugging Services & DNS Debugging method, checklist, CoreDNS not Ready, kube-proxy CrashLoopBackOff, wrong targetPort
  9. Imperative Commands --dry-run, generating Deployments and Services, containerPort, fixed nodePort, labels, test Pods, Pod DNS
  10. Namespaces Built-ins, namespaced vs cluster-scoped, -n/-A, cross-namespace DNS, not isolation, default namespace, quotas
  11. Manual Scheduling & Static Pods nodeName, bypassing taints, the control plane as a node, static Pods, mirror Pods
  12. Taints & Tolerations Effects, Equal vs Exists, tolerationSeconds, filter vs score, dedicated nodes, Pending debugging
  13. From kubectl apply to Running Pod Each component's step, watching events, Pending vs CrashLoopBackOff
  14. Container Runtime Internals Namespaces, cgroups, requests vs limits, containerd, runc, dockershim
  15. etcd & Raft Key-value store, WAL, Secrets are base64, leader election, quorum
  16. REST, gRPC & Protobuf How components talk, .proto files, where Kubernetes uses each
  17. RBAC & Request Flow Authentication, authorization, Roles and bindings, kubectl auth can-i
  18. Webhooks, CRDs & Operators Mutating vs validating admission, custom resources, controllers

docs.title: The big picture
docs.text:
• A Kubernetes cluster = a group of machines (nodes) working as one
  • Two kinds of nodes:
    • Control plane → the brain → decides what runs, where, and what is allowed
    • Worker nodes → the muscles → actually run my app containers
  • Every node runs Linux, containerd and the kubelet | only the control plane runs the "brain" components
                       ┌──────────────── CONTROL PLANE ────────────────┐
  kubectl ───────────▶ │  kube-apiserver ◀──▶ etcd                     │
                       │       ▲   ▲   ▲                               │
                       │       │   │   └── kube-controller-manager     │
                       │       │   └────── kube-scheduler              │
                       │       └────────── cloud-controller-manager    │
                       └───────┬───────────────────────────────────────┘
                               │ (everything talks to the API server)
          ┌────────────────────┴────────────────────┐
  ┌───────▼──────── WORKER NODE 1 ──┐     ┌──────────▼──── WORKER NODE 2 ──┐
  │ kubelet      kube-proxy         │     │ kubelet      kube-proxy        │
  │ containerd → runc               │     │ containerd → runc              │
  │ [ pod ] [ pod ] [ pod ]         │     │ [ pod ] [ pod ]                │
  │ CNI (network)  CSI (storage)    │     │ CNI (network)  CSI (storage)   │
  └─────────────────────────────────┘     └────────────────────────────────┘
  • Golden rule → every component talks only to the API server, never directly to each other or to etcd (except the API server itself)

docs.title: Control plane
docs.text:
• The brain of Kubernetes → stores state, validates changes, assigns work to nodes, keeps everything in sync
  • Four core components + one optional

docs.title: kube-apiserver (the front door)
docs.text:
• Entry point for every request → kubectl, controllers, scheduler, kubelets all go through it
  • For every request it does, in order:
    1. Authentication → who are you? (certificate, token, OIDC)
    2. Authorization → are you allowed? (RBAC) → see RBAC & Request Flow
    3. Admission control → modify (mutating) or approve/reject (validating) the object → see Webhooks, CRDs & Operators
    4. Schema validation → is the object well-formed?
    5. Save to etcd
  • Lets others watch for changes → when something changes, the scheduler, controllers and kubelets get notified
  • Does not run containers or schedule anything → it receives, checks, secures, saves and broadcasts
  • Only component that talks to etcd
  • Analogy → reception desk + security guard + notice board of a building

docs.title: etcd (the database)
docs.text:
• Distributed key-value store → holds the entire cluster state (every Deployment, Pod, Secret, ConfigMap)
  • Desired state lives here → lose etcd without a backup = lose the cluster
  • Usually run as 3 or 5 copies kept in sync by the Raft algorithm → see etcd & Raft

docs.title: kube-scheduler (the matchmaker)
docs.text:
• Watches for new Pods that have no node yet (nodeName empty)
  • Picks the best node based on → free CPU/RAM, node labels, affinity rules, taints and tolerations
  • Writes its choice (nodeName) into the Pod object through the API server
  • Does not start the Pod → the kubelet on that node does
  • Three stages:
    • Queue → Pods wait in a queue, sorted by priority (QueueSort); PreEnqueue checks a Pod is ready to be considered
    • Scheduling cycle → PreFilter (basic checks) → Filter (remove nodes that can't run it: not enough resources, wrong labels, blocking taints) → Score (rank the remaining nodes: balance, spreading, affinity) → NormalizeScore → Reserve (hold the spot so no other Pod takes it) → Permit (can wait for outside approval, e.g. gang scheduling)
    • Binding cycle → PreBind (last checks, e.g. volumes ready) → Bind (write nodeName to the Pod) → PostBind (cleanup, metrics)
  • Analogy → hotel receptionist: filters out full rooms, ranks the rest, reserves one, hands over the key

docs.title: kube-controller-manager (the robots)
docs.text:
• One process running many small controllers → each watches one kind of object and fixes differences
  • This is where reconciliation happens
Controller What it keeps true Deployment controller Right ReplicaSet exists for each version ReplicaSet controller Right number of Pods running Node controller Notices dead nodes, evicts their Pods DaemonSet controller One Pod on every node Job / CronJob controller Jobs run to completion / on schedule Namespace controller Deleting a namespace cleans up everything inside it EndpointSlice controller Service knows the IPs of its healthy Pods
  • Operators add custom controllers on top (cert-manager, Argo CD, Prometheus Operator)

docs.title: cloud-controller-manager (optional)
docs.text:
• Connects Kubernetes to a cloud provider's API
  • Creates a cloud load balancer for Service type=LoadBalancer, attaches cloud routes, notices deleted cloud VMs
  • Present on managed clusters (EKS, GKE, AKS) | not present on kind or bare-metal clusters

docs.title: Worker nodes
docs.text:
• The machines that run my containers
  • Receive instructions from the control plane (via the API server) → start Pods, attach volumes, set up networking, check health, report status back

docs.title: kubelet (the node's manager)
docs.text:
• Agent on every node → watches the API server for Pods assigned to its node
  • For each Pod → asks the container runtime to pull images and start containers → calls CNI for networking → calls CSI for volumes
  • Runs probes (liveness, readiness, startup) → restarts crashed containers
  • Reports Pod and node status back to the API server
  • Does not decide where Pods run (scheduler's job) → only makes sure assigned Pods run correctly
  • Only Kubernetes component that is a normal systemd service, not a Pod

docs.title: kube-proxy (Service networking)
docs.text:
• Runs on every node → makes Services work
  • When a Service is created → programs iptables / IPVS / nftables rules on the node → traffic to the Service IP is load-balanced across the Service's ready Pods
  • Pod behind a Service dies or is replaced → kube-proxy updates the rules
  • It does not give Pods their IPs → that is CNI's job
  • Some CNIs (e.g. Cilium) can replace kube-proxy completely with eBPF

docs.title: Container runtime
docs.text:
• Software that actually runs containers → containerd or CRI-O
  • containerd pulls images and manages containers → calls runc to create each one → see Container Runtime Internals
  • Docker itself is no longer a node runtime (removed in Kubernetes 1.24)

docs.title: The three plug-in interfaces
docs.text:
• Kubernetes does not run containers, network Pods or create disks by itself → it defines standard interfaces and plugins do the work
Interface Full name Job Examples CRI Container Runtime Interface How the kubelet tells a runtime to pull images and start/stop containers (gRPC) containerd, CRI-O CNI Container Network Interface Gives each Pod an IP, connects Pods across nodes, enforces network policies Calico, Cilium, Flannel, kindnet CSI Container Storage Interface Creates, attaches and mounts volumes from storage systems AWS EBS, GCP PD, Azure Disk, Ceph, Longhorn
  • Why interfaces → swap the plugin without changing Kubernetes itself

docs.title: Control plane vs data plane
docs.text: Control plane Data plane (workers) Job Manages the cluster Runs the applications Components API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager, CCM kubelet, kube-proxy, container runtime Location Dedicated machines, often 3 for high availability Every worker node If it goes down Running apps keep running, but no changes possible Apps on that node stop; Pods get recreated elsewhere

docs.title: How two Pods talk through a Service
docs.text:
• Example → Python frontend Pod needs Redis
  • Frontend connects to redis-service:6379 → CoreDNS turns the name into the Service's ClusterIP
  • Packet leaves the frontend Pod → kube-proxy's rules on that node rewrite the ClusterIP to the IP of one ready Redis Pod (load balancing)
  • CNI carries the packet across the cluster network to that Redis Pod, even on another node
  • Redis replies → the reply goes straight back to the frontend Pod over the same connection
  • Service = stable name and IP in front of Pods whose IPs keep changing
  • kube-proxy picks the Pod | CNI delivers the packet

Quick revision

  • Control plane = API server (front door), etcd (database), scheduler (picks node), controller manager (reconciles), CCM (cloud)
  • Worker = kubelet (runs Pods on the node), kube-proxy (Service rules), container runtime (containerd)
  • Everything talks to the API server; only the API server talks to etcd
  • CRI = runtime, CNI = network, CSI = storage

Interview points

  • Components of the control plane? → kube-apiserver, etcd, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager, and cloud-controller-manager on cloud clusters
  • Components of a worker node? → kubelet, kube-proxy, container runtime (containerd/CRI-O), plus CNI and CSI plugins
  • What does the API server do? → authenticates, authorizes, runs admission, validates and stores objects in etcd, and lets other components watch for changes; it is the only component that talks to etcd
  • Does the scheduler start Pods? → no, it only writes the chosen nodeName into the Pod; the kubelet on that node starts it
  • How does the scheduler pick a node? → filter out nodes that can't run the Pod, score the rest, reserve and bind the best one
  • What happens if the control plane goes down? → running Pods keep running, but nothing can be created, changed or rescheduled until it is back
  • Does kube-proxy assign Pod IPs? → no, the CNI plugin does; kube-proxy programs iptables/IPVS/nftables rules so Service IPs reach healthy Pods
  • Is the kubelet a Pod? → no, it runs as a systemd service on each node
  • CRI vs CNI vs CSI? → CRI is how the kubelet talks to the container runtime, CNI gives Pods networking, CSI gives Pods storage
  • What is the cloud-controller-manager? → the control-plane piece that talks to the cloud provider's API, e.g. creating load balancers for LoadBalancer Services

docs.title: The chain, top to bottom
docs.text:
kubectl
  ↓
kube-apiserver
  ↓
kubelet (on the node)
  ↓  gRPC via CRI
containerd      ← high-level runtime: images, lifecycle
  ↓
runc            ← low-level runtime: creates the container, exits
  ↓
Linux kernel    ← namespaces + cgroups do the real isolation
  • With plain Docker → docker → dockerd → containerd → runc → same bottom half
  • Restaurant analogy → kubelet = waiter taking orders from the API server | containerd = kitchen manager, gets ingredients ready (pulls and unpacks images) | runc = cook, makes the dish (starts the container) and leaves | containerd-shim = helper who stays by the dish and watches it

docs.title: A container is just a process
docs.text:
• Linux has no "container" object
  • Container = normal Linux process + namespaces (what it can see) + cgroups (how much it can use) + its own root filesystem (the image)
  • runc sets these up, starts the process, done

docs.title: Linux namespaces: what a process can see
docs.text:
• Give a process its own private view of the system → it thinks it's alone on the machine
  • Analogy → office building with many companies → each floor has its own room numbers and reception board → floor 3 can't see floor 5 → but one building, one foundation = one shared kernel
Namespace Isolates What the container sees PID Process IDs Its own process list, its main process is PID 1 NET Network Its own interfaces, IP, ports, routing table MNT Mount points Its own filesystem (the image), not the host's UTS Hostname Its own hostname IPC Shared memory, message queues Can't touch other processes' shared memory USER User IDs Can be root inside, a normal user outside CGROUP cgroup view Only its own cgroup tree TIME System clocks (newer) Can have its own clock offset
  • Big three for interviews → PID, NET, MNT
  • Kubernetes angle:
    • each container → own PID and MNT namespace
    • all containers in a Pod → share one NET namespace (held by the pause container) → one IP, talk over localhost
    • kubectl exec / docker exec → enter an existing container's namespaces (setns syscall)
  • Weak spot → all containers share the host kernel → a kernel exploit can escape the namespace → why gVisor and Kata Containers (microVMs) exist
  • More detail and labs → Docker's Namespaces chapter
sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc bash    # own PID namespace
ps aux                                         # only 2 processes, bash is PID 1
exit
sudo unshare --uts bash                        # own hostname
hostname container-test && hostname
exit
ls -l /proc/$$/ns                              # my shell's namespaces
lsns                                           # all namespaces on the system

docs.title: cgroups: how much a process can use
docs.text:
• Control groups → Linux kernel feature that limits and measures resources for a group of processes
  • Namespaces = what you see | cgroups = what you use
  • Analogy → hostel warden: "room 4 gets at most 2 units of power" → take more → throttled or cut off
Resource At the limit CPU Throttled (slowed down), not killed Memory Killed by the OOM killer → OOMKilled, exit code 137 Disk I/O Reads/writes slowed PIDs Can't create more processes (stops fork bombs)
  • Also measures usage → that is where docker stats and kubectl top get numbers, and what autoscaling reads

docs.title: Requests and limits in Kubernetes
docs.text:
resources:
  requests:            # used by the SCHEDULER to pick a node
    cpu: "250m"        # 250 millicores = 1/4 CPU
    memory: "128Mi"
  limits:              # enforced by CGROUPS on the node
    cpu: "500m"
    memory: "256Mi"
  • requests → "find a node with at least this much free" → scheduling decision
  • limits → hard ceiling → runc writes them into the container's cgroup
  • Over CPU limit → throttled (slow, alive) | over memory limit → OOMKilled (shown in kubectl describe pod)
  • CPU throttled vs memory killed → very common interview question

docs.title: cgroup v1 vs v2
docs.text:
• v1 → older, separate tree per resource, messy
  • v2 → one unified tree, better memory handling → modern default (Ubuntu 22.04+)
  • Recent Kubernetes (1.35+) refuses to run on cgroup v1 by default
stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup        # cgroup2fs = v2
cat /proc/self/cgroup             # which cgroup my shell is in
systemd-cgls                      # tree of all cgroups
docker run --rm -m 50m polinux/stress stress --vm 1 --vm-bytes 100M
echo $?                           # 137 = killed (128 + signal 9)

docs.title: runc: the low-level runtime
docs.text:
• Small program that actually creates and starts a container
  • Reference implementation of the OCI runtime spec (Open Container Initiative = the standard for how to run a container)
  • Gets a ready folder (root filesystem) + config.json → creates namespaces → applies cgroups → sets the root filesystem → starts the process → exits
  • Does not pull images, does not do networking, does not stay running
  • Because it follows a standard, it can be swapped:
    • crun → written in C, faster and lighter
    • gVisor (runsc) → sandboxed user-space kernel, stronger isolation
    • Kata Containers → each container inside a tiny VM

docs.title: containerd: the high-level runtime
docs.text:
• The container manager running on every node, always on (a daemon)
  • Jobs:
    • pulls images from registries (Docker Hub, ECR)
    • stores images and unpacks layers into a filesystem (snapshotters, usually overlayfs)
    • prepares the container config, then calls runc
    • manages lifecycle → create, start, stop, delete, status
    • talks to the kubelet through CRI (gRPC)
    • starts one containerd-shim per container → keeps containers alive even if containerd restarts, holds stdout/stderr, records exit codes
  • Restarting crashed containers → that is the kubelet's job (restart policy), not containerd's
  • Came out of Docker in 2017, donated to CNCF → now the standard node runtime

docs.title: containerd vs runc
docs.text:
containerd runc Level High-level runtime Low-level runtime Job Images, lifecycle, talks to the kubelet Creates one container with namespaces + cgroups Runs how long Always (daemon) A split second, then exits Talks to kubelet above (CRI), runc below Linux kernel Knows about images? Yes, pulls, unpacks, stores No, only gets a ready folder + config Standard Implements CRI Implements OCI runtime spec Swappable with CRI-O crun, gVisor, Kata
  • One line → containerd prepares and manages, runc creates and exits

docs.title: containerd vs Docker, and the dockershim story
docs.text:
• Docker → full developer tool: CLI, docker build, Compose, networks, volumes
  • containerd → only the runtime part, pulled out of Docker
  • Kubernetes talks to runtimes only through CRI → Docker never spoke CRI → Kubernetes kept an adapter called dockershim
  • Kubernetes 1.24 (2022) removed dockershim → nodes now use containerd or CRI-O directly
  • Docker-built images still work everywhere → they are standard OCI images
  • Only Docker as the node runtime was dropped, not Docker as a build tool

docs.title: Tools to look inside a node
docs.text:
Tool For crictl Talks CRI, shows what the kubelet sees → use this on Kubernetes nodes ctr containerd's own low-level CLI, for debugging nerdctl Docker-like CLI for containerd 
docker exec -it my-first-cluster-control-plane bash
crictl ps                       # running containers (like docker ps)
crictl pods                     # Pod sandboxes
crictl images
systemctl status containerd
ps aux | grep -E "containerd|shim"
  • Break it → inside the node systemctl stop containerd → existing Pods keep running (shims keep them alive) → new Pods can't start → systemctl start containerd

Quick revision

  • Container = process + namespaces (see) + cgroups (use) + own root filesystem
  • kubelet → CRI → containerd → runc → kernel
  • CPU over limit = throttled, memory over limit = OOMKilled (137)
  • dockershim removed in 1.24; Docker images still work (OCI)

Interview points

  • What is a container, technically? → a normal Linux process isolated with namespaces, limited with cgroups, running on its own root filesystem
  • Namespaces vs cgroups? → namespaces isolate what a process can see; cgroups limit and measure what it can use
  • Which namespace do containers in a Pod share? → the network namespace, held by the pause container, so they share one IP and use localhost
  • Container exceeds its CPU limit vs its memory limit? → CPU gets throttled; memory gets OOMKilled with exit code 137
  • Requests vs limits? → requests are used by the scheduler to place the Pod; limits are enforced on the node through cgroups
  • What is runc? → the low-level OCI runtime that containerd calls to create the container; it sets up namespaces and cgroups, starts the process and exits
  • What is containerd? → a CNCF high-level runtime that pulls and stores images, manages container lifecycle and calls runc; Kubernetes talks to it over CRI
  • Why did Kubernetes drop Docker? → Docker doesn't implement CRI, so Kubernetes needed the dockershim adapter; it was removed in 1.24 in favour of containerd and CRI-O
  • Do Docker-built images still work on Kubernetes? → yes, they are OCI images
  • What keeps a container running if containerd restarts? → the containerd-shim, which is the container's parent process
  • Why are containers weaker isolation than VMs? → they share the host kernel, so a kernel exploit can escape; gVisor and Kata add a stronger boundary

docs.title: The method
docs.text:
• Nobody knows every error in advance → debugging is a method, not memory → narrow the problem down one layer at a time
  • Steps →
    1. Exact symptom → copy the exact error, not "it's not working"
    2. Split the path in half → every test should cut the problem in two (name fails but IP works → DNS)
    3. Status first → get → describe → logs (logs --previous if it crashes)
    4. Compare working vs broken → one Pod fine, one not? → what's different (node, config, version)
    5. Go one layer down → Pod → node → host → the cause can sit several layers below the symptom
    6. Search the exact error line in quotes → normal, everyone does it
    7. Fix → verify → write down the cause

docs.title: The path a Service request depends on
docs.text:
curl backend-svc:9090
  → DNS lookup                    (Pod's /etc/resolv.conf → kube-dns Service 10.96.0.10)
    → CoreDNS Pods Ready          (else kube-dns has no endpoints)
      → CoreDNS reaches the API server (kubernetes Service 10.96.0.1:443) to learn Service names
        → kube-proxy rules on the node (make ClusterIPs work at all)
          → kube-proxy running     (needs host kernel resources)
  → Service ClusterIP:port → iptables DNAT
    → Endpoints not empty         (selector matches, Pods Ready, same namespace)
      → targetPort = the app's real port
        → app listening and answering
  • Any link breaks → the request fails → the error message tells which half to look at

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
# 1. Service exists, right namespace, right ports?
kubectl get svc -A | grep <name>
kubectl describe svc <name>                       # Selector, Port, TargetPort, Endpoints

# 2. Does it have endpoints?
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<name>
kubectl get pods --show-labels -o wide            # labels match the selector? Pods Ready (1/1)?

# 3. Name vs IP (from a test Pod)
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- curl <svc>:<port>        # by name
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- curl <clusterIP>:<port>  # by IP → works = DNS problem
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- curl <podIP>:<targetPort>  # straight to a Pod → works = Service/port problem

# 4. DNS
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- cat /etc/resolv.conf     # nameserver 10.96.0.10
kubectl get svc -n kube-system                     # kube-dns 10.96.0.10
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns -o wide
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns --tail=20
kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- nslookup <svc>

# 5. kube-proxy (Service rules on each node)
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy -o wide
kubectl logs -n kube-system <kube-proxy-pod> --previous --tail=20

docs.title: Symptom → likely cause
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Check Could not resolve host: <svc> DNS broken, typo in name, or Service in another namespace get svc -A, CoreDNS Pods Ready, curl <clusterIP> Could not resolve host: backend + svc Space instead of - → curl saw two hosts Fix the typo Connection refused / browser "empty response" targetPort ≠ app's real port, or app not listening describe svc TargetPort vs app config Request hangs / times out No Ready endpoints, or kube-proxy rules stale Endpoints, kube-proxy Pods Endpoints: <none> Selector ≠ Pod labels, Pods not Ready, wrong namespace get pods --show-labels, readiness Pod 0/1 Running Running but failing readiness probe → removed from Services describe pod, logs Pod CrashLoopBackOff Starts, exits, restarts again and again logs --previous LoadBalancer EXTERNAL-IP <pending> No cloud controller (kind, bare metal) Normal locally → MetalLB / cloud-provider-kind

docs.title: Incident: Service name doesn't resolve on kind (DNS → kube-proxy → inotify)
Symptom
docs.text:
# curl backend-svc:9090
curl: (6) Could not resolve host: backend-svc

docs.title: Simple version
docs.text:
• Think of the cluster as an office building →
    • CoreDNS = phonebook operator → "what's backend-svc's number?"
    • API server = main office register → has every Service and its number
    • kube-proxy = switchboard operator on each floor → connects calls to the right place
    • Nodes = floors | my laptop = the land the building stands on
  • What went wrong →
    1. Asked the phonebook for backend-svc → no reply
    2. Called backend-svc directly by its number → worked → so the reception (Service) was fine, the phonebook was the problem
    3. Both phonebook operators were marked not ready
    4. Their complaint → "I can't reach the main register" → no list → refuse to work
    5. After a restart one operator (on floor worker2) was fine, the one on floor worker still stuck → problem is on that floor
    6. Switchboard operators (kube-proxy) → floor worker2 fine, floors worker and control-plane kept fainting (crashing 180+ times)
    7. Why → "too many open files" → the land (my laptop) ran out of a resource the operators need
    8. Fix → raise that limit on the laptop → replace the fainted operators → replace the stuck phonebook operator
  • One sentence → host ran out of inotify instances → kube-proxy kept crashing → CoreDNS couldn't reach the API server → DNS stopped → Pods couldn't find Services by name

docs.title: Investigation, step by step
docs.text:
1. Does the Service exist?

$ kubectl get svc
NAME          TYPE        CLUSTER-IP      PORT(S)
backend-svc   ClusterIP   10.96.253.171   9090/TCP
  • Exists, same namespace (default) as the test Pod → Service object is fine

2. Name vs IP

$ kubectl exec -it mynginx -- curl 10.96.253.171:9090
Hello from backend :)
  • IP works, name fails → DNS is the problem, the Service data path is fine
  • (Worked because that node still had the iptables rule from before kube-proxy started failing → stale but present)

3. DNS components

$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
NAME                       READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
coredns-559f6c778d-8cpvc   0/1     Running   3 (136m ago)
coredns-559f6c778d-kfxfx   0/1     Running   3 (136m ago)

$ kubectl exec -it mynginx -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
search default.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
nameserver 10.96.0.10
options ndots:5

$ kubectl get svc -n kube-system
NAME       TYPE        CLUSTER-IP   PORT(S)
kube-dns   ClusterIP   10.96.0.10   53/UDP,53/TCP,9153/TCP
  • resolv.conf points to the right place, kube-dns Service exists
  • But CoreDNS is 0/1 → Running but not Ready
  • DNS is itself a Service → kube-dns (10.96.0.10) in front of the CoreDNS Pods → Services only route to Ready Pods → 0 endpoints → nobody answers DNS queries
  • RESTARTS 3 (136m ago) → laptop slept / Docker restarted about 2 hours earlier → common trigger with kind

4. Why isn't CoreDNS Ready?

$ kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns --tail=20
[INFO] plugin/ready: Plugins not ready: "kubernetes"
  • CoreDNS doesn't store records itself → its kubernetes plugin watches the API server for Services and Pods to build its answers
  • Plugin not ready = initial sync with the API server never finished → CoreDNS fails its readiness probe
  • CoreDNS reaches the API server through the kubernetes Service → 10.96.0.1:443 → a ClusterIP → needs kube-proxy's rules on CoreDNS's node

5. Restart CoreDNS and compare

$ kubectl rollout restart deployment coredns -n kube-system
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns -o wide
NAME                       READY   NODE
coredns-66bc77855f-gpbdc   1/1     my-first-cluster-worker2
coredns-66bc77855f-wbd72   0/1     my-first-cluster-worker
  • rollout restart → old Pods Terminating → Completed, new Pods ContainerCreating → Running
  • Same image, same config → one Ready, one not → the difference is the node
  • One Ready CoreDNS Pod is enough for DNS to work again → but the cluster isn't healthy yet

6. kube-proxy on each node

$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy -o wide
NAME               READY   STATUS             RESTARTS          NODE
kube-proxy-nb9dn   1/1     Running            210 (142m ago)    my-first-cluster-worker2
kube-proxy-qb7jn   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   183 (83s ago)     my-first-cluster-control-plane
kube-proxy-vngnk   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   182 (2m37s ago)   my-first-cluster-worker
  • CrashLoopBackOff → container starts, crashes, kubelet restarts it, waits longer each time, repeats
  • kube-proxy dead on worker → that node's Service rules never update → CoreDNS on worker can't reach 10.96.0.1 → stays 0/1

7. Why does kube-proxy crash?

$ kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-proxy-vngnk --previous --tail=20
"command failed" err="failed complete: fsnotify watcher init: too many open files"
  • --previous → logs of the last crashed container → where crash reasons live
  • kube-proxy uses inotify (kernel feature: "tell me when this file changes") to watch its config
  • Kernel limits inotify per user → fs.inotify.max_user_instances (default 128) and fs.inotify.max_user_watches
  • kind nodes share the host's kernel → 3 nodes × (kubelet, kube-proxy, other components) + VS Code + browser → limit exhausted → kube-proxy can't create its watcher → exits → crash loop

docs.title: Fix
docs.text:
# 1. Raise the limits now
sudo sysctl fs.inotify.max_user_watches=524288
sudo sysctl fs.inotify.max_user_instances=512

# 2. Persist across reboots
echo "fs.inotify.max_user_watches=524288" | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.conf
echo "fs.inotify.max_user_instances=512" | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.conf
sudo sysctl -p

# 3. Replace the crashed kube-proxy Pods (DaemonSet recreates them immediately)
kubectl delete pod -n kube-system <kube-proxy-on-control-plane> <kube-proxy-on-worker>
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy -o wide -w      # all 1/1, RESTARTS 0

# 4. Replace the stuck CoreDNS Pod (ReplicaSet recreates it)
kubectl delete pod -n kube-system <coredns-pod-that-is-0/1>
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns -o wide -w        # both 1/1

# 5. Verify
kubectl exec -it <test-pod> -- curl backend-svc:9090                 # Hello from backend :)
kubectl get endpointslices -n kube-system -l kubernetes.io/service-name=kube-dns
  • Deleting a DaemonSet Pod is safe → DaemonSet = one Pod per node, always → recreated straight away
  • New CoreDNS Pod may land on a different node → normal, the scheduler picks any node that fits
  • Old restart counts on the healthy kube-proxy stay (e.g. 210) → history from before the fix → ignore if they don't grow

docs.title: Dependency chain (technical)
docs.text:
curl backend-svc:9090
  → needs DNS
    → CoreDNS Pods Ready
      → CoreDNS lists Services from the API server (10.96.0.1:443)
        → reaching a ClusterIP needs iptables rules
          → kube-proxy writes those rules
            → kube-proxy needs inotify watchers from the host kernel
              → host inotify limit too low   ← ROOT CAUSE

docs.title: What this incident teaches
docs.text:
• Running ≠ Ready → Services only send traffic to Ready Pods → a Running-but-not-Ready Pod is invisible to callers
  • Cluster DNS is just a Service + Pods → kube-dns in front of CoreDNS → same rules as my own Services
  • DaemonSet → one Pod per node, recreated on delete
  • CrashLoopBackOff → logs --previous
  • kind shares the host kernel → host limits (inotify, file descriptors) affect the whole cluster
  • Compare healthy vs broken → same Pod on two nodes behaving differently = look at the node

docs.title: Symptom
docs.text:
• Browser → localhost:31000 → "localhost:31000 sent back an empty page" (NS_ERROR_NET_EMPTY_RESPONSE)
  • Pods 1/1 Running, Service created, Endpoints filled

docs.title: Cause
docs.text:
spec:
  type: NodePort
  ports:
    - port: 9090
      targetPort: 5678     # ← copied from the backend Service
      nodePort: 31000
  selector:
    app: frontend          # but these Pods run nginx, which listens on 80

Browser → localhost:31000 → frontend-svc → nginx Pod:5678   ← nothing listening → connection cut
  • Ports copied from the backend Service → selector now points at nginx Pods → nginx listens on 80, not 5678

docs.title: Fix
docs.text:
ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 80
      nodePort: 31000

kubectl apply -f frontend.yaml
kubectl get svc frontend-svc       # 80:31000/TCP
curl localhost:31000               # Welcome to nginx!

docs.title: How to catch it
docs.text:
1. Pods Running + Endpoints filled + connection refused / empty response → suspect ports
  2. kubectl describe svc <name> → read TargetPort
  3. Does it match the app's real port? (nginx 80, http-echo 5678) → check the app's config if unsure
  4. Mismatch → fix targetPort

docs.title: Building the skill
docs.text:
• Debugging only grows by facing broken things → break things on purpose, predict the error first, then debug it
  • Break a kind cluster →
    • wrong targetPort | wrong selector label | Pod in another namespace
    • scale CoreDNS to 0 → kubectl scale deploy coredns -n kube-system --replicas=0
    • bad image name → ImagePullBackOff
    • stop a node container → docker stop <node>
  • Practice →
    • SadServers → real broken Linux servers to fix in the browser → the base layer under everything
    • Killercoda → free Kubernetes scenarios, including CKA-style troubleshooting
    • learnk8s troubleshooting flowchart → one visual map for "my Pod or Service doesn't work"
    • Kubernetes docs → Debug Services and Debugging DNS Resolution
  • Write every incident as a short postmortem → symptom → investigation → root cause → fix → lesson

Quick revision

  • Name fails, IP works → DNS | IP fails, Pod IP works → Service/ports | Pod IP fails → app
  • describe svc → Endpoints empty = selector/readiness/namespace | filled but refused = targetPort
  • DNS = kube-dns Service → CoreDNS Pods → must be Ready → must reach the API server through kube-proxy rules
  • CrashLoopBackOff → kubectl logs --previous
  • kind + "too many open files" → raise fs.inotify.max_user_instances / max_user_watches on the host, restart kube-proxy and CoreDNS

Interview points

  • A Pod can't resolve a Service name, how do you debug? → confirm the Service exists in that namespace, curl the ClusterIP to separate DNS from Service problems, check resolv.conf, check that CoreDNS Pods are Ready and read their logs
  • CoreDNS Pods show 0/1 Running, what does that mean? → the process runs but fails its readiness probe, so the kube-dns Service has no endpoints and DNS queries go unanswered
  • CoreDNS logs say plugin kubernetes not ready, why? → CoreDNS can't sync with the API server, often because kube-proxy rules for the kubernetes Service ClusterIP are missing on that node
  • How do you see why a container keeps crashing? → kubectl logs --previous shows the last crashed run
  • Why can kube-proxy crash with too many open files on kind? → kind nodes share the host kernel, and the default inotify instance limit is exhausted; raise fs.inotify limits with sysctl
  • Is it safe to delete a kube-proxy Pod? → yes, it's a DaemonSet Pod and is recreated immediately on the same node
  • Service Endpoints are filled but connections are refused? → targetPort doesn't match the port the app listens on
  • Service Endpoints are empty? → selector doesn't match Pod labels, Pods aren't Ready, or they're in another namespace
  • General debugging approach? → reproduce the exact error, split the path in half with tests, check get/describe/logs, compare healthy vs broken, go one layer down, fix, verify and document

docs.title: From kubectl apply to Running Pod
The short version
docs.text:
• kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml sets off a chain → no component does everything, each one does one small job and writes the result back to the API server
  • The next component watches the API server, sees the change, does its job → like a relay race where the baton is always handed through the API server
kubectl ─▶ API server ─▶ etcd
                │
   Deployment controller   → creates ReplicaSet
   ReplicaSet controller   → creates Pod objects (no node yet)
   Scheduler               → picks a node, writes nodeName
   kubelet on that node    → containerd pulls image, CNI gives IP, containers start
   kubelet                 → reports status back → Pod Running

docs.title: Step 1: kubectl
docs.text:
• I run kubectl apply -f python-frontend-deployment.yaml
  • kubectl checks the YAML → syntax (indentation, format) and basic schema (valid apiVersion, kind)
  • Turns it into a REST request (POST/PATCH) and sends it to the API server
  • See the actual HTTP calls → kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml -v=8

docs.title: Step 2: API server
docs.text:
1. Authentication → who sent this? (my client certificate from the kubeconfig)
  2. Authorization → RBAC: is this user allowed to create Deployments in this namespace?
  3. Admission → mutating webhooks may change it, validating webhooks may reject it
  4. Validation → full schema check
  5. Store in etcd → the Deployment's desired state (name, replicas, Pod template)
  6. Respond → deployment.apps/python-frontend created
  7. At this point → nothing is running yet, only a record in the database

docs.title: Step 3: Deployment controller
docs.text:
• Part of kube-controller-manager → watches Deployment objects through the API server
  • Sees a new Deployment with no ReplicaSet → asks the API server to create a ReplicaSet object → stored in etcd
  • Keeps updating the Deployment's status → how many replicas are ready (containers running and passing readiness checks) and available (ready for at least minReadySeconds)

docs.title: Step 4: ReplicaSet controller
docs.text:
• Watches ReplicaSets through the API server (never reads etcd directly)
  • Sees desired 3, actual 0 → asks the API server to create 3 Pod objects
  • These Pods are only records in etcd → no node assigned (nodeName empty), no containers yet
  • Status → Pending

docs.title: Step 5: Scheduler
docs.text:
• Watches for Pods with an empty nodeName
  • For each one → filters nodes that can't run it (resources, taints, affinity) → scores the rest → picks the best
  • Writes nodeName into the Pod object through the API server → stored in etcd
  • Scheduler's job ends here → it does not start anything

docs.title: Step 6: kubelet on the chosen node
docs.text:
• Every kubelet watches for Pods whose nodeName = its own node
  • Sees the new Pod → reads its spec (containers, ports, volumes, env)
  • Through CRI (gRPC) tells containerd to:
    • pull the image from the registry
    • create the Pod sandbox (pause container, network namespace) → CNI plugin gives it an IP
    • mount volumes (through CSI if needed)
    • create and start the containers (containerd → runc)
  • Pod status → ContainerCreating → Running

docs.title: Step 7: Running and kept running
docs.text:
• kubelet keeps checking container health (probes) → restarts crashed containers → reports status to the API server → stored in etcd
  • Pod gets deleted or its node dies → ReplicaSet controller sees actual 2, desired 3 → creates a new Pod → scheduler places it → kubelet starts it
  • Who does what after startup:
    • kubelet → health of containers on its node
    • ReplicaSet controller → recreates missing Pods
    • Deployment controller → manages ReplicaSets (versions), does not recreate Pods itself

docs.title: Watch it happen
docs.text:
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx --replicas=3
kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
kubectl get deploy,rs,pods -o wide
kubectl describe pod <web-pod>        # Events: Scheduled → Pulling → Pulled → Created → Started
  • kubectl describe pod → Events section at the bottom shows each step and which component did it (default-scheduler, kubelet)
  • Best debugging habit → stuck Pod = look at Events first
Pod stuck in Usually means Look at Pending Scheduler can't find a node (no resources, taints, affinity) kubectl describe pod → Events ContainerCreating Image pull, volume mount or CNI still in progress or failing Events, node's kubelet ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull Wrong image name/tag or no registry access Image name, registry credentials CrashLoopBackOff Container starts, then exits, again and again kubectl logs <pod> --previous

Quick revision

  • kubectl → API server (authn, authz, admission, etcd) → Deployment controller (ReplicaSet) → ReplicaSet controller (Pods) → scheduler (nodeName) → kubelet (containerd, CNI, CSI) → Running
  • Every component only talks to the API server and watches it for changes

Interview points

  • Walk me through what happens on kubectl apply of a Deployment → kubectl sends it to the API server, which authenticates, authorizes, runs admission and stores it in etcd; the Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet; the ReplicaSet controller creates Pod objects; the scheduler assigns each Pod a node; the kubelet on that node asks containerd to pull the image and start the containers, CNI gives the Pod an IP, and the kubelet reports status back
  • When kubectl says "deployment created", is anything running? → no, only the object is stored in etcd; controllers, the scheduler and the kubelet do the rest asynchronously
  • Who recreates a deleted Pod, the Deployment or the ReplicaSet? → the ReplicaSet controller; the Deployment controller manages ReplicaSets
  • Do controllers read etcd directly? → no, everything goes through the API server, which is the only component talking to etcd
  • A Pod is stuck in Pending, what do you check? → kubectl describe pod and its Events, usually the scheduler couldn't find a node because of resources, taints or affinity
  • CrashLoopBackOff, what do you check? → kubectl logs --previous for the crashed container, then the command, config and probes

docs.title: What etcd is
docs.text:
• Distributed key-value store → stores data as key → value pairs, like a giant dictionary
  • Kubernetes keeps its entire state here → every Deployment, Pod, Service, Secret, ConfigMap, node
  • Keys look like paths → /registry/deployments/default/web, /registry/pods/kube-system/coredns-xxxx
  • Desired state + current status of the whole cluster = the cluster's single source of truth
  • Only the API server talks to etcd → everyone else goes through the API server
  • Name → /etc (Linux config folder) + d for distributed

docs.title: Why it matters so much
docs.text:
• Lose etcd without a backup = lose the cluster's memory → nodes keep running Pods, but Kubernetes no longer knows what should exist
  • So in production → run 3 or 5 etcd members + take regular snapshots
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd.db    # backup (needs certs/endpoints on a real cluster)
etcdctl snapshot status /backup/etcd.db -w table

docs.title: Write-Ahead Log (WAL)
docs.text:
• Every change is first written to a log on disk, before it is applied
  • If etcd crashes or the power goes → replay the log → nothing lost, changes stay in the right order
  • Same idea as a bank writing every transaction in a ledger before updating balances

docs.title: Protobuf, not JSON
docs.text:
• Kubernetes objects are stored in etcd as Protocol Buffers → compact binary format
  • Smaller and faster than JSON → stays quick even with thousands of objects
  • Protobuf is not encryption → just a space-efficient format → see REST, gRPC & Protobuf

docs.title: Not encrypted by default
docs.text:
• etcd stores data in plain form unless encryption at rest is turned on
  • Secrets are only base64-encoded → base64 is encoding, not encryption → anyone who reads etcd's files can decode them
  • Production → enable encryption at rest in the API server config (EncryptionConfiguration, ideally with a KMS provider)
  • Also → restrict who can reach etcd, use TLS between API server and etcd
echo 'cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM=' | base64 -d     # password123 → base64 hides nothing

docs.title: Raft: keeping copies in agreement
docs.text:
• Problem → one etcd copy = single point of failure | 3 copies = how do they stay identical? If two writes arrive at two copies at the same time, which wins?
  • Raft = consensus algorithm → the rulebook that lets several machines agree on the same data, even if some crash
  • Analogy → 5 students keeping one shared notebook:
    1. One leader (class monitor) → only the monitor writes new entries | everyone else is a follower
    2. All writes go through the leader → anyone with a new entry hands it to the monitor
    3. Leader asks for agreement → "adding entry #42" → followers write it and reply "done"
    4. Majority = committed → once 3 of 5 have it, it's official
    5. Leader disappears → followers stop hearing from it → one says "vote for me" → whoever gets a majority becomes the new leader (leader election)

docs.title: The three states
docs.text: State Role Leader Accepts writes, copies them to followers, sends regular heartbeats ("I'm alive") Follower Copies what the leader sends, votes in elections Candidate A follower that stopped getting heartbeats and is asking for votes

docs.title: Quorum
docs.text:
• Quorum = majority = (N / 2) + 1 (rounded down, then +1)
etcd members Quorum Failures it survives 1 1 0 2 2 0 3 2 1 4 3 1 5 3 2
  • Use odd numbers (3 or 5) → a 4th member costs more but survives no extra failure
  • Bigger isn't always better → every write waits for a majority → 7+ members slow writes down
  • Quorum lost (e.g. 2 of 3 down) → etcd stops accepting writes → Kubernetes can't create, change or delete anything → running Pods keep running, but the cluster is frozen

docs.title: Split-brain
docs.text:
• Network splits 5 members into a group of 3 and a group of 2
  • Group of 3 has a majority → elects a leader, keeps working
  • Group of 2 can't reach a majority → can't accept writes
  • So there are never two leaders writing different data (that failure is called split-brain) → majority voting prevents it
etcdctl member list
etcdctl endpoint status --cluster -w table     # shows which member is leader
kubectl -n kube-system get pods | grep etcd    # kind: one etcd Pod on the control-plane node

Quick revision

  • etcd = key-value store holding all cluster state, only the API server talks to it
  • WAL first, protobuf format, not encrypted by default (Secrets are just base64)
  • Raft = one leader, majority commit, re-election if the leader dies
  • Quorum = N/2 + 1 → use 3 or 5 members

Interview points

  • What is etcd? → a distributed, consistent key-value store that holds all Kubernetes cluster state; only the API server talks to it
  • What happens if you lose etcd with no backup? → the cluster loses its record of what should exist; you restore from an etcd snapshot
  • Are Kubernetes Secrets encrypted? → not by default; they are base64-encoded in etcd, so you enable encryption at rest (ideally with KMS) and restrict etcd access
  • What is Raft? → a consensus algorithm: one elected leader takes writes and replicates them, a write commits once a majority acknowledges it, and followers elect a new leader if the leader fails
  • What is quorum and why odd numbers? → a majority, N/2+1; 4 members tolerate the same single failure as 3, so even numbers add cost without extra safety
  • What happens when etcd loses quorum? → it stops accepting writes, so the Kubernetes API can't make changes; existing Pods keep running
  • How does Raft prevent split-brain? → only a side with a majority can elect a leader and commit writes, so two leaders can never both write
  • What is the WAL? → the write-ahead log: every change is logged to disk before being applied, so etcd can replay it after a crash

docs.title: Why learn them at all
docs.text:
• Real clusters are run declaratively → YAML in Git → applied by CI/CD or GitOps (Argo CD, Flux), often templated with Helm/Kustomize → nobody runs production with kubectl create
  • Imperative commands are still used every day, for 3 jobs:
    • Generate YAML → let kubectl write the skeleton, edit it, apply it (see YAML, Manifests & Objects)
    • CKA / CKAD exam → timed → typing a full manifest from memory wastes minutes
    • Troubleshooting → throwaway test Pods, port-forward, logs, exec, rollout restart, scale during an incident
  • Rule → imperative to generate and debug, declarative to run

docs.title: The dry-run flags
docs.text:
Flag What happens Use it for --dry-run=client kubectl builds the object locally, nothing is created Getting a YAML skeleton fast --dry-run=server Sent to the API server → schema + admission checks (quotas, policies, webhooks) → then thrown away "Would this actually be accepted?" before a real apply -o yaml Print the object as YAML instead of creating it Always paired with a dry-run here
  • Catch → client doesn't always mean "no API call" → kubectl expose still reads the live Deployment to copy its selector → the Deployment must already exist, or → Error from server (NotFound): deployments.apps "backend-deploy" not found

docs.title: > vs >>
docs.text:
• > file.yaml → create / overwrite the file
  • >> file.yaml → append to the end of the file
  • Appending a second object needs a --- separator between them → without it the file is one YAML document with duplicate keys (apiVersion, kind, metadata…) → apply errors or silently keeps only one object
  • --dry-run=client -o yaml does not print a leading --- → add it myself:
echo '---' >> backend-deploy.yaml
kubectl expose ... --dry-run=client -o yaml >> backend-deploy.yaml
  • Forgot it? Fix in place → the Service starts with apiVersion: v1, the Deployment with apps/v1, so this match is unique:
sed -i 's/^apiVersion: v1$/---\napiVersion: v1/' backend-deploy.yaml
grep -n -e '^---' -e '^kind' backend-deploy.yaml      # Deployment, ---, Service

docs.title: Step 1 → Deployment
docs.text:
kubectl create deployment backend-deploy \
  --image=hashicorp/http-echo \
  --replicas=3 \
  --port=5678 \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml > backend-deploy.yaml
Flag Meaning backend-deploy Deployment name → also becomes the Pod label app: backend-deploy --image Container image → hashicorp/http-echo = tiny web server that replies with fixed text --replicas=3 3 Pods --port=5678 Writes containerPort: 5678 into the Pod template

docs.title: What --port / containerPort really does
docs.text:
• It only writes containerPort: 5678 into the YAML → mostly documentation
  • It does not →
    • make the app listen on 5678 → the app decides that (http-echo listens on 5678 by default)
    • expose anything outside the Pod
    • block other ports → a port not listed is still reachable inside the cluster
  • Where it does matter →
    • kubectl expose without --target-port → copies containerPort into the Service's targetPort → no containerPort and no flag → expose fails ("couldn't find port via --port flag or introspection")
    • Named ports → containerPort: 5678 + name: http → Service uses targetPort: http → change the number in one place only
    • Probes can point at the named port
  • Proof it's informational → kubectl port-forward deploy/backend-deploy 8080:5678 works even with containerPort deleted
  • Mental model → app = the port actually listened on | containerPort = a label on it | Service = what exposes it

docs.title: Generated YAML, cleaned up
docs.text:
• Dry-run output has empty noise → strategy: {}, resources: {}, status: {}, creationTimestamp: null → delete them, Kubernetes fills defaults, and status is never mine to write
  • Add args → http-echo needs -text to know what to reply → older versions exit with Missing -text option → CrashLoopBackOff
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: backend-deploy
  labels:
    app: backend-deploy
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend-deploy        # must match the template labels
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: backend-deploy      # the Service selects on this too
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: http-echo
        image: hashicorp/http-echo
        args:
        - "-text=Hello from Backend"
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5678

docs.title: Step 2 → ClusterIP Service
docs.text:
kubectl apply -f backend-deploy.yaml              # expose needs the live Deployment
echo '---' >> backend-deploy.yaml
kubectl expose deployment backend-deploy \
  --type=ClusterIP \
  --port=9090 \
  --target-port=5678 \
  --name=backend-svc \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml >> backend-deploy.yaml
Part Meaning expose deployment backend-deploy Build a Service for this Deployment → copies its selector (app: backend-deploy) and labels --type=ClusterIP Internal-only virtual IP → the default, so optional --port=9090 Port the Service listens on → callers use backend-svc:9090 --target-port=5678 Port in the Pod traffic is forwarded to → must match the app --name=backend-svc Service name → also its DNS name 
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: backend-svc
  labels:
    app: backend-deploy
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: backend-deploy
  ports:
  - port: 9090
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 5678

client Pod → backend-svc:9090 → (selector picks 1 of 3 Pods) → <pod-IP>:5678 → http-echo

docs.title: Step 3 → apply and verify
docs.text:
kubectl apply -f backend-deploy.yaml
# deployment.apps/backend-deploy unchanged     ← already exists, file matches → nothing to do
# service/backend-svc created
kubectl get deploy,svc,pods -l app=backend-deploy
kubectl get endpoints backend-svc               # 3 Pod IPs on :5678 → selector matches
  • unchanged → apply compares file vs live object and only changes what differs → re-applying the same file is safe (idempotent)
  • Empty endpoints → selector doesn't match Pod labels, or Pods not Ready (see Debugging Services & DNS)

docs.title: Frontend: Deployment + NodePort Service
docs.text:
kubectl create deployment frontend-deploy \
  --image=nginx \
  --replicas=3 \
  --port=80 \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml > frontend-deploy.yaml
kubectl apply -f frontend-deploy.yaml
echo '---' >> frontend-deploy.yaml
kubectl expose deployment frontend-deploy \
  --type=NodePort \
  --port=80 \
  --target-port=80 \
  --name=frontend-svc \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml >> frontend-deploy.yaml
  • --type=NodePort → opens the same port (30000–32767) on every node → reachable from outside via any node IP
  • kubectl expose has no --node-port flag → Kubernetes picks a random port → to fix it, edit the YAML:
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector:
    app: frontend-deploy
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
    nodePort: 31000        # added by hand
  • Result in kubectl get svc → 80:31000/TCP → read as service port 80, node port 31000
<any-node-IP>:31000 → frontend-svc:80 → nginx Pod :80

kubectl get nodes -o wide        # node INTERNAL-IPs (kind nodes = Docker containers, 172.18.0.x)
curl 172.18.0.2:31000            # from the laptop on native Linux → nginx welcome page
  • localhost:31000 only works if the kind cluster was created with extraPortMappings for it (see Services)

docs.title: The other way → kubectl create service
docs.text:
• kubectl create service nodeport frontend-svc --tcp=80:80 --node-port=31000 → does accept a node port
  • Catch → it sets the selector to app: frontend-svc (the Service's name) → doesn't match Pods labelled app: frontend-deploy → empty endpoints
  • So → expose gets the selector right, create service gets the nodePort right → either way one manual edit

docs.title: Labels with imperative commands
docs.text:
• kubectl create deployment X → always labels the Pods app=X → no flag for custom Pod labels → edit template.metadata.labels and selector.matchLabels together in the YAML
  • kubectl label deployment X env=prod → labels the Deployment object, not its Pods → the Pod template is untouched
  • kubectl run (plain Pod) → takes labels directly:
kubectl run nginx-pod \
  --image=nginx \
  --restart=Never \
  --labels="app=nginx,env=production"       # comma-separated key=value
kubectl get pods --show-labels
kubectl get pods -l env=production          # filter by label
  • Why labels matter → Services and Deployments find Pods only by labels → wrong label = no traffic, or a ReplicaSet that keeps creating Pods

docs.title: See it break
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -l app=backend-deploy
kubectl label pod <one-backend-pod> app=broken --overwrite
kubectl get endpoints backend-svc           # that Pod's IP drops out
kubectl get pods --show-labels              # ReplicaSet saw only 2 → created a 3rd
kubectl delete pod <the-broken-pod>         # cleanup → it's orphaned now

docs.title: Generate a Pod manifest
docs.text:
kubectl run my-nginx \
  --image=nginx \
  --restart=Never \
  --labels=app=test-pod \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml > test-pod.yaml

docs.title: Throwaway Pod for troubleshooting
docs.text:
kubectl run test-pod \
  --rm -it \
  --restart=Never \
  --labels=app=test-pod \
  --image=nginx \
  -- /bin/sh
Flag Meaning --rm Delete the Pod as soon as I exit the shell → pod "test-pod" deleted -it Interactive + terminal → I get a shell prompt --restart=Never Plain Pod, not restarted if it exits → right for one-off checks -- /bin/sh Command to run instead of the image's default → everything after -- goes to the container
  • Why a test Pod at all → a ClusterIP isn't reachable from the laptop → I must test from inside the cluster
  • Image choice →
    • nginx → has curl → curl backend-svc:9090
    • busybox → no curl → use wget -qO- backend-svc:9090 | has nslookup
    • nicolaka/netshoot → everything (curl, dig, nslookup, tcpdump) → best for network debugging
  • One-shot, no shell:
kubectl run tmp --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox -- wget -qO- backend-svc:9090
  • Newer kubectl prints → "All commands and output from this session will be recorded in container logs" → anything typed (including secrets) ends up in kubectl logs → don't paste credentials into test Pods

docs.title: What happened on curl backend-svc:9090
docs.text:
From inside the test Pod:

# curl backend-svc:9090
Hello from Backend
# cat /etc/resolv.conf
search default.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
nameserver 10.96.0.10
options ndots:5

kubectl get svc -n kube-system              # kube-dns  ClusterIP  10.96.0.10  53/UDP,53/TCP,9153/TCP
kubectl describe svc kube-dns -n kube-system   # Selector k8s-app=kube-dns → Endpoints 10.244.0.2:53, 10.244.0.3:53
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide     # coredns-... Pods on exactly those IPs
  1. nameserver 10.96.0.10 → the Pod sends DNS queries here → it's the kube-dns Service
  2. kube-dns is a normal ClusterIP Service → its endpoints are the 2 CoreDNS Pods → same label-selector mechanism as backend-svc, just in kube-system
  3. backend-svc isn't a full name → resolver appends the search domains in order → first try backend-svc.default.svc.cluster.local → exists → done
  4. CoreDNS answers with backend-svc's ClusterIP
  5. kube-proxy (one Pod per node) has written rules on every node → ClusterIP:9090 → one of the 3 backend Pods on :5678
test Pod → CoreDNS (via kube-dns 10.96.0.10) → backend-svc = 10.96.x.x
        → 10.96.x.x:9090 → kube-proxy rules → backend Pod :5678 → "Hello from Backend"
  • ndots:5 → names with fewer than 5 dots try the search domains first → great for short in-cluster names | costs extra lookups for external names (google.com → 3 failed lookups first) → fix: query the FQDN with a trailing dot (google.com.) or lower ndots in the Pod's dnsConfig
  • Short name works only in the same namespace → more in Namespaces

docs.title: Imperative commands worth knowing
docs.text:
# generate
kubectl run <pod> --image=<img> --dry-run=client -o yaml > pod.yaml
kubectl create deployment <name> --image=<img> --replicas=3 --port=80 --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml
kubectl expose deployment <name> --port=80 --target-port=8080 --dry-run=client -o yaml > svc.yaml
kubectl create configmap <name> --from-literal=key=value --dry-run=client -o yaml > cm.yaml
kubectl create secret generic <name> --from-file=./creds --dry-run=client -o yaml > secret.yaml
kubectl create namespace <name> --dry-run=client -o yaml > ns.yaml

# debug / operate
kubectl run tmp --rm -it --restart=Never --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- sh
kubectl port-forward deploy/<name> 8080:80
kubectl logs <pod> [-f] [--previous]
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh
kubectl scale deploy <name> --replicas=5
kubectl rollout restart deploy <name>
kubectl rollout undo deploy <name>
kubectl label pod <pod> key=value [--overwrite]
  • After any imperative change to something that came from a file → update the file → otherwise file and cluster drift apart (see last-applied-configuration)
  • Secrets in real setups → Sealed Secrets / External Secrets / Vault, not create secret by hand

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
kubectl delete -f backend-deploy.yaml -f frontend-deploy.yaml
kubectl get all
  • delete -f removes everything the file describes → no need to delete Deployment and Service one by one (and no services "backend-deploy" not found from guessing the wrong name)

Quick revision

  • Imperative → generate YAML, exams, debugging | declarative YAML in Git → how real clusters run
  • --dry-run=client = build locally | --dry-run=server = full API validation, not saved | -o yaml = print it
  • > overwrites, >> appends → add --- between objects
  • kubectl expose reads the live Deployment → apply the Deployment first
  • --port on create deployment = containerPort = documentation | the app decides the real port
  • Service port = what callers use | targetPort = the app's port in the Pod | nodePort set by editing YAML
  • create deployment labels Pods app=<name> only → custom labels by editing the YAML
  • Test Pod → kubectl run tmp --rm -it --restart=Never --image=... -- sh → ClusterIP is only reachable from inside
  • Pod DNS → /etc/resolv.conf → kube-dns Service → CoreDNS Pods → search domains make short names work

Interview points

  • Are imperative commands used in production? → not to manage workloads; production uses declarative manifests in Git applied by CI/CD or GitOps, while imperative commands are used to generate manifests and for debugging
  • --dry-run=client vs --dry-run=server? → client builds the object locally without creating it; server sends it to the API server for schema and admission validation but does not persist it
  • Does containerPort open or expose a port? → no, it is informational; the application decides which port it listens on and a Service exposes it, though kubectl expose and named ports use it
  • Why must the Deployment exist before kubectl expose, even with a client dry-run? → expose reads the live Deployment to copy its selector into the Service
  • How do you set a fixed nodePort when kubectl expose has no flag for it? → generate the YAML and add nodePort under ports, or use kubectl create service nodeport --node-port and fix its selector
  • Why put --- between objects in one file? → it separates YAML documents; without it the objects merge into one document with duplicate keys
  • How do you test a ClusterIP Service? → from a temporary Pod inside the cluster, e.g. kubectl run tmp --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox -- wget -qO- svc:port
  • How does a Pod resolve a short Service name? → /etc/resolv.conf points to the kube-dns Service (CoreDNS) and its search domains expand the name to service.namespace.svc.cluster.local
