  • What does ndots:5 do and why can it hurt? → names with fewer than five dots try the search domains first, so external names cause several failed lookups before the real one
  • What happens if you change a Pod's label so it no longer matches? → it drops out of the Service endpoints and the ReplicaSet creates a replacement, leaving the relabelled Pod orphaned

docs.title: What kind is
docs.text:
• kind = Kubernetes in Docker → runs a whole Kubernetes cluster on my laptop
  • Each node is a Docker container running the kindest/node image → inside it: systemd, kubelet, containerd, and the control-plane Pods
  • Free, starts in about a minute, safe to break and delete → perfect for learning and labs
  • Other local options → minikube, k3d | real clusters → kubeadm, EKS, GKE, AKS
  • Install docs → kubectl and kind

docs.title: kubectl vs the cluster version
docs.text:
• kubectl → the client, the remote control on my laptop
  • kindest/node image → the cluster itself, the TV
  • They don't have to match exactly → kubectl must be within ±1 minor version of the API server
  • My setup → kubectl v1.37.2 + cluster v1.37.0 → same minor (1.37) → fine
kubectl version --client
kind version

docs.title: Creating a cluster from a config file
docs.text:
• kind-cluster.yaml → 1 control-plane + 2 workers, pinned image
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
  - role: control-plane
    image: kindest/node:v1.37.0@sha256:a1ed56cfb0e7b93589bdf97c8cd566405a265939e3620fc4f5de89adff580ae5
  - role: worker
    image: kindest/node:v1.37.0@sha256:a1ed56cfb0e7b93589bdf97c8cd566405a265939e3620fc4f5de89adff580ae5
  - role: worker
    image: kindest/node:v1.37.0@sha256:a1ed56cfb0e7b93589bdf97c8cd566405a265939e3620fc4f5de89adff580ae5

kind create cluster --name my-first-cluster --config kind-cluster.yaml
kind get clusters
docker ps                  # 3 containers = 3 nodes
kubectl get nodes -o wide
  • Image tag + digest → copy both from the kind release notes for my kind version → GitHub kubernetes-sigs/kind releases → "Images pre-built for this release"
  • kind v0.33.0 ships v1.37.0 → that image needs kind v0.33.0 or newer
  • Only the control-plane container publishes a port → 127.0.0.1:40627->6443/tcp → 6443 = API server → that is how kubectl reaches the cluster

docs.title: Config file vs plain command
docs.text:
• kind create cluster --name my-second-cluster → no file → one node, kind's default image (change it with --image)
  • Config file is better:
    • version control → in Git, easy to track and roll back
    • declarative → same cluster every time, on every machine
    • shareable → whole team gets the same setup
    • single source of truth → no "which flags did I use?"
  • Same idea as Terraform, Ansible, Helm and Kubernetes manifests → YAML (or JSON) files describe the setup

docs.title: Lab: my first two clusters
docs.text:
1. Created my-first-cluster from the config file → 3 nodes
  2. Created my-second-cluster with no file → 1 node
  3. kubectl get nodes → showed only my-second-cluster-control-plane → kind switched my current context to the newest cluster
  4. Second cluster showed NotReady at 20s old → normal, node turns Ready once the CNI (kindnet) is up, about 30–60s
  5. Switched back with kubectl config use-context kind-my-first-cluster
Symptom Cause Fix Changed the tag to v1.37.2 but kept the v1.37.0 digest Digest belongs to one exact image; with both given, Docker pulls by digest and ignores the tag Use a tag + digest pair exactly as listed in the kind release notes Wanted the node image to match my kubectl v1.37.2 kubectl is the client; only ±1 minor skew matters Keep v1.37.0 kubectl get clusters → the server doesn't have a resource type "clusters" A cluster doesn't know about other clusters; kubectl only lists objects inside one cluster kind get clusters or kubectl config get-contexts kubectl get nodes shows only the second cluster kind create cluster sets the current context to the new cluster kubectl config use-context kind-my-first-cluster kubectl config set-context kind-my-first-cluster said "modified" but nothing changed set-context edits a context, it doesn't switch use-context switches kubectl get pods → No resources found in default namespace No Pods created yet; system Pods live in kube-system kubectl get pods -n kube-system

docs.title: The kubeconfig file
docs.text:
• File that tells kubectl which clusters exist, how to reach them, and who I am on each
  • Default path → ~/.kube/config | without it kubectl doesn't know where any cluster is
  • Analogy → phone contacts + saved Wi-Fi passwords → clusters = addresses, users = logins, contexts = saved shortcuts, current-context = who I'm on a call with right now

docs.title: Its four sections
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
clusters:                              # WHERE
- name: kind-my-first-cluster
  cluster:
    server: https://127.0.0.1:40627    # API server address
    certificate-authority-data: ...    # to trust the server's certificate
users:                                 # WHO
- name: kind-my-first-cluster
  user:
    client-certificate-data: ...       # my identity
    client-key-data: ...               # my private key
contexts:                              # WHERE + WHO + NAMESPACE
- name: kind-my-first-cluster
  context:
    cluster: kind-my-first-cluster
    user: kind-my-first-cluster
    namespace: default                 # optional
current-context: kind-my-first-cluster # which one kubectl uses now
  • kind gives the cluster, user and context the same name → confusing | in real setups they usually differ (e.g. context prod-context → cluster cluster-3 + user varun-user)
  • The certificate here is the authentication step ("who are you") → then RBAC decides what I'm allowed to do → see RBAC & Request Flow

docs.title: When the file changes
docs.text:
• Changes when I change clusters or contexts:
    • create a cluster → kind create cluster, aws eks update-kubeconfig --name my-cluster
    • delete a cluster → kind delete cluster
    • switch context → kubectl config use-context
    • edit a context → kubectl config set-context
  • Does not change when I create, delete or scale Pods, Deployments, Services → those live inside the cluster, in etcd
  • kubeconfig = address book for reaching clusters, not a record of what runs in them
  • Check → md5sum ~/.kube/config before and after kubectl create deployment (same) vs use-context (different)

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Holds credentials → anyone with my kubeconfig has my access to the cluster (on prod, maybe full admin)
  • Never commit it to Git, never paste it in chats or screenshots
  • chmod 600 ~/.kube/config → only I can read it

docs.title: Contexts
docs.text:
• Context = cluster + user + namespace saved under one name
  • Lets me switch between many clusters (dev, staging, prod) without retyping addresses and credentials
  • Prevents running a command on the wrong cluster by accident → always check before anything destructive
kubectl config get-contexts               # list, * = current
kubectl config current-context            # just the current one
kubectl config use-context <name>         # SWITCH
kubectl get nodes --context <name>        # one command on another cluster, no switch
kubectl config view                       # whole file, secrets hidden
kubectl config view --minify              # only the current context

docs.title: set-context vs use-context
docs.text:
• use-context → switches to a context (changes the current-context line)
  • set-context → edits a context's settings | with no settings given it changes nothing
  • Real use of set-context → default namespace so I don't type -n every time
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=kube-system
kubectl get pods                              # now kube-system Pods
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=default
kubectl get pods --namespace=dev              # override for one command

docs.title: Namespaces (first look)
docs.text:
• Kubernetes namespace = a virtual cluster inside one real cluster → logical separation of resources
  • Example → dev, staging, prod or one namespace per app on the same cluster
  • Same name can exist in two namespaces (web in dev and web in prod) without conflict
  • Built-in ones → default, kube-system (control-plane Pods), kube-public, kube-node-lease
  • Not the same as Linux namespaces (process isolation) → different idea, same word
  • Full chapter → Namespaces

docs.title: Other ways kubectl finds a cluster
docs.text:
kubectl get nodes --kubeconfig /path/to/other-config
export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config:~/work-config     # merge several files

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
kind delete cluster --name my-second-cluster
kind get clusters

Quick revision

  • kind = Kubernetes in Docker, each node is a container
  • Pin node images with tag + digest from the kind release notes
  • kubeconfig = clusters + users + contexts + current-context
  • use-context switches, set-context edits

Interview points

  • What is kind? → a tool that runs Kubernetes clusters locally, with each node as a Docker container; used for learning, testing and CI
  • Why create a kind cluster from a config file? → version control, reproducible and declarative setup, shareable across the team, single source of truth
  • Must kubectl match the cluster version exactly? → no, kubectl is supported within one minor version of the API server
  • What is a kubeconfig? → kubectl's config file, ~/.kube/config by default, with clusters (API server + CA), users (credentials) and contexts that pair a cluster with a user and namespace; current-context decides where kubectl points
  • What is a context? → a saved combination of cluster, user and namespace
  • use-context vs set-context? → use-context switches the current context; set-context edits a context, e.g. its default namespace
  • Does the kubeconfig change when you create a Deployment? → no, only when clusters or contexts change; workloads live in etcd inside the cluster
  • Why is the kubeconfig sensitive? → it holds credentials; whoever has it has your access to the cluster
  • How do you avoid running a command on the wrong cluster? → check current-context before acting, use clear context names, or pass --context explicitly
  • Kubernetes namespace vs Linux namespace? → a Kubernetes namespace groups API objects logically; a Linux namespace isolates what a process can see

docs.title: Normal scheduling (recap)
docs.text:
kubectl apply → API server stores the Pod (nodeName empty)
             → scheduler filters + scores nodes (resources, taints, affinity)
             → scheduler writes spec.nodeName
             → kubelet on that node sees a Pod assigned to it → starts it
  • The scheduler decides where a Pod goes → the kubelet only runs what is assigned to its node
  • Two ways to get a Pod onto a node without the scheduler choosing → manual scheduling and static Pods
Manual scheduling Static Pods Created by Me, through the API server (kubectl apply) The kubelet, from a file on the node How spec.nodeName set in the manifest Manifest placed in the kubelet's static Pod folder Needs the API server Yes No Scheduler involved No No Delete with kubectl delete pod Remove the manifest file from the node Used for Testing, debugging, scheduler down Control-plane components, per-node agents

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
• Set nodeName myself → the Pod is already bound to a node → the scheduler never picks it up
  • Analogy → a hotel guest who arrives with a room key → the receptionist (scheduler) does nothing → the room staff (kubelet) let them in
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: nginx-manual
spec:
  nodeName: my-new-cluster-worker
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80

kubectl apply -f manual-pod.yaml
kubectl get po -o wide        # NODE column = exactly the node I wrote

docs.title: Why it's useful
docs.text:
• Debugging → put a Pod on one specific node to test that node (networking, disk, a bad kubelet)
  • Node-specific test → check a workload on a node with special hardware
  • Scheduler down → Pods with nodeName still start, because only the kubelet is needed after the API server stores them
  • For real workloads → use nodeSelector / affinity instead → they go through the scheduler, so resources and taints are still checked

docs.title: What the scheduler would have checked, and nobody checks now
docs.text:
• Taints (NoSchedule) → ignored → a Pod with nodeName runs even on a tainted node
  • Resources → not pre-checked → the kubelet checks on admission → not enough CPU/memory → Pod goes Failed with reason OutOfcpu / OutOfmemory instead of waiting in Pending
  • Affinity, spreading → ignored
  • NoExecute taints still apply → they're enforced after the Pod is running (by the node lifecycle controller), so a nodeName Pod on a NoExecute node gets evicted

docs.title: Node that doesn't exist
docs.text:
• nodeName: no-such-node → the API server accepts it (no check) → no kubelet ever claims it → Pod stays Pending
  • The Pod garbage collector deletes Pods bound to nodes that don't exist → the Pod disappears shortly after

docs.title: Running a Pod on the control plane
docs.text:
spec:
  nodeName: my-new-cluster-control-plane
  • It runs, even though the control plane carries the taint node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule
kubectl describe node my-new-cluster-control-plane | grep -i taint
# Taints: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule
  • Why → only the scheduler reads NoSchedule → nodeName skips the scheduler → nobody checks the taint
  • Proof → same Pod with nodeSelector: {kubernetes.io/hostname: my-new-cluster-control-plane} instead of nodeName → stays Pending → Events: untolerated taint {node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: }
  • Proper way onto the control plane → a toleration for that taint (see Taints & Tolerations)
  • Single-node kind / minikube → the one node has no taint, so anything schedules there → a multi-node kind cluster does taint the control plane

docs.title: The control plane is a node too
docs.text:
• Architecture diagrams draw the control plane as a separate box → on kubeadm / kind it's a normal node that also runs the control-plane components
  • Every node, control plane included, has:
    • kubelet → runs Pods
    • container runtime → containerd
    • kube-proxy → Service rules
  • The control-plane node additionally runs API server, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager → as Pods
kubectl get po -n kube-system -o wide
# etcd-my-new-cluster-control-plane                      ... my-new-cluster-control-plane
# kube-apiserver-my-new-cluster-control-plane            ... my-new-cluster-control-plane
# kube-controller-manager-my-new-cluster-control-plane   ... my-new-cluster-control-plane
# kube-scheduler-my-new-cluster-control-plane            ... my-new-cluster-control-plane
  • The taint exists to protect it → a heavy app eating CPU/memory there could slow or crash the API server or etcd → whole cluster suffers
  • So it's a policy, not a technical limit → that's why nodeName gets around it
Setup Pods on the control plane? kind / kubeadm, multi-node Possible → tainted by default Single-node kind / minikube Yes → no taint EKS / GKE / AKS No → the provider runs the control plane; it isn't even in kubectl get nodes

docs.title: The chicken-and-egg problem
docs.text:
• Normal Pods need the API server (to be stored) and the scheduler (to be placed)
  • But the API server and scheduler are themselves Pods → who starts them before they exist?
  • Answer → the kubelet starts them directly from files on disk → static Pods

docs.title: What a static Pod is
docs.text:
• A Pod created and managed by the kubelet of one node, from a manifest in a folder on that node
  • The kubelet watches the folder:
    • file added → start the Pod
    • file changed → recreate the Pod
    • file removed → stop the Pod
  • No API server, no scheduler, no controller involved → always bound to that one node
  • Can be on any node → control plane or worker

docs.title: Where the folder is
docs.text:
• Set in the kubelet config → staticPodPath → kubeadm / kind default /etc/kubernetes/manifests
# kind nodes are Docker containers → get in with docker exec
docker exec -it my-new-cluster-control-plane bash
grep staticPodPath /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml     # staticPodPath: /etc/kubernetes/manifests
ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests
# etcd.yaml  kube-apiserver.yaml  kube-controller-manager.yaml  kube-scheduler.yaml
  • On a real cluster (VMs / bare metal) → ssh into the node instead of docker exec
  • Workers have the same folder → usually empty

docs.title: Mirror Pods
docs.text:
• The kubelet also creates a mirror Pod in the API server for every static Pod → so kubectl get pods can show it
  • Name → <pod-name>-<node-name> → nginx-static-pod-my-new-cluster-control-plane
  • The mirror is a read-only reflection → I can't really control the static Pod through it
  • kubectl delete pod on a mirror → the mirror goes away → the kubelet recreates it immediately → the real Pod never stopped
  • Only way to remove a static Pod → delete (or move out) its manifest file

docs.title: Limits of static Pods
docs.text:
• No Deployment / ReplicaSet → no rolling updates, no replicas, no self-healing across nodes → just the kubelet restarting it on this node
  • The spec can't reference other API objects → no ServiceAccount, ConfigMap or Secret
  • Node dies → its static Pods die with it → nothing moves them

docs.title: Static Pods vs DaemonSets
docs.text: Static Pod DaemonSet Managed by kubelet, from a local file DaemonSet controller, through the API server Needs the API server No Yes Update with Editing the file on each node kubectl apply once Typical use Control-plane components Per-node agents → log shippers, monitoring, CNI

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
• Control-plane bootstrapping → API server, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager on kubeadm / kind
  • Must run even if the API server is down → the kubelet keeps them alive regardless
  • Fixing a broken control plane → edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml → kubelet restarts the API server with the new config → a common CKA task

docs.title: Lab: manual scheduling
docs.text:
kubectl get nodes

# worker
kubectl apply -f manual-pod.yaml                 # nodeName: my-new-cluster-worker
kubectl get po -o wide

# control plane
# copy the file, change name to nginx-manual-cp and nodeName to my-new-cluster-control-plane
kubectl apply -f manual-pod-cp.yaml
kubectl get po -o custom-columns=POD:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName

# proof that the scheduler would refuse → stays Pending
kubectl run sel-cp --image=nginx \
  --overrides='{"apiVersion":"v1","spec":{"nodeSelector":{"kubernetes.io/hostname":"my-new-cluster-control-plane"}}}'
kubectl describe po sel-cp | tail -5

kubectl delete po nginx-manual nginx-manual-cp sel-cp
  • kubectl get po -o yaml | grep node also shows node.kubernetes.io/not-ready and unreachable → those are tolerations added to every Pod automatically, not related to manual scheduling

docs.title: Lab: static Pod
docs.text:
docker exec -it my-new-cluster-control-plane bash

cat <<EOF > /etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-pod.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: nginx-static-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
EOF
exit

kubectl get po                                                  # nginx-static-pod-my-new-cluster-control-plane
kubectl delete po nginx-static-pod-my-new-cluster-control-plane
kubectl get po                                                  # back again

docker exec my-new-cluster-control-plane rm /etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-pod.yaml
kubectl get po                                                  # gone
  • Never leave a stray or temporary file in /etc/kubernetes/manifests → the kubelet treats every manifest there as a Pod to run
  • Editing control-plane manifests → keep a backup outside that folder (cp kube-apiserver.yaml /root/) → a copy left inside becomes a second API server

Quick revision

  • Scheduler decides the node → writes nodeName | kubelet only runs Pods assigned to its node
  • Manual scheduling = I set nodeName → scheduler skipped → NoSchedule taints, affinity and resource fit not checked
  • Not enough resources on a nodeName Pod → kubelet rejects it → OutOfcpu / OutOfmemory, not Pending
  • NoExecute still evicts nodeName Pods → enforced after scheduling
  • Control plane = a node with kubelet, containerd, kube-proxy + control-plane Pods → protected by the control-plane:NoSchedule taint
  • Static Pod = kubelet runs it from a file in staticPodPath (/etc/kubernetes/manifests) → no API server needed
  • Mirror Pod = read-only copy in the API server, named <pod>-<node> → kubectl delete doesn't stop the real Pod
  • Remove a static Pod → delete its manifest file

Interview points

  • What is manual scheduling? → setting spec.nodeName in the Pod manifest so the Pod is bound to a node directly and the scheduler is skipped
  • Why can a Pod with nodeName run on a tainted control-plane node? → NoSchedule taints are enforced by the scheduler, and nodeName bypasses the scheduler; the kubelet doesn't check them
  • Does nodeName bypass NoExecute taints? → no, NoExecute is enforced after the Pod is running and the Pod gets evicted
  • What happens if nodeName points to a node without enough resources? → the kubelet rejects the Pod on admission and it fails with OutOfcpu or OutOfmemory
  • What happens if nodeName points to a node that doesn't exist? → the Pod stays Pending because no kubelet claims it, and the Pod garbage collector deletes it
  • What is the proper way to run a Pod on a specific node? → nodeSelector or node affinity, plus a toleration if the node is tainted, so the scheduler still checks the rules
  • How do control-plane components run on a kubeadm cluster? → as static Pods from manifests in /etc/kubernetes/manifests on the control-plane node
  • What is a static Pod? → a Pod managed directly by the kubelet of one node from a local manifest file, without the API server or scheduler
  • How do you find the static Pod directory? → the staticPodPath field in the kubelet config, usually /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
  • What is a mirror Pod? → a read-only object the kubelet creates in the API server so a static Pod shows in kubectl, named pod-name dash node-name
  • Why does kubectl delete not remove a static Pod? → it only deletes the mirror Pod; the kubelet still has the manifest and recreates it
  • How do you delete a static Pod? → remove its manifest file from the static Pod directory on that node
  • Static Pod vs DaemonSet? → a static Pod is managed by one node's kubelet from a file and needs no API server; a DaemonSet is managed by a controller through the API server and runs one Pod per node
  • Can you use static Pods on EKS or GKE control planes? → no, the provider manages the control plane and you have no access to its nodes

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
• One cluster, many teams / apps / environments → without separation it's one flat pile:
    • Two teams can't both have a Service called backend-svc → names must be unique
    • kubectl get pods shows everyone's Pods
    • No clean way to give a team access to only its own stuff, or cap how much CPU/memory it uses
  • Running a separate cluster per team or app → expensive and a lot to operate

docs.title: What a namespace is
docs.text:
• A logical partition inside one cluster → a folder that groups resources
  • Names only need to be unique within a namespace → team-a/backend-svc and team-b/backend-svc can both exist
  • Analogy → a big house shared by 4 families → without rooms there's no privacy or order → give each family a room
    • house = cluster | families = apps / teams | rooms = namespaces
  • Not the same as Linux namespaces (process isolation for containers, see Container Runtime Internals) → same word, different idea

docs.title: Why use them
docs.text:
• Organisation → group related resources by team, app or environment → manage them together
  • No naming conflicts → same names in different namespaces
  • Access control → RBAC Roles and RoleBindings are per namespace → a developer gets dev only
  • Resource limits → ResourceQuota and LimitRange are per namespace
  • Network rules → NetworkPolicies are written per namespace
  • Multi-tenancy → many apps / teams on one cluster
  • Bulk cleanup → delete the namespace → everything inside goes with it

docs.title: Built-in namespaces
docs.text:
kubectl get namespaces        # or: kubectl get ns
Namespace Holds default My stuff when I don't say otherwise → lets a new cluster be used without creating a namespace kube-system Objects created by Kubernetes itself → CoreDNS, kube-proxy, and on kind/kubeadm the control-plane Pods (apiserver, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager) kube-public Readable by everyone, even unauthenticated → mostly the cluster-info ConfigMap, almost empty kube-node-lease One Lease object per node → node heartbeats the control plane uses to judge node health local-path-storage kind only → the Local Path Provisioner that backs PersistentVolumes

docs.title: Namespaced vs cluster-scoped
docs.text:
• Not every resource lives in a namespace
Namespaced Cluster-scoped (no namespace) Pods, Deployments, ReplicaSets, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, PVCs, Roles, RoleBindings, ServiceAccounts, Ingress, NetworkPolicies, ResourceQuotas Nodes, Namespaces themselves, PersistentVolumes, StorageClasses, ClusterRoles, ClusterRoleBindings, CRDs 
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=true
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false
  • -n on a cluster-scoped resource is ignored → kubectl get nodes -n dev still lists every node
  • Namespaces can't be nested → one level only

docs.title: Imperative
docs.text: kubectl create namespace app1-ns          # or: kubectl create ns app1-ns

docs.title: Declarative
docs.text:
# app1-ns.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: app1-ns

kubectl apply -f app1-ns.yaml
  • Generate it instead of typing → kubectl create ns app1-ns --dry-run=client -o yaml > app1-ns.yaml
  • Name rules → lowercase letters, numbers, - | max 63 chars | can't start with kube- (reserved)

docs.title: List and inspect
docs.text:
kubectl get ns
kubectl describe ns app1-ns               # labels, status, quotas and limits applied

docs.title: Delete
docs.text:
kubectl delete namespace app1-ns
  • Deletes the namespace and everything inside it → Pods, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, PVCs… → no undo, no confirmation prompt
  • Namespace shows Terminating while its contents are removed → stuck in Terminating for long = some object has a finalizer that can't complete (often a CRD whose controller is gone) → find it with kubectl api-resources --verbs=list --namespaced -o name | xargs -n1 kubectl get -n app1-ns --ignore-not-found
  • default, kube-system, kube-public, kube-node-lease can't be deleted

docs.title: The -n and -A flags
docs.text:
Flag Meaning -n <ns> / --namespace <ns> Run the command in that namespace -A / --all-namespaces Run it across every namespace → adds a NAMESPACE column (neither) The namespace set in the current context → default unless changed 
kubectl get pods -n app1-ns
kubectl get services -A
kubectl get all -n kube-system
  • Every namespaced command is scoped to one namespace → that's why kubectl get pods showed only my app, while -n kube-system showed CoreDNS, kube-proxy and the rest
  • NotFound on something I know exists → first suspect → wrong namespace

docs.title: Way 1 → -n at apply time
docs.text:
kubectl create ns app1-ns
kubectl apply -f frontend-deploy.yaml -n app1-ns
kubectl apply -f backend-deploy.yaml -n app1-ns
kubectl get all -n app1-ns
  • Same YAML files as in Imperative Commands → no change to the files → the objects just land in app1-ns
  • Can apply the same files to default and app1-ns → two independent copies, same names

docs.title: Way 2 → namespace in the manifest
docs.text:
metadata:
  name: backend-deploy
  namespace: app1-ns
  • Better for real setups → the file says where it belongs → no relying on someone remembering -n
  • Conflict → file says app1-ns, command says -n dev → error: the namespace from the provided object "app1-ns" does not match the namespace "dev"
  • The namespace must exist first → otherwise namespaces "app1-ns" not found → put the Namespace object first in the file (or a 00-namespace.yaml)

docs.title: The Service and its Pods
docs.text: • A Service's selector only matches Pods in its own namespace → backend-svc in app1-ns never sends traffic to backend Pods in default

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
From a test Pod in default (with backend running only in app1-ns):

kubectl run test-pod --image=busybox -it --rm --restart=Never -- /bin/sh
# wget -qO- backend-svc:9090             ✗ bad address 'backend-svc'
# wget -qO- backend-svc.app1-ns:9090     ✓ Hello from Backend

From a test Pod in app1-ns:

kubectl run test-pod -n app1-ns --image=busybox -it --rm --restart=Never -- /bin/sh
# wget -qO- backend-svc:9090             ✓ Hello from Backend
  • busybox has no curl → use wget -qO- (or an image with curl → nginx, curlimages/curl, nicolaka/netshoot)

docs.title: Why → the search domains
docs.text:
# cat /etc/resolv.conf   (Pod in app1-ns)
search app1-ns.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
nameserver 10.96.0.10
options ndots:5
  • The first search domain is the Pod's own namespace → short name backend-svc becomes backend-svc.app1-ns.svc.cluster.local
  • From default the first try is backend-svc.default.svc.cluster.local → doesn't exist → the remaining search domains don't form a valid Service name either → bad address
  • backend-svc.app1-ns → second search domain turns it into backend-svc.app1-ns.svc.cluster.local → works

docs.title: Name formats
docs.text:
Called from Name Same namespace backend-svc Other namespace backend-svc.app1-ns Anywhere (FQDN) backend-svc.app1-ns.svc.cluster.local 
<service-name>.<namespace>:<service-port>      →  backend-svc.app1-ns:9090
  • The port is the Service port (9090), not the container port (5678)
  • Gotcha → if default also has a backend-svc (left from an earlier lab), the short name from default succeeds → it silently hits the default copy → when testing isolation, check kubectl get svc -A first
  • In app config → prefer <svc>.<ns> or the FQDN for anything crossing namespaces → never rely on the caller's namespace

docs.title: Namespaces are not isolation (by default)
docs.text:
• Namespaces separate names and management → not the network
  • A Pod in dev can reach a Service in prod → backend-svc.prod → by default nothing stops it
  • Pod IPs are one flat network across all namespaces (CNI job)
  • Real isolation = namespaces plus:
    • NetworkPolicy → allow / deny traffic between Pods and namespaces → needs a CNI that enforces it (Calico, Cilium) → kind's default kindnet ignores NetworkPolicies
    • RBAC → who can read / change what, per namespace
    • ResourceQuota / LimitRange → stop one namespace starving the others
    • Pod Security Admission → namespace labels that block privileged Pods
  • Strong isolation for untrusted tenants or prod → often separate clusters, not just namespaces

docs.title: Setting a default namespace
docs.text:
• Typing -n app1-ns on every command is tiring → store it in the context (see kind, kubeconfig & Contexts)
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=app1-ns
kubectl config view --minify | grep namespace        # namespace: app1-ns
kubectl config get-contexts                          # NAMESPACE column
kubectl get pods                                     # now app1-ns Pods
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=default    # switch back
  • It's saved in ~/.kube/config → stays after closing the terminal → easy to forget → run a delete in the wrong namespace
  • kubectl doesn't check the namespace exists → a typo in the name = every command returns "No resources found"
  • Typo in the flag (--namepsace) → error: unknown flag → read the flag name
  • Habit → show the current context and namespace in the shell prompt (kube-ps1), or use kubens (from kubectx) to switch

docs.title: ResourceQuota and LimitRange (first look)
docs.text:
• ResourceQuota → cap on the total a namespace can use
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: app1-quota
  namespace: app1-ns
spec:
  hard:
    pods: "10"
    requests.cpu: "2"
    requests.memory: 2Gi
    limits.cpu: "4"
    limits.memory: 4Gi
  • Once a CPU/memory quota exists → every new Pod must set requests/limits, or it's rejected
  • LimitRange → defaults and min/max per Pod or container in the namespace → fills in requests/limits for Pods that don't set them
kubectl describe ns app1-ns        # shows quota used / hard and the limit ranges
kubectl get resourcequota -n app1-ns

docs.title: How they're used in real setups
docs.text:
• Per environment → dev, staging, prod → prod often on its own cluster instead
  • Per team or app → payments, search, checkout
  • Per tool → argocd, monitoring (Prometheus, Grafana), ingress-nginx, cert-manager → Helm charts usually install into their own namespace (helm install ... -n monitoring --create-namespace)
  • Naming → clear and consistent → team-app-env style, e.g. payments-api-prod
  • Label namespaces (team=payments, env=prod) → NetworkPolicies and tools can select by them
  • Every manifest carries metadata.namespace → the namespace object is in Git too

docs.title: Lab: same app, two namespaces
docs.text:
kubectl create ns app1-ns
kubectl apply -f backend-deploy.yaml -f frontend-deploy.yaml -n app1-ns
kubectl get all -n app1-ns
kubectl get svc -A | grep -e backend -e frontend     # any copies left in default?

# from default
kubectl run t1 --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox -- wget -qO- backend-svc.app1-ns:9090

# from inside app1-ns
kubectl run t2 -n app1-ns --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox -- wget -qO- backend-svc:9090

# default namespace in the context
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=app1-ns
kubectl get pods
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=default

# cleanup → everything inside goes too
kubectl delete ns app1-ns
kubectl get ns

Quick revision

  • Namespace = logical partition inside one cluster → names unique per namespace, not per cluster
  • Built-ins → default, kube-system, kube-public, kube-node-lease (+ local-path-storage on kind)
  • Namespaced → Pods, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, PVCs, Roles | cluster-scoped → Nodes, PVs, StorageClasses, ClusterRoles, Namespaces
  • -n <ns> = one namespace | -A = all | neither = the context's namespace
  • kubectl delete ns deletes everything inside, no prompt → stuck Terminating = finalizer
  • Cross-namespace DNS → <svc>.<ns>:<service-port> | short name works only in the same namespace because of the search line
  • Namespaces don't isolate the network → NetworkPolicy (with a CNI that enforces it) + RBAC + quotas do
  • Default namespace → kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<ns> → saved in kubeconfig

Interview points

  • What is a namespace in Kubernetes? → a logical partition of one cluster that scopes resource names and is the unit for RBAC, resource quotas and network policies
  • Do namespaces provide network isolation? → no, Pods in any namespace can reach each other by default; isolation needs NetworkPolicies enforced by the CNI, plus RBAC and quotas
  • How does a Pod reach a Service in another namespace? → service.namespace or service.namespace.svc.cluster.local on the Service port
  • Why does the short Service name only work in the same namespace? → the Pod's resolv.conf search list starts with its own namespace.svc.cluster.local
  • Which resources are not namespaced? → Nodes, PersistentVolumes, StorageClasses, ClusterRoles, ClusterRoleBindings, CRDs and Namespaces themselves
  • What are the default namespaces? → default, kube-system, kube-public and kube-node-lease
  • What is kube-node-lease for? → it holds a Lease per node that the kubelet renews as a lightweight heartbeat for node health
  • What happens when you delete a namespace? → every namespaced object inside it is deleted; it stays Terminating until finalizers complete
  • Why is a namespace stuck in Terminating? → a resource inside has a finalizer whose controller can't finish, often a CRD whose operator was removed
  • How do you change the default namespace for kubectl? → kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=name, which is saved in the kubeconfig context
  • Can a Service select Pods in another namespace? → no, a Service selector only matches Pods in its own namespace
  • What do ResourceQuota and LimitRange do? → ResourceQuota caps the total resources and object counts of a namespace; LimitRange sets default and min/max requests and limits per Pod or container
  • Namespaces or separate clusters for prod? → namespaces are cheap soft isolation within one control plane; separate clusters give a hard boundary for blast radius, security and upgrades

docs.title: Nodes vs Pods
docs.text:
• Node → a machine (physical server, VM, or in kind a Docker container pretending to be a machine) → gives CPU, RAM, disk, network
  • Pod → my app running on that machine
  • Analogy → node = apartment building | Pod = a flat inside it | containers = the people living in the flat
  • One node holds many Pods → the scheduler decides which building each new flat goes into
Node Pod What A machine An app instance Contains Many Pods One or more containers Created by Me / the cloud / kind Kubernetes (usually through a Deployment) Lifespan Long (days, months) Short (can be replaced any time) Command kubectl get nodes kubectl get pods

docs.title: Pod
docs.text:
• Smallest thing Kubernetes runs → Kubernetes never runs a bare container, always a Pod
  • Wraps one or more containers that:
    • share one network namespace → same IP, same ports, talk to each other over localhost
    • can share volumes → same files
  • Usually one main container per Pod | extra containers = helpers (sidecars: log shipper, proxy)
  • Every Pod gets its own IP inside the cluster (given by the CNI plugin)
  • Pods are disposable → a bare Pod that dies or whose node dies is gone for good, nobody recreates it
  • So in production → never create bare Pods, let a Deployment manage them

docs.title: How containers in a Pod share the network
docs.text:
• Each Pod has its own network namespace → own IP, interfaces, routing table
  • A tiny pause container starts first and just holds that namespace open
  • App containers join the pause container's network namespace → that is why they share one IP
  • Pods are isolated from each other's networks but can reach each other by Pod IP
  • Linux namespaces explained in Container Runtime Internals

docs.title: ReplicaSet
docs.text:
• One job → keep exactly N copies of a Pod running
  • Keeps counting:
    • only 2 running → creates 1
    • 4 running → deletes 1
    • 3 running → does nothing
  • Same reconciliation loop as the rest of Kubernetes
  • Finds "its" Pods by labels, not by name
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: ReplicaSet
metadata:
  name: web-rs
spec:
  replicas: 3              # how many
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web             # which labels to count
  template:                # what a new Pod looks like
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx
  • Three parts → replicas (how many) | selector (which labels to count) | template (blueprint for new Pods)

docs.title: The label gotcha
docs.text:
• Counts by labels → a bare Pod I create with app=web gets counted as one of its 3 → the ReplicaSet deletes one Pod to get back to 3
  • Remove the label from one of its Pods → it stops counting that Pod → creates a new one → the old Pod keeps running, orphaned
  • It does not care who created a Pod, only what label it carries
  • It doesn't check what's inside the Pod either → a 2-container Pod with app=web gets adopted even though the template has 1 container
  • Adoption is recorded on the Pod → ownerReferences → deleting the ReplicaSet deletes adopted Pods too
kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].name}{"\n"}'   # which RS owns it

docs.title: Many ReplicaSets per cluster
docs.text:
• A cluster runs as many ReplicaSets as it needs → usually one per app version
  • Names → unique per namespace (web-rs can exist in default and in dev)
  • Selectors → must not overlap → two ReplicaSets selecting app=web fight over the same Pods → give each app its own label
  • A ReplicaSet lives in one cluster → other clusters know nothing about it
  • Cluster ≠ node → the ReplicaSet's Pods are in one cluster but the scheduler spreads them across its nodes → one machine dies, the rest keep serving

docs.title: Why I don't use ReplicaSets directly
docs.text:
• A ReplicaSet can keep count but can't update → change the image in its template → existing Pods keep the old image, only new Pods get the new one
  • That is why a Deployment sits on top of it

docs.title: ReplicationController vs ReplicaSet
docs.text:
• ReplicationController (RC) → the original, same job (keep N Pods) → legacy now
  • ReplicaSet (RS) → its replacement → the difference is how it selects Pods
apiVersion: v1                  # core group
kind: ReplicationController
metadata:
  name: web-rc
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:                     # plain key: value → exact match only
    app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx
ReplicationController ReplicaSet apiVersion v1 (core) apps/v1 Selector Equality-based only Equality-based and set-based Selector required? No (defaults to template labels) Yes Used by Deployments? No Yes Updates Manual Manual (Deployment automates them) Today Legacy, old tutorials and exam questions Everywhere, but created by Deployments
  • kubectl create rc no longer exists → RCs only via YAML
  • In practice → kubectl get rc is empty on real clusters | kubectl get rs shows dozens, all owned by Deployments

docs.title: Selectors: equality-based vs set-based
docs.text:
• Label = name tag on an object → app: web
  • Selector = filter that finds objects by their labels
  • Analogy → a team of 5 engineers tagged "Kubernetes", "Automation", "CI/CD" → selector "all Kubernetes experts" finds 2 of them without knowing their names
  • Used by ReplicaSets, Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Services, Jobs, NetworkPolicies → labels and selectors are everywhere

docs.title: Equality-based
docs.text:
• Exact match → app = web, env != prod
selector:
  matchLabels:
    app: web

docs.title: Set-based
docs.text:
• Rules instead of exact values → app in (web, api), "not prod", "has a tier label"
Operator Matches when Example In value is one of the list app is nginx or apache NotIn value is none of the list env is not development Exists key is present (any value) Pod has a tier label DoesNotExist key is absent Pod has no debug label 
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: ReplicaSet
metadata:
  name: web-setbased
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchExpressions:
      - key: app
        operator: In
        values: ["nginx", "apache"]
      - key: env
        operator: NotIn
        values: ["development"]
      - key: tier
        operator: Exists          # no values list for Exists / DoesNotExist
      - key: debug
        operator: DoesNotExist
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:                     # must satisfy every rule above
        app: nginx
        env: production
        tier: frontend            # no debug label, or the selector fails
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx
  • Between rules → AND | inside one In list → OR
  • matchLabels and matchExpressions can be combined → still AND
  • Template labels must satisfy the selector → otherwise the API server rejects the manifest
Pod labels Match? Why app=nginx, env=production, tier=frontend Yes passes all rules app=apache, env=staging, tier=backend Yes apache in list, not development, tier present app=nginx, env=development, tier=frontend No env is development app=nginx, env=production No no tier label app=nginx, env=production, tier=frontend, debug=true No debug label present
  • Same syntax on the command line → test a selector before writing it:
kubectl get pods -l app=web                                   # equality
kubectl get pods -l 'env!=prod'
kubectl get pods -l 'app in (nginx,apache)'                   # In
kubectl get pods -l 'env notin (development)'                 # NotIn
kubectl get pods -l tier                                      # Exists
kubectl get pods -l '!debug'                                  # DoesNotExist
kubectl get pods -l 'app in (nginx,apache),tier,!debug'       # comma = AND
  • In practice → most manifests use plain matchLabels → set-based is for "one of these", "not that", "has this key"

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
• A manager for Pods → I declare what I want, it keeps making it true
  • Gives:
    • Replicas → always keep N Pods | one dies → a new one appears
    • Rolling updates → change the image → Pods replaced gradually, no downtime
    • Rollbacks → new version broken → undo it
    • Scaling → 3 → 10 Pods with one command

docs.title: The three layers
docs.text:
Deployment  →  ReplicaSet  →  Pods  →  Containers
(versions)     (count)        (run)     (the app)
  • Deployment wraps ReplicaSets → handles versions, rolling updates, rollback
  • ReplicaSet wraps Pods → keeps the count
  • Pod wraps containers → shares network and storage
  • On an update → Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet for the new version, scales it up, scales the old one down
  • Old ReplicaSet stays (at 0 Pods) → that is what makes rollback instant
  • I never create ReplicaSets myself → the Deployment does it
  • Pod names show this → web-7d4b9c8f6-x2kqp = Deployment web + ReplicaSet hash 7d4b9c8f6 + random Pod suffix

docs.title: Why rolling updates are safe
docs.text:
• New Pods must be Ready before old Pods are removed
  • New image broken (e.g. wrong tag) → new Pods stuck in ImagePullBackOff → old Pods keep serving → no downtime
  • Then kubectl rollout undo brings the old version back

docs.title: Deployment manifest and update strategy
docs.text:
• Same shape as a ReplicaSet → only kind changes, plus an optional strategy
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/change-cause: "initial release nginx 1.19"
spec:
  replicas: 3
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10     # old ReplicaSets kept for rollback (default 10)
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate        # default
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1              # at most 1 Pod above replicas during an update
      maxUnavailable: 0        # never drop below 3 Ready Pods
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.19      # pin a tag so updates are visible
Strategy How Downtime Use when RollingUpdate replace Pods gradually No default, most stateless apps Recreate kill all old Pods, then start new ones Yes two versions must never run at once
  • maxSurge → how many extra Pods allowed during the update (default 25%) → speed
  • maxUnavailable → how many Pods may be not-Ready during the update (default 25%) → safety
  • maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 → slowest but always full capacity

docs.title: Labels vs annotations
docs.text:
• Label → name tag → used by selectors to find and group objects
  • Annotation → sticky note → extra information for humans or tools → never used for selecting
Labels Annotations Purpose Identify and select Describe Used by selectors Yes No Content Short key-values (app: web) Anything: change notes, build info, URLs, tool config Example env: prod kubernetes.io/change-cause: "update to 1.20"
  • Common real use → config for controllers → e.g. alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing is ignored by Kubernetes but read by the AWS Load Balancer Controller
  • Annotation values are always strings → quote numbers ('15')

docs.title: change-cause → readable rollout history
docs.text:
• kubernetes.io/change-cause → shown in the CHANGE-CAUSE column of rollout history
  • Without it → every revision shows <none> → no idea which revision was which
  • Set it in the YAML (best) or with kubectl annotate after each change → the note attaches to whichever revision is current at that moment
  • Second annotation onwards needs --overwrite
  • --record used to do this automatically → deprecated
kubectl set image deploy/web nginx=nginx:1.20
kubectl annotate deploy web kubernetes.io/change-cause="update nginx 1.19 to 1.20" --overwrite
kubectl rollout history deploy/web

REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
1         initial release nginx 1.19
2         update nginx 1.19 to 1.20

docs.title: Rollback in detail
docs.text:
• kubectl rollout undo deploy/web → go to the previous revision → run it twice = flip between the same two versions
  • kubectl rollout undo deploy/web --to-revision=N → jump to any revision still in history
  • kubectl rollout history deploy/web --revision=N → see that revision's image and settings before jumping
  • Rollback is not a restore → it creates a new revision with the old settings → the old number disappears from the list
    • history 1, 2, 3 → undo --to-revision=1 → history becomes 2, 3, 4 (4 = the old revision 1)
  • Under the hood → current ReplicaSet scaled to 0, the target revision's ReplicaSet scaled back up → no new image pull needed
  • History is limited → revisionHistoryLimit (default 10) → older ReplicaSets are deleted and can't be rolled back to
  • Can always move again → undo the undo, jump to another revision, or set image to a brand-new version

docs.title: Imperative rollback vs Git
docs.text:
• rollout undo changes the live Deployment but not my YAML or its last-applied-configuration → warning: "previously managed with 'kubectl apply'…"
  • After any imperative change → update the YAML to match → kubectl apply -f again → file and cluster agree
  • In real teams → rollback = revert the change in Git → CI/CD or Argo CD applies it → rollout undo is for emergencies and labs

docs.title: Pause and resume
docs.text:
• kubectl rollout pause deploy/web → stop rolling out while I make several changes (image, resources, env)
  • kubectl rollout resume deploy/web → all queued changes go out as one rollout, one revision
  • Also useful → pause a rollout that looks wrong, investigate, then resume or undo
Pod ReplicaSet Deployment Job Run containers Keep N Pods Manage versions of ReplicaSets Self-healing No Yes Yes (via ReplicaSet) Scaling No Yes Yes Rolling update / rollback No No Yes Use directly in production? Rarely No Yes, for stateless apps

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
# bare Pod: dies and stays dead
kubectl run solo --image=nginx
kubectl delete pod solo
kubectl get pods                      # gone

# Deployment: comes back
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx --replicas=3
kubectl get deploy,rs,pods
kubectl delete pod <one-web-pod>
kubectl get pods                      # replaced, new name
kubectl get pods -o wide              # NODE column = which machine each Pod is on

# scale
kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5

# rolling update + rollback
kubectl set image deployment/web nginx=nginx:1.27   # nginx = the CONTAINER name, not the Deployment name
kubectl rollout status deployment/web
kubectl get rs                        # old RS at 0, new RS at 3
kubectl annotate deploy web kubernetes.io/change-cause="update to 1.27" --overwrite
kubectl rollout history deployment/web
kubectl rollout history deployment/web --revision=2
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web                  # previous revision
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web --to-revision=1  # specific revision

# find the container name for set image
kubectl get deploy web -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[*].name}{"\n"}'

# image currently running
kubectl get deploy -o wide             # CONTAINERS + IMAGES columns

# pause, batch changes, resume
kubectl rollout pause deployment/web
kubectl set image deployment/web nginx=nginx:1.27
kubectl set resources deployment/web -c nginx --limits=memory=256Mi
kubectl rollout resume deployment/web

# not ready yet? (READY 0/3)
kubectl get pods                       # ContainerCreating = still pulling | ImagePullBackOff = bad image
kubectl describe pod <pod>             # Events → exact reason
kubectl get pods -w                    # watch live

# legacy
kubectl get rc
kubectl scale rc web-rc --replicas=4

# break it on purpose
kubectl set image deployment/web nginx=nginx:doesnotexist
kubectl get pods                      # new Pods ImagePullBackOff, old Pods still Running
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web

# labels
kubectl get pods --show-labels
kubectl get pods -l app=web
  • Node failure → docker stop <kind-worker> → node NotReady after ~40s → after a few minutes its Pods are recreated on another node → docker start to bring it back

Quick revision

  • Node = machine, Pod = app instance on it
  • Pod = one or more containers sharing one IP (network namespace) and volumes
  • ReplicaSet = keeps N Pods, finds them by label, can't update
  • Deployment = manages ReplicaSets, one per version → rolling updates and rollbacks
  • ReplicationController = legacy RS, equality selectors only → RS adds set-based (In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist)
  • RollingUpdate (default, no downtime) vs Recreate → tune with maxSurge / maxUnavailable
  • Labels select, annotations describe → kubernetes.io/change-cause fills rollout history
  • Rollback = new revision with old settings → limited by revisionHistoryLimit (10)

Interview points

  • Node vs Pod? → a node is a worker machine that provides compute; a Pod is the smallest deployable unit, one or more containers, scheduled onto a node
  • What is a Pod? → the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes: one or more containers sharing a network namespace (one IP) and volumes
  • How do containers in the same Pod talk? → over localhost, because they share the Pod's network namespace
  • What is the pause container? → a tiny container that holds the Pod's network namespace open so app containers can join it
  • What happens if a bare Pod dies? → nothing recreates it; only controllers like ReplicaSets bring Pods back
  • How does a ReplicaSet know which Pods are its own? → by label selector, not by name or owner
  • You create a Pod with the same labels as a ReplicaSet's Pods, what happens? → the ReplicaSet counts it and deletes one Pod to get back to the desired count
  • Why use a Deployment instead of a ReplicaSet? → a ReplicaSet can't do rolling updates; a Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet per version and shifts Pods gradually, which also enables rollback
  • How does a rollback work? → the old ReplicaSet is kept at 0 replicas; rollback scales it back up and scales the new one down
  • New image tag doesn't exist, does the app go down? → no, new Pods fail with ImagePullBackOff while old Pods keep running, because old Pods are only removed once new ones are Ready
  • ReplicationController vs ReplicaSet? → same job; RC is legacy core v1 with equality-based selectors only, RS is apps/v1 and also supports set-based selectors, and is what Deployments use
  • Equality-based vs set-based selectors? → equality matches exact values (=, !=); set-based uses In, NotIn, Exists and DoesNotExist; rules are ANDed
  • Can a cluster run many ReplicaSets? → yes; names must be unique per namespace and selectors shouldn't overlap or they fight over Pods
  • You change the image in a bare ReplicaSet, what happens? → existing Pods keep the old image; only Pods created later use the new one
  • RollingUpdate vs Recreate? → RollingUpdate replaces Pods gradually without downtime; Recreate deletes all old Pods first, used when two versions can't run together
  • What do maxSurge and maxUnavailable control? → maxSurge is how many extra Pods may exist during an update, maxUnavailable is how many may be unavailable; both default to 25%
  • Labels vs annotations? → labels identify objects and are used by selectors; annotations hold non-identifying metadata for humans and tools and are never used for selection
  • How do you record why a revision was made? → set the kubernetes.io/change-cause annotation, shown in kubectl rollout history
  • Does a rollback restore the old revision number? → no, it creates a new revision with the old template; the old number disappears from history
  • How far back can you roll back? → as far as revisionHistoryLimit allows, 10 old ReplicaSets by default
  • Why pause a Deployment? → to batch several changes into one rollout, or to stop a rollout while investigating a problem
  • Why does kubectl warn after rollout undo? → the live object changed but last-applied-configuration didn't, so the next kubectl apply may behave unexpectedly; update the YAML and re-apply

docs.title: Every request passes three gates
docs.text:
• Every request to the API server (from me, a controller or an app) goes through, in order:
    1. Authentication → who are you? (client certificate from kubeconfig, token, OIDC)
    2. Authorization → are you allowed to do this? → RBAC lives here
    3. Admission control → should this exact object be accepted, or changed first? → see Webhooks, CRDs & Operators
  • Fails any gate → request rejected, nothing is stored

docs.title: What RBAC is
docs.text:
• Role-Based Access Control → decides who can do what on which resources, where
  • Permissions are given to roles, then roles are given to people or apps
  • Without it → every user would be admin → one wrong command could delete production

docs.title: Office analogy
docs.text:
• I join a company and get an ID card
  • Me → the subject
  • Job description → "can enter the server room and read logs, can't delete anything" → the Role
  • HR assigning that job to me → "Aditya gets server-room-reader, on Floor 2 only" → the RoleBinding
  • Floor 2 → a namespace | whole building → the cluster
  • When I swipe at a door → system checks: does Aditya have a job that allows this, on this floor? → door opens or stays shut
  • A job description nobody holds does nothing → a Role alone gives no one access until a binding connects it to someone

docs.title: The four objects
docs.text: Object What it does Scope Role A set of permissions One namespace ClusterRole A set of permissions Whole cluster (or reusable in many namespaces) RoleBinding Gives a Role or ClusterRole to a subject One namespace ClusterRoleBinding Gives a ClusterRole to a subject Whole cluster

docs.title: The four questions RBAC answers
docs.text:
1. Who → subject:
    • User → a human | Kubernetes has no User object, users come from certificates or OIDC
    • Group → a set of users
    • ServiceAccount → identity for Pods and apps (CI/CD, operators) | a real Kubernetes object
  2. Can do what → verbs → get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete
  3. On what → resources → pods, deployments, secrets, pods/log
  4. Where → namespace (Role/RoleBinding) or whole cluster (ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding)

docs.title: Example: read-only Pods in dev
docs.text:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: pod-reader
  namespace: dev
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]                 # "" = core group (pods, services, configmaps)
  resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: read-pods
  namespace: dev
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: monitor
  namespace: dev
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

docs.title: Rules that matter
docs.text:
• Additive only → no "deny" rules → anything not explicitly allowed is denied
  • Least privilege → give only the verbs and resources actually needed → avoid cluster-admin and * wildcards
  • ClusterRole + RoleBinding → define permissions once cluster-wide, grant them inside one namespace only → common trick
  • roleRef can't be changed after creation → delete and recreate the binding
  • Built-in ClusterRoles worth knowing → view, edit, admin, cluster-admin

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
kubectl create namespace dev
kubectl create serviceaccount monitor -n dev

kubectl auth can-i list pods -n dev --as=system:serviceaccount:dev:monitor     # no

kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods -n dev
kubectl create rolebinding read-pods --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=dev:monitor -n dev

kubectl auth can-i list pods -n dev --as=system:serviceaccount:dev:monitor     # yes
kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n dev --as=system:serviceaccount:dev:monitor   # no

kubectl get roles,rolebindings -n dev
kubectl describe clusterrole view
kubectl auth can-i --list -n dev --as=system:serviceaccount:dev:monitor
  • Break it → remove list from the Role → rerun can-i → try kubectl get pods as that ServiceAccount → read the Forbidden error, it names the verb, resource and namespace

docs.title: Where I'll use it
docs.text:
• Any in-cluster tool runs as a ServiceAccount → I write its ClusterRole myself
  • Good interview story → "my tool needed read access to nodes, Pods and its CRDs, plus create only in its own namespace; here's how I scoped it"

Quick revision

  • Request flow = authentication → authorization (RBAC) → admission → etcd
  • Role/ClusterRole = what is allowed | RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding = who gets it
  • Additive only, no deny → least privilege
  • Test with kubectl auth can-i

Interview points

  • What is RBAC in Kubernetes? → the authorization layer; Roles and ClusterRoles define allowed verbs on resources, RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings attach them to users, groups or ServiceAccounts
  • Role vs ClusterRole? → a Role is limited to one namespace; a ClusterRole is cluster-wide or reusable across namespaces
  • Can a RoleBinding reference a ClusterRole? → yes, and it grants those permissions only inside the binding's namespace
  • Can you write a deny rule? → no, RBAC is additive; anything not allowed is denied
  • Authentication vs authorization? → authentication proves who you are; authorization (RBAC) decides what you may do
  • Where do users come from? → outside Kubernetes, through certificates or OIDC; ServiceAccounts are the only identities stored as objects
  • How do you check permissions? → kubectl auth can-i, with --as to test another user or ServiceAccount
  • Can you change a binding's roleRef? → no, delete and recreate the binding
  • What is least privilege? → give each identity only the exact verbs and resources it needs, avoiding cluster-admin and wildcards

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
• Kubernetes is a group of programs talking over the network → kubectl ↔ API server, API server ↔ etcd, kubelet ↔ containerd
  • They use two styles → REST and gRPC → knowing which is used where helps when reading logs, debugging and building tools

docs.title: REST
docs.text:
• An architectural style built on HTTP
  • Resources identified by URLs → /users/42, /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods
  • HTTP verbs act on them → GET (read), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE
  • Payload usually JSON → text, human-readable
  • Easy to debug with curl or a browser, works everywhere
  • Slower and heavier → text payloads repeat field names every time, JSON parsing costs CPU, mostly HTTP/1.1 (one request at a time per connection), no native streaming

docs.title: gRPC
docs.text:
• RPC framework from Google → RPC = Remote Procedure Call → call a function on another machine as if it were local → client.GetUser(ctx, req)
  • Contract defined first in a .proto file → client and server code generated from it
  • Runs over HTTP/2 → many requests at once on one connection (multiplexing)
  • Messages in protobuf → binary, compact, fast
  • Native streaming → server streaming, client streaming, both directions at once
  • Harder to debug → binary payloads, needs grpcurl instead of curl

docs.title: REST vs gRPC
docs.text:
REST gRPC Model Resources + HTTP verbs Calling functions Payload JSON (text) Protobuf (binary) Transport HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 HTTP/2 only Contract Optional (OpenAPI) Required (.proto), strongly typed Code generation Optional Built in, many languages Streaming Not native (needs SSE / WebSockets) Native, all directions Performance Slower, bigger payloads Faster, smaller payloads Browser support Native Needs gRPC-Web proxy Debugging Easy (curl, browser) Harder (grpcurl) Caching HTTP caching works No native HTTP caching
  • REST → public APIs, browsers, mobile apps, third-party integrations, simplicity
  • gRPC → internal service-to-service calls, low latency, high volume, streaming
  • Common pattern → REST at the edge (public), gRPC inside (between microservices)

docs.title: Protobuf (Protocol Buffers)
docs.text: • Google's format for serializing structured data → same job as JSON, but binary and schema-first

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Define the schema in a .proto file
syntax = "proto3";

message User {
  int32 id = 1;
  string name = 2;
  bool active = 3;
}

  • = 1, = 2, = 3 → field numbers, not values → they identify each field on the wire

  • Generate code → protoc --go_out=. user.proto → a Go struct User with encode/decode methods

  • Use it
u := &pb.User{Id: 42, Name: "Aditya", Active: true}
data, _ := proto.Marshal(u)   // binary bytes

docs.title: Why it's smaller
docs.text:
• JSON → {"id":42,"name":"Aditya","active":true} → 39 bytes, field names sent every time
  • Protobuf → only field number + type + value → about 12 bytes → both sides already have the schema, so names never travel
  • Small integers use varint encoding → as little as 1 byte

docs.title: Key properties
docs.text:
• Strongly typed → wrong types fail at compile time, not at runtime
  • Faster → no text parsing
  • Not human-readable → need the .proto to decode
  • Schema evolution → add new fields without breaking old clients (they ignore unknown field numbers)
  • Rule → never change or reuse a field number → mark removed ones reserved
JSON Protobuf Format Text Binary Schema Optional Required Size Larger Several times smaller Speed Slower parsing Faster Readable Yes No Browser-native Yes No

docs.title: Where Kubernetes uses each
docs.text:
Connection Style kubectl / users → API server REST over HTTPS (JSON) Internal clients → API server REST, can use protobuf instead of JSON API server → etcd gRPC Objects stored inside etcd Protobuf kubelet → containerd / CRI-O (CRI) gRPC kubelet → storage drivers (CSI) gRPC kubelet → device plugins (e.g. GPUs) gRPC
  • kubectl is just a REST client → see the real HTTP calls:
kubectl get pods -v=8          # shows GET /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods
kubectl get --raw /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods | head -c 300
kubectl api-resources          # every resource type the REST API exposes

Quick revision

  • REST = resources + verbs + JSON, easy and universal
  • gRPC = call functions, protobuf over HTTP/2, fast, typed, streaming
  • Protobuf = binary, schema-first, field numbers instead of names
  • Kubernetes: REST for its API, gRPC for etcd, CRI, CSI and device plugins

Interview points

  • REST vs gRPC? → REST is resource-oriented, JSON over HTTP, easy to debug and works everywhere, best for public APIs; gRPC is contract-first with protobuf over HTTP/2, faster, strongly typed and has native streaming, best for internal service calls
  • Why is gRPC faster? → binary protobuf payloads are smaller and cheaper to parse, and HTTP/2 multiplexes many calls over one connection
  • What is protobuf? → a binary, schema-first serialization format; you define messages in a .proto file and generate typed code, and field numbers replace field names on the wire
  • How does protobuf stay backward compatible? → old code ignores unknown field numbers; never reuse or change a field number, mark removed ones reserved
  • Is protobuf encryption? → no, it is only an encoding format
  • Where does Kubernetes use gRPC? → API server to etcd, and the kubelet to the container runtime (CRI), storage drivers (CSI) and device plugins
  • What protocol does kubectl use? → REST over HTTPS to the API server; -v=8 shows the requests

docs.title: The problem Services solve
docs.text:
• Pods are temporary → crash, rescheduled, replaced in a rollout → every new Pod gets a new IP
  • Frontend talks to backend by Pod IP → breaks the next time a backend Pod is replaced
  • 3 backend replicas → which one should the frontend call? → it would need its own load-balancing logic
  • Some Pods must be reachable inside the cluster only (backend), some from outside (frontend)
Without a Service:  User ─▶ Frontend Pod (IP keeps changing) ─▶ Backend Pod (IP keeps changing)   ✗

With Services:      User ─▶ frontend-svc ─▶ Frontend Pod ─▶ backend-svc ─▶ Backend Pod           ✓

docs.title: What a Service is
docs.text:
• A stable front door in front of a group of Pods
  • Gives →
    • a fixed virtual IP (ClusterIP) that never changes while the Service exists
    • a DNS name → backend-svc (short) or backend-svc.default.svc.cluster.local (full)
    • load balancing across all matching Ready Pods
    • automatic tracking → Pods come and go, the Service's list updates by itself
  • Analogy → customer-care number → which employee picks up keeps changing, the number stays the same
    • number = Service | employees = Pods | caller = frontend

docs.title: Pod networking vs Services
docs.text:
• Common confusion → "Services let Pods on different nodes talk" → not quite
  • Pods can already reach each other by Pod IP, same node or different node → that is the CNI plugin's job (Calico, Flannel, Cilium, kindnet in kind) → every Pod gets a unique IP, all nodes joined into one flat network
  • The Service adds what raw Pod IPs can't give → a stable name/IP + load balancing + auto-updating list of Pods
CNI (Pod network) Service Analogy The roads The address board / reception Gives Every Pod a unique IP, cross-node delivery Stable IP + DNS name, load balancing Without it Pods can't reach each other at all Pods can reach each other, but must track changing IPs themselves
  • A Service works the same whether its Pods are on one node or spread across many

docs.title: How a Service finds its Pods (labels and selectors)
docs.text:
• A Service never lists Pod names or IPs → it has a selector → "send traffic to every Pod with these labels"
  • Kubernetes keeps checking → which Pods have this label right now? → those become the Service's endpoints

docs.title: The label that connects everything
docs.text:
# Deployment
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend       # (2) Deployment finds ITS Pods by this label
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: backend     # (1) every Pod gets this label (sticker)
---
# Service
spec:
  selector:
    app: backend         # (3) Service finds Pods to send traffic to by this label
Where What it does template.metadata.labels Puts the label on each new Pod Deployment selector.matchLabels Deployment counts its own Pods by the label Service selector Service finds Pods to route to by the label
  • Deployment and Service don't know about each other → they're linked only through the Pods' labels
  • Change the label in one place and not the others → things break silently

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Automatic and live →
    • Pod dies → removed from the Service
    • New Pod comes up → added
    • Scale 3 → 5 → all 5 added, Service YAML untouched
  • Only Ready Pods → a Pod still starting or failing its readiness probe is not added → no traffic until Ready
  • Same namespace only → a Pod with app: backend in another namespace is ignored
  • Any Pod with the label gets traffic → even a random test Pod I accidentally label app: backend → keep labels specific
  • Doesn't care who created the Pod → delete the Deployment, create matching Pods another way → Service still routes to them

docs.title: Where the list lives → EndpointSlices
docs.text:
• The EndpointSlice controller (inside kube-controller-manager) writes the current Ready PodIP:targetPort list into EndpointSlice objects
  • Old API = Endpoints object → still shown in kubectl describe svc as the Endpoints: line
kubectl describe svc backend-svc                                        # Endpoints: line
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=backend-svc
  • Watch it update live →
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=backend-svc -w   # terminal 1
kubectl scale deployment backend-deploy --replicas=5                      # terminal 2 → 2 new IPs appear
  • Endpoints empty = selector matches no Pods OR matching Pods aren't Ready → the most common Service bug

docs.title: What a port is
docs.text:
• A machine has one IP but runs many apps → a message arrives → which app is it for? → the port decides
  • Each app listens on its own number → web server 80, MySQL 3306, SSH 22
  • Full address = IP : port → which machine : which app on it
  • Analogy → IP = apartment building | port = flat number | courier needs both

docs.title: The two ports of a Service
docs.text:
frontend  ─▶  backend-svc : 9090   ─▶   pod : 5678
              (Service IP) port         (Pod IP) targetPort
  • port → the port the Service listens on → what callers use → backend-svc:9090 → I choose it, any number
  • targetPort → the port the app inside the Pod listens on → where traffic finally lands → the app decides it, I just have to tell the Service what it is
  • The node swaps both parts → Service IP → Pod IP and 9090 → 5678
Hotel Kubernetes Reception Service Counter 9090 (guests go here) port Room 5678 (the person is actually here) targetPort Person in the room The app (http-echo) Guest The caller (frontend)
  • Memory trick → target = the app → shooting an arrow: fire from port, it lands on the targetPort
  • Who uses what →
    • Service → one IP (10.96.74.12), accepts traffic on 9090
    • Caller → sends to backend-svc:9090 → any other port → nothing answers
    • Pods → each has its own different IP (10.244.2.14, 10.244.1.14, 10.244.2.15) but all listen on the same 5678 (same app)
caller ─▶ 10.96.74.12:9090 ─┬─▶ 10.244.2.14:5678
          (Service)         ├─▶ 10.244.1.14:5678
                            └─▶ 10.244.2.15:5678
                               (different IPs, same port)

docs.title: Why two numbers at all
docs.text:
• Caller doesn't need to know the app's real port
  • App moves from 5678 → 8000 → change only targetPort → callers still use :9090 → nothing else breaks
  • In practice they are often the same → port: 80, targetPort: 80 → keeps it simple

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: YAML Caller uses App listens on port: 9090, targetPort: 5678 backend-svc:9090 5678 port: 80, targetPort: 3000 backend-svc:80 3000 port: 80, targetPort: 8080 backend-svc:80 8080

docs.title: Wrong targetPort = classic bug
docs.text:
• targetPort doesn't match the app's real port (app on 80, I wrote 5678) →
    • Service is created fine ✓ | Pods are 1/1 Running ✓ | Endpoints shows IPs ✓
    • but every request fails → connection refused / browser says empty response → the node forwards to a port where nothing is listening
  • Fix → set targetPort to the port the app really uses

docs.title: How to find which port an app uses
docs.text:
• nginx listens on 80 by default → set in its config (listen 80; in /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf)
  • hashicorp/http-echo listens on 5678 by default
  • Ways to check any image →
    1. The image's page on Docker Hub → docs mention the port
    2. EXPOSE in the image → only a label from the image author, usually right, not guaranteed
    3. Look inside the running container → what is actually listening (most reliable)
docker inspect nginx --format '{{.Config.ExposedPorts}}'                          # map[80/tcp:{}]
kubectl exec -it deploy/frontend-deploy -- cat /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf | grep listen
  • containerPort in a Deployment (ports: - containerPort: 80) → documentation only → does not open or block anything → Service's targetPort must still match the real port
App Default port nginx / Apache (HTTP) 80 HTTPS 443 hashicorp/http-echo 5678 Node.js apps often 3000 Flask 5000 Spring Boot / Tomcat 8080 MySQL 3306 PostgreSQL 5432 Redis 6379 MongoDB 27017 DNS 53
  • Defaults only → any app can be reconfigured → when something breaks, check the real config

docs.title: Service manifest anatomy
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: backend-svc          # also becomes its DNS name
spec:
  type: ClusterIP            # what kind of Service
  ports:                     # which door
    - protocol: TCP          # default TCP, can be skipped
      port: 9090             # Service's port (callers use this)
      targetPort: 5678       # app's port inside the Pod
  selector:                  # which Pods
    app: backend
  • Three parts under spec → type, ports, selector
    • type → what kind? → ClusterIP / NodePort / LoadBalancer / ExternalName
    • ports → which door? → port (counter) + targetPort (room) (+ nodePort for NodePort)
    • selector → which Pods? → label to match
  • Memory trick → T-P-S → "Tea, Pakoda, Samosa" → what kind, which door, which pods
  • type is optional → skipped = ClusterIP | ports and selector are almost always written
  • port can have a name → shown as <unset> in describe when not set → optional, nothing wrong
  • Imperative shortcut →
kubectl expose deployment backend-deploy --name=backend-svc --port=9090 --target-port=5678
kubectl expose deployment backend-deploy --port=9090 --target-port=5678 --dry-run=client -o yaml   # generate YAML

docs.title: Service types
docs.text:
Type Reachable from What it adds ClusterIP (default) Inside the cluster only Stable virtual IP + DNS name + load balancing NodePort Outside, at <anyNodeIP>:<nodePort> ClusterIP + same port (30000–32767) opened on every node LoadBalancer Outside, at one external IP/hostname NodePort + a cloud load balancer in front ExternalName Inside the cluster Just a DNS alias (CNAME) to an outside name, no IP, no Pods Headless (clusterIP: None) Inside the cluster No virtual IP, DNS returns each Pod's IP directly
  • They stack →
LoadBalancer  =  NodePort + cloud load balancer
NodePort      =  ClusterIP + port on every node
ClusterIP     =  internal fixed address

docs.title: Office-building analogy
docs.text: Building Kubernetes Office building complex Cluster Individual buildings Nodes Departments (HR, Finance) Pods Internal phone extensions ClusterIP → only works inside the complex Front-desk phone number of each building NodePort → outsiders call a building's front desk Call centre with one number LoadBalancer → routes to any working front desk IT support speed-dial 111 ExternalName → shortcut to an outside party

docs.title: ClusterIP
docs.text:
• Default type → reachable only inside the cluster → for Pod-to-Pod traffic (frontend → backend, backend → cache)
  • Gets a virtual IP from the Service CIDR (10.96.0.0/12 in kind) → not on any machine, Pod or network card

docs.title: The simple story
docs.text:
1. Frontend wants backend-svc → computers need an IP, not a name → asks the cluster's phonebook (CoreDNS) → answer 10.96.74.12
  2. Frontend sends the request to 10.96.74.12
  3. 10.96.74.12 is fake → nobody owns it → it exists only as a rule on every node
  4. As the packet leaves, the node checks its rule → "anything to 10.96.74.12? send it to one of the 3 backend Pods" → picks one, changes the address on the packet
