  5. That Pod replies → on the way back the node changes the reply's address back to 10.96.74.12 → frontend thinks the fake address answered

  6. Analogy → letter to "PO Box 9090" → post office rule: letters to that box go to any free employee → reply comes back stamped "PO Box 9090"

  7. Two things to remember →
    • the Service IP is fake → just a rule on every node
    • the node swaps the fake address for a real Pod's address, and swaps it back on the reply

docs.title: What happens when the Service is created
docs.text:
1. kubectl → API server → YAML validated, stored in etcd → at this point only a database record, nothing running
  2. IP allocated → API server picks a free IP from the Service CIDR → 10.96.74.12 → virtual, not attached anywhere
  3. Pods found → EndpointSlice controller reads selector: app=backend → finds all Ready Pods with that label → adds targetPort → 10.244.2.14:5678, 10.244.1.14:5678, 10.244.2.15:5678 → the Endpoints: line
  4. DNS record → CoreDNS (Pods in kube-system) watches the API server → adds backend-svc.default.svc.cluster.local → 10.96.74.12

  5. Rules on every node → kube-proxy (one per node, a DaemonSet) watches Services and EndpointSlices → writes iptables NAT rules on its node: "packet to 10.96.74.12:9090 → change destination to one of the 3 endpoints, pick randomly"

  6. Setup done → no process "runs" the Service → it's a DNS record + iptables rules on every node

docs.title: What happens on curl backend-svc:9090 (packet by packet)
docs.text:
1. App needs an IP → can't connect to a name
  2. Pod knows where DNS is → kubelet wrote /etc/resolv.conf into the Pod: 
    search default.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
nameserver 10.96.0.10
options ndots:5
    • nameserver 10.96.0.10 → send DNS questions here → that is the kube-dns Service (in front of the CoreDNS Pods)
    • search ... → short name backend-svc → try backend-svc.default.svc.cluster.local first
    • ndots:5 → names with fewer than 5 dots get the search suffixes tried first
  3. DNS question and answer → "what is backend-svc.default.svc.cluster.local?" → CoreDNS → 10.96.74.12
  4. App sends the packet → from 10.244.1.5:<random port> (frontend Pod) → to 10.96.74.12:9090
  5. Packet leaves the Pod → through the Pod's veth pair (virtual cable: one end in the Pod, one end on the node) → arrives in the node's kernel
  6. iptables catches it → rule matches 10.96.74.12:9090 → picks an endpoint at random, e.g. 10.244.2.15:5678 → DNAT (destination NAT):
    • before → to 10.96.74.12:9090
    • after → to 10.244.2.15:5678
    • kernel records the rewrite in conntrack (connection tracking table) so it can undo it for the reply
  7. Routing → is 10.244.2.15 on this node?
    • yes → delivered straight through that Pod's veth
    • no → the CNI carries it to the right node, which delivers it
  8. Backend Pod receives it on :5678 → http-echo accepts → doesn't know a Service was involved → sees the request coming from 10.244.1.5
  9. Reply → from 10.244.2.15:5678 to 10.244.1.5 → passes back through the frontend's node
  10. conntrack undoes the rewrite → source changed back:
    • before → from 10.244.2.15:5678
    • after → from 10.96.74.12:9090
    • why → the app talked to 10.96.74.12:9090; a reply from any other address would be rejected ("I never talked to you")

  11. Frontend gets the answer → from 10.96.74.12:9090 → never knows which Pod replied

  12. The "Service" is really just a destination rewrite on the node → no load-balancer machine, no proxy process in the data path

docs.title: When a backend Pod dies
docs.text:
• Pod 10.244.2.15 crashes → EndpointSlice controller removes it → 2 endpoints
  • kube-proxy on every node updates its rules → only the 2 remaining Pods
  • Deployment's ReplicaSet creates a replacement → new IP, e.g. 10.244.1.20 → once Ready → added to endpoints → rules updated again
  • Frontend keeps calling backend-svc:9090 → notices nothing → that's the whole point of a Service

docs.title: Two IP ranges
docs.text:
Range (kind defaults) What Stable? 10.96.x.x Service IPs (ClusterIPs) Yes, for the Service's lifetime 10.244.x.x Pod IPs No, change on every restart
  • Each node usually gets its own Pod range → 10.244.1.x on one node, 10.244.2.x on another → endpoints from both ranges = Pods spread over 2 nodes, Service treats them as one group

docs.title: Seeing the iptables rules
docs.text:
• kind nodes are Docker containers → look inside one
docker exec -it <node-name> iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n | grep backend-svc   # gives KUBE-SVC-XXXX
docker exec -it <node-name> iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SVC-XXXX -n
  • 3 rules with probabilities ≈ 0.333, 0.5, then the rest →
    • rule 1 catches 1/3 of traffic
    • rule 2 catches half of the remaining 2/3 → 1/3
    • rule 3 takes what's left → 1/3
    • → each Pod gets an equal share, chosen randomly per new connection

docs.title: Reading kubectl describe svc
docs.text:
Name:                     backend-svc
Namespace:                default
Selector:                 app=backend
Type:                     ClusterIP
IP:                       10.96.74.12
Port:                     <unset>  9090/TCP
TargetPort:               5678/TCP
Endpoints:                10.244.2.14:5678,10.244.1.14:5678,10.244.2.15:5678
Session Affinity:         None
Internal Traffic Policy:  Cluster
Field Meaning Selector Label used to find Pods Type ClusterIP → internal only IP Fixed virtual IP → survives Pods being replaced Port: <unset> 9090/TCP <unset> = this port has no name (optional) → Service listens on 9090 TargetPort App's port inside the Pod Endpoints Real PodIP:targetPort of every Ready matching Pod → first thing to check when debugging Session Affinity: None Each new connection can go to any Pod → ClientIP = same client keeps hitting the same Pod Internal Traffic Policy: Cluster In-cluster traffic may go to Pods on any node (Local = only Pods on the caller's node)

docs.title: DNS names of a Service
docs.text: Called from Name that works Same namespace backend-svc Other namespace backend-svc.<namespace> Anywhere (full name, FQDN) backend-svc.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local

docs.title: Lab: frontend + backend with ClusterIP
docs.text:
# backend.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: backend-deploy
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: backend
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: backend-container
          image: hashicorp/http-echo          # tiny test server, listens on 5678
          args:
            - "-text=Hello from backend :)"   # text it replies with
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: backend-svc
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 9090
      targetPort: 5678
  selector:
    app: backend
  • --- → separates two objects in one file
  • http-echo → replies to every request with the -text value → 5678 is its default port → that's where targetPort: 5678 comes from
# frontend.yaml (Deployment part)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: frontend-deploy
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: frontend
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: frontend
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: frontend-container
          image: nginx
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80   # documentation only

kubectl apply -f backend.yaml -f frontend.yaml
kubectl get pods -o wide                     # match Pod IPs with the Endpoints line
kubectl get svc backend-svc
kubectl describe svc backend-svc             # Endpoints → 3 IPs with :5678

# call the backend from inside the cluster
kubectl exec -it deploy/frontend-deploy -- curl backend-svc:9090      # Hello from backend :)
kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- wget -qO- backend-svc:9090

# see each step
kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- cat /etc/resolv.conf     # DNS settings in a Pod
kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- nslookup backend-svc     # name → ClusterIP
  • Break it on purpose → change targetPort to 5000 → apply → curl fails (nothing on 5000) → change back → works

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
• ClusterIP works only inside the cluster → my laptop, browser or a user on the internet can't reach 10.96.x.x
  • Need a way in from outside

docs.title: What NodePort does
docs.text:
• "Open the same port number on every node. Anything arriving there goes to my Service."
  • Port range → 30000–32767 (configurable on the API server, best left alone) → avoids clashing with normal system ports
  • From outside → http://<any node IP>:<nodePort>
  • Analogy → side door numbered 31000 on every floor of the building → walk into any floor's door 31000 → all lead to the same reception → works even on a floor with no backend Pods
  • A NodePort Service is still a ClusterIP Service → gets a ClusterIP, in-cluster callers still use svc:port → NodePort only adds the outside door

docs.title: Now three ports
docs.text:
outside user ─▶ nodeIP:31000 ─▶ Service:80 ─▶ pod:80
                 nodePort        port          targetPort
Field What Who uses it nodePort Port opened on every node (30000–32767) Outside users port Service's own port on its ClusterIP Pods inside the cluster targetPort App's port in the Pod Where traffic finally lands 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: frontend-svc
spec:
  type: NodePort
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80          # ClusterIP port, in-cluster callers
      targetPort: 80    # nginx listens on 80
      nodePort: 31000   # opened on every node (30000-32767)
  selector:
    app: frontend
  • nodePort omitted → Kubernetes picks a random free one in 30000–32767
  • Set it explicitly when something outside depends on the number (kind extraPortMappings, firewall rules)
  • One nodePort belongs to one Service cluster-wide → two Services can't both use 31000
  • kubectl get svc shows 80:31000/TCP → read as port:nodePort

docs.title: kubectl describe of a NodePort Service
docs.text:
Type:                     NodePort
IP:                       10.96.199.133
Port:                     <unset>  80/TCP
TargetPort:               80/TCP
NodePort:                 <unset>  31000/TCP
Endpoints:                10.244.2.10:80,10.244.1.9:80,10.244.1.10:80
External Traffic Policy:  Cluster
  • Still has an IP → proof NodePort is built on ClusterIP

docs.title: What happens on a request from outside
docs.text:
1. User → 172.18.0.4:31000 (Node 2's IP) → arrives at Node 2's network interface
  2. kube-proxy wrote a rule on every node → "anything to port 31000 on a node IP → frontend-svc"
  3. iptables picks an endpoint, e.g. 10.244.1.10:80 → DNAT
  4. 10.244.1.10 may be on a different node → CNI carries it there → that's why any node's door works
  5. SNAT (extra step NodePort adds) → Node 2 also rewrites the source to its own IP → otherwise the other node would reply straight to the user and the user would reject it
    • side effect → nginx sees Node 2's IP, not the user's real IP
  6. Reply → conntrack reverses both rewrites → user gets the answer from 172.18.0.4:31000
NodePort (31000) → ClusterIP (80) → Pod (80)

docs.title: External Traffic Policy
docs.text:
Cluster (default) Local Node sends traffic to Pods on any node Only Pods on itself Works through every node Yes Only nodes running a matching Pod (others drop it) Extra hop Possible None App sees real client IP No (SNAT) Yes
  • One-liner → Cluster spreads load evenly but hides the client IP | Local keeps the client IP but fails on nodes without Pods

docs.title: Which node should the user use?
docs.text:
• NodePort doesn't answer that → it opens the door everywhere and leaves the choice to someone else
  • I have to hand out a node IP, or put something in front that knows all nodes (a load balancer)

docs.title: What happens when a node goes down
docs.text:
• Users pointing at that node's IP → requests time out → NodePort can't help → they must switch to another node's IP manually
  • Users on other nodes → mostly fine → but Pods that lived on the dead node are gone too
  • Timeline inside the cluster →
    • 0 s → node stops, its kubelet stops sending heartbeats
    • ~40 s → node controller marks it NotReady (node-monitor-grace-period) → its Pods marked not Ready → removed from every Service's endpoints → kube-proxy on healthy nodes updates rules
    • 0–40 s → healthy nodes may still pick dead Pods → some requests hang or fail (the blip)
    • ~5 min → Pods on the NotReady node evicted (default toleration 300 s) → ReplicaSet creates replacements on healthy nodes → added once Ready
  • Routing heals in ~40 s | capacity heals in ~5 min
  • NodePort address = a node IP → belongs to one machine → dies with it → Kubernetes can't move it → NodePort gives the port everywhere but no single address that survives node failure

docs.title: Ways to put one stable address in front
docs.text: Option Where How LoadBalancer Service Cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure) Cloud LB with health checks → all nodes' NodePort External LB (HAProxy / nginx VM) On-prem Configured with all node IPs + NodePort + health checks MetalLB Bare metal / on-prem / kind Gives LoadBalancer Services a real IP that moves to a healthy node DNS with all node IPs Cheap hack 3 A records → clients may still try the dead IP, caching slows recovery

docs.title: When NodePort is used
docs.text:
• Labs, testing, quick demos, some on-prem setups
  • Not exposed directly to users in production → ugly ports, users would need node IPs, no failover
  • Still used underneath → a LoadBalancer Service sends traffic to NodePorts

docs.title: Simulate a node failure on kind
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -o wide                       # which Pods are on <worker>
docker stop <worker-node-container>            # "kill" the node
kubectl get nodes -w                           # NotReady after ~40 s
kubectl describe svc frontend-svc              # Endpoints shrink
docker start <worker-node-container>           # bring it back

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
• Each kind node = a Docker container → NodePort opens 31000 inside each container
  • macOS / Windows → Docker runs inside a hidden Linux VM (Docker Desktop) → the 172.18.0.x node network exists only inside that VM → laptop can't reach 172.18.0.x:31000
  • Native Linux (e.g. Ubuntu) → Docker runs on my own kernel → the bridge network is on my machine → curl 172.18.0.x:31000 works directly
  • localhost:31000 → on any OS, nothing on my laptop listens on 31000 unless I map it

docs.title: The fix → a pipe from my laptop into a node
docs.text:
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
  - role: control-plane
    image: kindest/node:v1.37.0@sha256:a1ed56cfb0e7b93589bdf97c8cd566405a265939e3620fc4f5de89adff580ae5
    extraPortMappings:
      - containerPort: 31000   # port inside the node container → must equal the Service's nodePort
        hostPort: 31000        # port on my laptop
  - role: worker
    image: kindest/node:v1.37.0@sha256:a1ed56cfb0e7b93589bdf97c8cd566405a265939e3620fc4f5de89adff580ae5
  - role: worker
    image: kindest/node:v1.37.0@sha256:a1ed56cfb0e7b93589bdf97c8cd566405a265939e3620fc4f5de89adff580ae5
  • extraPortMappings = kind passing Docker's -p hostPort:containerPort when it creates the node container → same as docker run -p 31000:31000 ...
  • hostPort → outside end of the pipe (my laptop) | containerPort → inside end (the node)
  • containerPort must equal the Service's nodePort → otherwise the pipe ends at a closed door
  • hostPort can be anything → hostPort: 9090 → open localhost:9090 → still reaches containerPort: 31000
  • Only the control-plane has the mapping → enough, NodePort opens 31000 on every node and forwards to Pods on workers
  • Only mapped ports reach the cluster through localhost → a Service on nodePort 30950 is not reachable at localhost:30950 unless 30950 is also mapped
  • This is why the nodePort is fixed in the Service YAML (nodePort: 31000) instead of letting Kubernetes pick one
  • image: ...@sha256:... → pins the exact Kubernetes version, the digest guarantees the identical image every time

docs.title: Can only be set at creation
docs.text:
• extraPortMappings can't be added to a running cluster → delete and recreate:
kind get clusters
kind delete cluster --name my-first-cluster
kind create cluster --name my-second-cluster --config kind-cluster.yaml

docs.title: The full chain
docs.text:
Browser ─▶ localhost:31000                          (laptop)
   ─▶ Docker port forward ─▶ control-plane container:31000
   ─▶ kube-proxy NodePort rule ─▶ frontend-svc
   ─▶ DNAT to an nginx Pod:80 (CNI delivers it if the Pod is on a worker)

docs.title: Lab: expose the frontend, hide the backend
docs.text:
• Real pattern → frontend = NodePort (outside door) | backend = ClusterIP (internal only, safer)
User ─▶ any node:31000 (frontend-svc, NodePort) ─▶ nginx Pod:80
                                                     │
                     backend-svc:9090 (ClusterIP) ◀──┘
                              │
                              └─▶ http-echo Pod:5678

# frontend.yaml (Service part)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: frontend-svc
spec:
  type: NodePort
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 80        # nginx's port, NOT the backend's 5678
      nodePort: 31000
  selector:
    app: frontend

kubectl apply -f backend.yaml
kubectl apply -f frontend.yaml
kubectl get all

kubectl get nodes -o wide                          # INTERNAL-IP column → 172.18.0.x
curl 172.18.0.2:31000                              # any node works (native Linux)
curl localhost:31000                               # through extraPortMappings
kubectl exec -it deploy/frontend-deploy -- curl backend-svc:9090   # backend from inside only
  • Expected →
    • localhost:31000 → "Welcome to nginx!" page
    • backend reachable only from inside → Hello from backend :)
  • Plain nginx doesn't call the backend → it just serves its own page → the diagram's nginx → backend arrow shows the idea; making nginx forward needs a proxy_pass http://backend-svc:9090; config
  • Moving the outside door from one Service to another → delete the old NodePort Service first → nodePort: 31000 can belong to only one Service, and changing a Service's type in place keeps its old nodePort

docs.title: Reading kubectl get all
docs.text:
• pod/... → individual Pods
  • service/... → PORT(S) = port:nodePort/TCP for NodePort | port/TCP for ClusterIP
  • deployment.apps/... → READY 3/3 = 3 of 3 desired Pods Ready
  • replicaset.apps/... → created by the Deployment to keep the Pods running → hash in the name (79f94c6cdc) changes whenever the Pod template changes (that's how rollouts work)
  • ContainerCreating for a while → image still downloading → becomes Running

docs.title: The problem left by NodePort
docs.text: • Users must know a node IP | node dies → its users are cut off | ugly ports like :31000

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Asks the cloud (AWS, GCP, Azure) → "create a real load balancer with one external address and point it at all my nodes"
User ─▶ one external address (cloud LB)
          ─▶ health-checks every node
          ─▶ sends traffic only to healthy nodes on the NodePort
          ─▶ Service ─▶ Pod
  • User only knows one address (e.g. abc123.elb.amazonaws.com) → normal ports like 80/443 → dead node skipped automatically
  • Analogy → main gate with a guard outside the building → visitors only go to the gate → guard sends them through a working floor door
  • A LoadBalancer Service gets all three → ClusterIP + NodePort + external address
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: frontend-lb
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80              # port on the load balancer AND the ClusterIP
      targetPort: 80        # nginx's port
      # nodePort: 31000     # optional → usually left out, Kubernetes picks one
  selector:
    app: frontend

docs.title: What happens when it's applied
docs.text:
1. API server stores it → assigns a ClusterIP and a NodePort (random, e.g. 32145)
  2. kube-proxy writes ClusterIP + NodePort rules on every node → same as before
  3. cloud-controller-manager (control-plane component that talks to the cloud API) sees type: LoadBalancer → calls the cloud → "create a load balancer"
  4. Cloud creates it (on AWS an ELB) with →
    • listener on port 80
    • targets → every node on port 32145 (the NodePort)
    • health checks on each node
  5. Cloud returns the address → written into the Service's status → EXTERNAL-IP column
NAME          TYPE           CLUSTER-IP    EXTERNAL-IP                PORT(S)
frontend-lb   LoadBalancer   10.96.80.12   abc123.elb.amazonaws.com   80:32145/TCP
  • 80:32145 → LB/Service port : NodePort

docs.title: The packet path
docs.text:
User ─▶ abc123.elb.amazonaws.com:80
   ─▶ cloud LB picks a healthy node ─▶ node:32145 (NodePort)
   ─▶ kube-proxy iptables ─▶ DNAT ─▶ nginx Pod:80
  • Node fails health checks → LB removes it within seconds → the failover NodePort couldn't give

docs.title: On AWS (EKS)
docs.text:
• Plain type: LoadBalancer → Classic LB by default, NLB with annotations
  • Most teams install the AWS Load Balancer Controller →
    • type: LoadBalancer Service → NLB (L4)
    • Ingress → ALB (L7)
    • can target Pod IPs directly (target-type: ip) → skips the NodePort hop
  • Internal LB (annotation) → private LB reachable only inside the VPC

docs.title: On kind
docs.text:
• No cloud → nobody creates the LB → EXTERNAL-IP stays <pending> forever → normal, not a bug
kubectl expose deployment frontend-deploy --name=frontend-lb --type=LoadBalancer --port=80
kubectl get svc frontend-lb          # EXTERNAL-IP <pending>
  • To get a real IP locally → something must act like a cloud →
    • cloud-provider-kind → official Kubernetes SIG tool built for this
    • MetalLB → common for bare-metal and on-prem clusters

docs.title: Is it used in production?
docs.text:
• Rare → one LoadBalancer Service per app →
    • cost → one cloud LB each (roughly $16–20/month each on AWS before traffic)
    • many external addresses to manage
    • L4 only → can't route by URL path or hostname, no central TLS
  • Normal web apps → Ingress (or Gateway API) → one entry point routes by path/host → app Services stay ClusterIP
app.com/       → frontend-svc (ClusterIP)
app.com/api    → api-svc      (ClusterIP)
admin.app.com  → admin-svc    (ClusterIP)
  • Still used in production for →
    1. In front of the Ingress controller → ingress-nginx is just Pods → one type: LoadBalancer Service brings outside traffic to them → LB used once, at the edge
    2. Non-HTTP traffic → Ingress understands only HTTP/HTTPS → databases, MQTT, game servers, DNS, some gRPC → LoadBalancer Service
    3. Internal load balancers → expose a service privately inside the VPC (other clusters, VMs, VPN users)
Situation What's used Normal web apps ClusterIP + Ingress / Gateway API Getting traffic into the Ingress controller 1 LoadBalancer Service TCP/UDP apps LoadBalancer Service Private access inside the VPC Internal LoadBalancer Service Labs and testing NodePort

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
• App inside the cluster needs something outside → e.g. a database on AWS RDS → mydb.abc123.ap-south-1.rds.amazonaws.com
  • Hard-coded in the app → DB moves (test → prod, new instance) → change and redeploy the app

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Creates a nickname inside the cluster → my-db → the long outside name
  • App connects to my-db → DB changes → update only the Service → app untouched
  • Analogy → saved phone contact "Papa" → number changes → update the contact once, keep tapping "Papa" | or speed-dial 111 for IT support
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: cka-db-svc
spec:
  type: ExternalName
  externalName: cka-db.judhtdmxwly6.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com   # RDS DNS name
  • No selector, no ports, no ClusterIP → just type + externalName
ClusterIP / NodePort / LoadBalancer ExternalName Points to Pods inside the cluster A DNS name outside the cluster Selector Yes No Virtual IP Yes No Endpoints / kube-proxy rules Yes No Traffic flows through it Yes (address rewrite) No (only the name is swapped)

docs.title: What actually happens
docs.text:
1. Applied → API server stores it → no ClusterIP, no endpoints, no iptables rules
  2. CoreDNS creates a CNAME record (DNS alias) → cka-db-svc.default.svc.cluster.local → CNAME → cka-db.judhtdmxwly6.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com
  3. App connects to cka-db-svc:3306 →
    • asks CoreDNS → "that's another name for the RDS hostname"
    • resolution continues → RDS hostname → real IP (e.g. 10.0.5.23)
    • app connects directly to 10.0.5.23:3306
  4. Kubernetes is involved only in the DNS step → no DNAT, no load balancing

docs.title: Watch out
docs.text:
• Ports are ignored → app must use the outside service's real port (3306 for MySQL) → ExternalName can't map 80 → 3306
  • Must be a DNS name, not an IP → externalName: 10.0.5.23 → creates a CNAME to "10.0.5.23" → wrong
    • fixed outside IP → use a Service with no selector + an EndpointSlice I write by hand with that IP
  • HTTP/HTTPS can break → HTTP sends Host: cka-db-svc | HTTPS certificate is for the real hostname, not the alias → many websites and APIs reject it → best for databases and plain TCP, risky for HTTPS APIs

docs.title: Real uses
docs.text:
• Short in-cluster name for a managed database (RDS, Cloud SQL)
  • Migrations → my-db → outside DB today → later move the DB into the cluster and turn my-db into a normal ClusterIP Service → app never changes
  • Per-environment config → my-db in the dev namespace → dev DB | in prod namespace → prod DB → same app YAML everywhere
  • Cross-namespace alias → my-db → postgres.database.svc.cluster.local
  • Third-party APIs and legacy systems (watch the HTTPS caveat)

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
kubectl create service externalname my-google --external-name www.google.com
kubectl get svc my-google                                  # EXTERNAL-IP = www.google.com, no CLUSTER-IP
kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- nslookup my-google
# my-google.default.svc.cluster.local  canonical name = www.google.com → then Google's IPs

docs.title: Headless Services
docs.text:
• clusterIP: None → no virtual IP, no load balancing
  • DNS returns every Pod's IP directly instead of one Service IP
  • Used with StatefulSets (databases) → client must reach a specific Pod → mysql-0.mysql.default.svc.cluster.local (e.g. the primary), not "any free one"
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: mysql
  ports:
    - port: 3306

docs.title: Which type when
docs.text: Need Use Pod-to-Pod traffic inside the cluster ClusterIP Quick access from outside in a lab NodePort Public endpoint on a cloud (TCP/UDP, or for the Ingress controller) LoadBalancer Many HTTP apps behind one entry point ClusterIP + Ingress / Gateway API Short name for an outside DNS name ExternalName Reach individual Pods (StatefulSets) Headless

docs.title: Request flow summary
docs.text:
ClusterIP     Pod ─▶ svc-name:port ─▶ (DNS → ClusterIP) ─▶ iptables DNAT ─▶ Pod:targetPort

NodePort      User ─▶ anyNodeIP:nodePort ─▶ ClusterIP:port ─▶ Pod:targetPort
              (node down → user must switch to another node IP manually)

LoadBalancer  User ─▶ LB address:port ─▶ healthy node:nodePort ─▶ ClusterIP:port ─▶ Pod:targetPort

ExternalName  Pod ─▶ svc-name ─▶ (DNS CNAME) ─▶ outside hostname ─▶ connects directly

Quick revision

  • Service = stable virtual IP + DNS name + load balancing in front of Pods with changing IPs
  • Finds Pods by label selector → only Ready Pods, same namespace → list kept in EndpointSlices
  • port = Service's port (callers) | targetPort = app's port in the Pod | nodePort = port on every node (30000–32767)
  • ClusterIP is virtual → kube-proxy writes iptables DNAT rules on every node → conntrack reverses them for replies
  • CoreDNS maps svc.namespace.svc.cluster.local → ClusterIP | Pods use it via /etc/resolv.conf (10.96.0.10)
  • LoadBalancer ⊃ NodePort ⊃ ClusterIP | ExternalName = CNAME only | Headless = Pod IPs from DNS
  • Wrong targetPort → Pods Running, Endpoints filled, but connection refused / empty response

Interview points

  • Why do we need Services? → Pod IPs change on every restart, so a Service gives a stable IP and DNS name and load-balances across the current Ready Pods
  • How does a Service know which Pods to send traffic to? → its label selector; the EndpointSlice controller keeps a list of Ready Pods with matching labels in the same namespace
  • port vs targetPort vs nodePort? → port is the Service's port that callers use, targetPort is the port the app in the Pod listens on, nodePort is the port opened on every node for outside traffic
  • Is the ClusterIP assigned to any interface? → no, it's virtual; kube-proxy programs iptables/IPVS/nftables rules on every node that DNAT it to a Pod IP
  • Who does the load balancing for a ClusterIP Service? → kube-proxy's rules in the node kernel, choosing a random endpoint per new connection; no proxy process sits in the data path in iptables mode
  • What does CoreDNS do for Services? → watches the API server and answers name lookups, mapping service names to ClusterIPs, or to a CNAME for ExternalName
  • Pods are Running but the Service's Endpoints are empty, why? → the selector doesn't match the Pod labels, the Pods aren't Ready, or they're in another namespace
  • Endpoints are filled but requests get connection refused? → targetPort doesn't match the port the app actually listens on
  • Does a NodePort Service also have a ClusterIP? → yes, NodePort builds on ClusterIP and LoadBalancer builds on NodePort
  • Default NodePort range? → 30000–32767
  • What happens with NodePort if a node goes down? → clients using that node's IP fail and must switch manually; inside the cluster its Pods are removed from endpoints after the node goes NotReady (~40 s) and replaced after eviction (~5 min)
  • externalTrafficPolicy Cluster vs Local? → Cluster forwards to Pods on any node but SNATs and hides the client IP; Local only uses Pods on the receiving node and preserves the client IP
  • Who creates the cloud load balancer for a LoadBalancer Service? → the cloud-controller-manager, through the cloud provider's API
  • Why is EXTERNAL-IP pending on kind or bare metal? → there's no cloud controller to provision a load balancer; use MetalLB or cloud-provider-kind
  • Why not one LoadBalancer per app in production? → cost and no L7 routing; use one LoadBalancer for the ingress controller and ClusterIP Services behind Ingress
  • What is an ExternalName Service? → a DNS CNAME alias to an external hostname with no ClusterIP, selector or proxying
  • What is a headless Service? → clusterIP: None, DNS returns the individual Pod IPs, used with StatefulSets
  • Why does kind need extraPortMappings? → nodes are Docker containers, so the host port must be mapped into a node container to reach a NodePort via localhost; it can only be set at cluster creation

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
• Taint → on a node → "keep out unless you have a pass"
  • Toleration → on a Pod → the pass that lets it ignore a matching taint
  • Analogy → hotel → taint = a sign on a room's door ("reserved"), toleration = the guest's pass, scheduler = the receptionist who reads both
  • A Pod with no matching toleration is not placed on a tainted node
  • A toleration only allows, it never attracts → a Pod with a toleration can still land on any untainted node → to send a Pod to a node use nodeSelector / node affinity

docs.title: When they're used
docs.text: Use How Protect the control plane kubeadm / kind add node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule Dedicated GPU nodes Taint GPU nodes (nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule) → only ML Pods tolerate it → GKE / EKS add it to GPU node pools Node pool per team / workload Taint the pool (team=payments:NoSchedule) → only that team's Pods tolerate it Spot / preemptible nodes Taint them → only Pods that survive sudden shutdown (batch jobs) tolerate it Maintenance kubectl cordon adds node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable:NoSchedule Node health Kubernetes taints unhealthy nodes by itself → not-ready, unreachable, memory-pressure, disk-pressure, pid-pressure Per-node agents DaemonSets (log shippers, monitoring, CNI) carry broad tolerations to run on every node

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
key=value:effect          →  storage=ssd:NoSchedule
key:effect                →  node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule   (value is optional)

docs.title: The three effects
docs.text:
Effect New Pods without toleration Running Pods without toleration NoSchedule Not placed Stay PreferNoSchedule Avoided, but used if nothing better fits Stay NoExecute Not placed Evicted
  • Mild → harsh → Prefer → No → Execute

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
kubectl taint nodes my-new-cluster-worker storage=ssd:NoSchedule        # add
kubectl taint nodes my-new-cluster-worker storage=ssd:NoSchedule-       # remove (trailing -)
kubectl taint nodes my-new-cluster-worker storage-                      # remove every taint with key storage
kubectl taint nodes my-new-cluster-worker storage=nvme:NoSchedule --overwrite   # change the value

kubectl describe node my-new-cluster-worker | grep -i taint
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,TAINTS:.spec.taints
  • One node can have many taints → describe lists them one per line under Taints:

docs.title: Fields → K-O-V-E
docs.text:
• Key, Operator, Value, Effect → "Keep Out, Very Effective"
spec:
  tolerations:
  - key: "storage"          # Keep
    operator: "Equal"       # Out
    value: "ssd"            # Very
    effect: "NoSchedule"    # Effective
  • Taint has no operator → key=value:effect | toleration adds the operator
  • Lives under spec of the Pod → in a Deployment → spec.template.spec.tolerations
  • Field help without docs → kubectl explain pod.spec.tolerations

docs.title: Operators
docs.text:
Operator Matches when Equal (default) Key and value are the same as the taint's Exists Key is the same → value ignored → leave value out (K-O-E) 
# any storage taint → storage=ssd and storage=hdd both tolerated
- key: "storage"
  operator: "Exists"
  effect: "NoSchedule"

docs.title: Matching rules
docs.text:
• Key, value (for Equal) and effect must all match
  • Effect left empty → matches all effects of that key
  • Key empty + operator: Exists → matches every taint on every node → what DaemonSets use
tolerations:
- operator: "Exists"
  • A node with several taints → the Pod must tolerate every one of them → one missing = node blocked
  • A toleration for a taint that exists on no node → does nothing → the Pod behaves like a Pod with no tolerations

docs.title: tolerationSeconds (NoExecute only)
docs.text:
- key: "maint"
  operator: "Equal"
  value: "true"
  effect: "NoExecute"
  tolerationSeconds: 60
  • Pod may stay on the NoExecute node for 60 s after the taint appears → then evicted
  • No tolerationSeconds → stays forever

docs.title: Tolerations added automatically
docs.text:
kubectl get po <pod> -o yaml | grep -A3 tolerations
#  - key: node.kubernetes.io/not-ready
#    effect: NoExecute
#    tolerationSeconds: 300
#  - key: node.kubernetes.io/unreachable
#    effect: NoExecute
#    tolerationSeconds: 300
  • Added to every Pod by an admission plugin (DefaultTolerationSeconds)
  • Meaning → if my node goes not-ready or unreachable, wait 5 minutes before evicting me → avoids moving Pods on a short network blip
  • DaemonSet Pods get these with no time limit, plus the pressure / unschedulable taints → so they keep running on unhealthy or cordoned nodes

docs.title: How the scheduler uses them
docs.text:
• The scheduler works in two steps:
    • Filter (hard rules) → drop nodes the Pod isn't allowed on → untolerated NoSchedule and NoExecute taints act here
    • Score (soft rules) → rank the remaining nodes → untolerated PreferNoSchedule taints lower a node's score → also free resources, image already on the node, spreading replicas
  • A tolerated taint gives a node no bonus → after filtering, a tainted node the Pod tolerates and an untainted node are equal as far as taints go
  • Taints are checked only by the scheduler → a Pod with nodeName set skips them (except NoExecute, which evicts after the Pod runs) → see Manual Scheduling & Static Pods

docs.title: Where a Pod can go → worked example
docs.text:
Node Taint Green color=green:NoSchedule Blue color=blue:PreferNoSchedule Purple color=green:NoExecute Plain none Pod Green Blue Purple Plain No toleration ✗ low score ✗ ✓ Tolerates color=yellow ✗ low score ✗ ✓ Tolerates color=green:NoSchedule ✓ low score ✗ (effect differs) ✓ Tolerates color=green, effect empty ✓ low score ✓ ✓ Tolerates color=blue:PreferNoSchedule ✗ ✓ ✗ ✓
  • Yellow → no node has a yellow taint → the toleration is useless → same as no toleration
  • Green Pod with 10 replicas → spreads over Green and Plain → not "Green first" → tolerating a taint doesn't make a node preferred
  • Blue Pod → tolerates the blue taint → Blue gets no penalty → Blue and Plain are equal → replicas split between them
  • Existing Pods → Green and Blue ones stay when the taint is added | Purple ones without a matching NoExecute toleration are evicted

docs.title: Reserving nodes properly → taint + affinity
docs.text:
• Goal → Green nodes only for Project A, and Project A only on Green nodes
  • Taint + toleration alone → keeps other Pods off Green ✓ → but Project A Pods can still land on Plain ✗
  • nodeSelector / affinity alone → pulls Project A onto Green ✓ → but other Pods can still land on Green ✗
  • Both together → full isolation
kubectl taint nodes my-new-cluster-worker color=green:NoSchedule
kubectl label nodes my-new-cluster-worker color=green

spec:
  nodeSelector:
    color: green
  tolerations:
  - key: "color"
    operator: "Equal"
    value: "green"
    effect: "NoSchedule"
  • Taint = push others away | label + selector = pull mine in

docs.title: Debugging a Pending Pod
docs.text:
kubectl describe po <pod> | tail -5
# 0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) had untolerated taint {node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: },
#   1 node(s) had untolerated taint {storage: ssd}, 1 node(s) had untolerated taint {storage: hdd}.
  • Read each part → which taint blocked which node → add the toleration, or remove the taint if it was left from a test
  • Check all nodes' taints in one go → kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,TAINTS:.spec.taints
  • Common cause in real clusters → a forgotten test taint, a cordoned node, or a node with disk-pressure / memory-pressure

docs.title: Lab: one taint per worker
docs.text:
kubectl taint nodes my-new-cluster-worker storage=ssd:NoSchedule
kubectl taint nodes my-new-cluster-worker2 storage=hdd:NoSchedule

kubectl run plain --image=nginx
kubectl get po plain                     # Pending → every node is tainted (control plane too)
kubectl describe po plain | tail -3      # untolerated taint per node
kubectl delete po plain

# deploy.yaml → tolerates only ssd
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ssd-deploy
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: ssd
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: ssd
    spec:
      tolerations:
      - key: "storage"
        operator: "Equal"
        value: "ssd"
        effect: "NoSchedule"
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx

kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml
kubectl get po -o wide                   # all on worker → the only node whose every taint is tolerated
  • Looks like the toleration "pulled" Pods to worker → only because every other node was tainted → untaint worker2 and they can land there too

docs.title: Lab: multiple taints per node
docs.text:
kubectl taint nodes my-new-cluster-worker env=prod:NoSchedule
kubectl taint nodes my-new-cluster-worker2 env=dev:NoSchedule

    spec:
      tolerations:
      - key: "storage"
        operator: "Exists"
        effect: "NoSchedule"
      - key: "env"
        operator: "Equal"
        value: "prod"
        effect: "NoSchedule"
  • worker → storage=ssd ✓ + env=prod ✓ → allowed
  • worker2 → storage=hdd ✓ + env=dev ✗ → blocked
  • Pods already running on a node when a NoSchedule taint is added → keep running

docs.title: Lab: NoExecute eviction
docs.text:
kubectl run evict-me --image=nginx
kubectl get po -o wide                                              # note the node
kubectl taint nodes <that-node> maint=true:NoExecute
kubectl get po -w                                                   # evict-me is terminated → a bare Pod is not recreated
kubectl taint nodes <that-node> maint=true:NoExecute-
  • Pods owned by a Deployment get recreated on another node | bare Pods are just gone

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
kubectl taint nodes my-new-cluster-worker storage- env-
kubectl taint nodes my-new-cluster-worker2 storage- env-
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,TAINTS:.spec.taints   # only the control-plane taint left

Quick revision

  • Taint on node = keep out | toleration on Pod = pass | a pass allows, never attracts
  • Taint format → key=value:effect | remove with a trailing -
  • Effects → PreferNoSchedule (soft) → NoSchedule (no new Pods) → NoExecute (no new Pods + evict running ones)
  • Toleration fields → K-O-V-E → key, operator, value, effect
  • Equal (default) = key + value match | Exists = key only | empty key + Exists = tolerate everything
  • Empty effect in a toleration = matches all effects of that key
  • Node with several taints → Pod must tolerate all of them
  • tolerationSeconds → only with NoExecute → how long to stay before eviction
  • Every Pod auto-tolerates not-ready / unreachable for 300 s
  • Scheduler → filter (NoSchedule, NoExecute) then score (PreferNoSchedule) → a tolerated taint gives no bonus
  • Dedicated nodes → taint + toleration and label + nodeSelector / affinity

Interview points

  • What are taints and tolerations? → a taint on a node repels Pods; a toleration on a Pod lets it be scheduled onto a node with a matching taint
  • Does a toleration make a Pod run on the tainted node? → no, it only allows it; to attract a Pod to a node use nodeSelector or node affinity
  • What are the three taint effects? → NoSchedule blocks new Pods, PreferNoSchedule avoids the node if possible, NoExecute blocks new Pods and evicts running ones that don't tolerate it
  • What happens to running Pods when a NoSchedule taint is added? → nothing, they keep running; only NoExecute evicts
  • Difference between Equal and Exists? → Equal needs key and value to match; Exists only needs the key and ignores the value
  • What does a toleration with only operator Exists do? → tolerates every taint, which is how DaemonSets run on all nodes
  • What is tolerationSeconds? → for NoExecute taints, how long a Pod may stay on the node after the taint appears before it is evicted
  • Why do Pods have not-ready and unreachable tolerations by default? → the DefaultTolerationSeconds admission plugin adds them with 300 seconds so Pods aren't evicted on a short node outage
  • Why can't normal Pods run on the control plane? → kubeadm taints it with node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule to protect the API server and etcd
  • A node has two taints and the Pod tolerates one, can it schedule there? → no, the Pod must tolerate every taint on the node
  • How do you remove a taint? → kubectl taint nodes node key=value:effect with a trailing dash, or key- to remove all taints with that key
  • How do you dedicate nodes to one team? → taint the nodes so other Pods stay off, and add a label plus nodeSelector or affinity with a toleration so the team's Pods go there
  • How does the scheduler use taints? → NoSchedule and NoExecute taints filter nodes out; PreferNoSchedule lowers a node's score
  • A Pod is Pending with untolerated taint, what do you do? → read kubectl describe pod events, check the node taints, then add the toleration or remove a stale taint
  • How does kubectl cordon relate to taints? → cordon marks the node unschedulable and adds the node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable:NoSchedule taint

docs.title: Why this comes before Services
docs.text:
• Kubernetes Services only make sense once I know what talks to what in a real app
  • A real app = frontend + backend + database (+ middleware in between) → each piece runs as its own Deployment → they find each other through Services
  • This chapter = the app design | next chapter = the networking that connects it

docs.title: Monolithic architecture
docs.text:
• Monolith → UI, business logic and database access all in one codebase, deployed as one unit
  • Simple to start → one repo, one build, one deploy
  • Gets painful as it grows:
Problem What it means Tightly coupled Change in one part (e.g. payments) can break another (e.g. login) Hard to maintain and upgrade Any fix → rebuild, retest and redeploy the whole app → downtime, big test cycles Limited scaling Only the search feature is busy? Still have to scale the entire app → wasted CPU/RAM Slow development Many teams in one codebase → wait on each other, merge conflicts, risky releases
  • Still found in legacy systems that were never split up

docs.title: Three-tier architecture
docs.text:
• Splits the app into separate logical layers → each layer has one job → separation of concerns
User ─▶ Frontend (web tier) ─▶ Middleware ─▶ Backend (application tier) ─▶ Database (data tier)
Tier Job Examples Frontend (web tier) What the user sees and clicks HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, Angular, Vue Middleware Sits between frontend and backend → auth, logging, caching, routing, messaging API Gateway, Nginx, Express.js, Kafka, RabbitMQ Backend (application tier) Business logic → processes requests, talks to the database Python, Node.js, Java, Go, .NET Database (data tier) Stores and retrieves data MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis
  • Middleware is often counted as part of the backend → that's why it's still called three-tier

docs.title: Each tier in an e-commerce site
docs.text:
• Frontend → homepage, product listing, cart page | click "Add to Cart" → request goes to the backend
  • Middleware →
    • Auth → checks who I am (OAuth, JWT, API keys)
    • Logging / monitoring → ELK, Prometheus, Grafana
    • Caching → Redis, Memcached → avoid hitting the DB for the same data again
    • Service communication → API gateway routes requests, message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ) pass events between services
    • Rate limiting → blocks too many requests from one client
    • Payment gateway → validates the card before the order reaches the backend
  • Backend → order management (create order, update stock, send email), wishlist
  • Database → users table, products table, order history

docs.title: How three-tier apps were deployed over time
docs.text:
Era Setup Good Bad Single server All 3 tiers on one physical machine Simple, cheap Scale only vertically (bigger machine) → one busy tier slows everything → server dies = everything dies Three servers (pre-virtualization) One physical server per tier Better performance, fault isolation Expensive → 3× hardware, power, maintenance Virtualization One physical host, each tier in its own VM (VMware, KVM) Isolation without buying 3 machines, resize VMs Still heavy (each VM = full OS), slow to scale, manual Cloud + Kubernetes Each tier containerized, run as Deployments; DB often a managed service Fast scaling, self-healing, automation, efficient More moving parts to learn
  • Not the full list → event-driven and serverless models exist too

docs.title: Problems with plain three-tier
docs.text:
• Each tier is still a monolith inside → the whole backend is one codebase
  • Scaling → orders are busy but wishlist isn't → still scale the whole backend tier
  • Single point of failure → backend tier crashes → whole app down
  • Tight coupling → one big backend codebase → risky deploys
  • Slow delivery → teams wait on each other inside one tier
  • One tech stack per tier → whole backend locked to one language
  • Fix → break each tier into small independent services → microservices

docs.title: Microservices
docs.text:
• App split into small, independent services → each does one business function → they talk over APIs (HTTP/gRPC) or messages
Monolith:        [ login + products + orders + payments + wishlist ]   ← one app

Microservices:   [user-svc]  [product-svc]  [order-svc]  [payment-svc]  [wishlist-svc]
                     each built, deployed, scaled and failed independently
  • E-commerce example →
    • User service → login, profiles
    • Product service → catalogue, inventory
    • Order service → orders, payments
    • Wishlist service → saved items
  • Fault isolation → wishlist service crashes → users can still browse and order, only the wishlist is unavailable until it recovers
    • In a monolith → a wishlist bug can take the whole app down
Benefit Meaning Independent scaling Scale only the busy service (orders on sale day) Fault isolation One service failing doesn't crash the rest Faster deployment Each team ships its own service on its own schedule Technology freedom Orders in Java, search in Go, ML in Python Easier maintenance Small codebases → easier to read, test, debug
  • Naming → called "Wishlist Service", not "Wishlist Microservice" → every microservice is a service anyway, shorter, industry convention
  • Trade-off (not free) → many services = more network calls, more things to monitor, harder debugging across services → that's why Services, DNS, observability and tracing matter so much

docs.title: Microservices on Kubernetes
docs.text:
• Each microservice → its own Deployment (its Pods) + its own Service (stable name to reach it)
  • Each tier can hold many microservices:
Tier Microservices In Kubernetes Frontend Web UI, mobile backend Deployments + Service exposed to users (usually through Ingress) Middleware API gateway, auth, logging, caching Deployments + internal Services Backend Order, payment, wishlist services Deployments + internal (ClusterIP) Services Database MySQL, PostgreSQL Usually outside the cluster (managed service)

docs.title: Request flow in an e-commerce app on Kubernetes
docs.text:
1. User opens https://example.com
  2. Request hits the Ingress controller → routes it to the frontend Service → one frontend Pod
  3. Frontend calls the API gateway (middleware)
  4. API gateway forwards to the right backend service → e.g. wishlist Service → one wishlist Pod
  5. Wishlist Pod reads from the database → sends data back
  6. User sees the updated wishlist

docs.title: Scaling each service
docs.text:
• Each microservice = its own Deployment → scaled separately
  • HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) → adds/removes Pods of one Deployment based on load (CPU, memory, custom metrics) → orders can go to 20 Pods while wishlist stays at 2

docs.title: Stateless vs stateful
docs.text:
• Stateless → keeps nothing between requests → any Pod can answer any request → kill it, start another, nothing lost → easy to scale (frontend, most backends)
  • Stateful → remembers data between requests → losing a Pod can lose data → needs stable identity + persistent storage (databases, Kafka, ZooKeeper)

docs.title: Why databases are usually not run in Kubernetes in production
docs.text:
• Stateful is hard → needs stable network identity, persistent volumes, replication, failover, backups → Kubernetes doesn't do all of that out of the box
  • Performance → managed DBs and tuned VMs give better storage I/O
  • HA and backups → replication, automatic failover, point-in-time restore are built into managed services

docs.title: Where they run instead
docs.text:
• Managed database → AWS RDS, Google Cloud SQL, Azure Database → backups, patching, failover handled for me
  • Dedicated VMs with HA setup → full control over tuning
  • Hybrid (most common) → apps in Kubernetes, database outside → apps reach it by DNS name (an ExternalName Service can give it a short in-cluster name → see Services)

docs.title: When a database does run in Kubernetes
docs.text:
• StatefulSet → like a Deployment but each Pod gets:
    • a stable name → mysql-0, mysql-1 (not random suffixes)
    • its own persistent volume that follows it across restarts
    • ordered start, scale and shutdown (mysql-0 first)
  • Use cases → MySQL, PostgreSQL, Kafka, ZooKeeper
  • Good fits →
    • dev and test environments
    • with a database Operator (MySQL Operator, CloudNativePG for PostgreSQL) → an Operator is a custom controller with the DBA's knowledge coded in → handles backups, failover, upgrades (see Webhooks, CRDs & Operators)
    • small self-managed setups

Quick revision

  • Monolith → one codebase, one deploy → coupled, scale everything together
  • Three-tier → frontend, (middleware), backend, database → separated layers, but each tier is still a monolith inside
  • Microservices → small services per business function → scale, deploy and fail independently
  • In Kubernetes → one Deployment + one Service per microservice
  • Databases → usually managed services outside the cluster; StatefulSets or Operators when inside

Interview points

  • What are the three tiers? → presentation (frontend), application (backend, often with middleware), and data (database)
  • What does middleware do? → sits between frontend and backend for auth, logging, caching, rate limiting and routing, e.g. an API gateway or message broker
  • Monolith vs microservices? → a monolith is one codebase deployed as one unit; microservices split the app into small services deployed and scaled independently
  • Main benefit of microservices? → independent scaling and deployment, plus fault isolation so one failing service doesn't take down the app
  • Downside of microservices? → more network calls, more services to deploy and monitor, and harder debugging across service boundaries
  • How do microservices map to Kubernetes? → each service gets its own Deployment for its Pods and its own Service for a stable name
  • Stateless vs stateful? → stateless keeps no data between requests so any Pod can serve any request; stateful keeps data and needs stable identity and storage
  • Why are production databases often kept outside Kubernetes? → stateful workloads need persistent storage, replication, failover and backups, which managed services like RDS handle better
  • What is a StatefulSet? → a controller for stateful apps that gives each Pod a stable name, its own persistent volume and ordered startup

docs.title: Webhooks in general
docs.text:
• Webhook = "when something happens, call this URL"
  • A system sends an HTTP request (usually POST with JSON) to a URL I registered, as soon as an event happens
  • Polling → I keep asking "anything new?" every few minutes | webhook → it tells me the moment it happens
  • Analogy → food delivery app: without a webhook I keep opening the app to check | with one, I get a notification "out for delivery"
  • API vs webhook → API = I call them when I want data (pull) | webhook = they call me when something happens (push)

docs.title: DevOps example: GitHub → Jenkins
docs.text:
1. Tell GitHub → "on every push, POST to https://jenkins.example.com/github-webhook/"
  2. I push code
  3. GitHub sends Jenkins a message → repo, branch, commit, author
  4. Jenkins starts the build
  5. Without it → Jenkins would poll GitHub every minute → wasteful and slow
  6. Others → Stripe → my app ("payment succeeded") | Alertmanager → Slack/PagerDuty | GitHub → Argo CD

docs.title: Admission controllers
docs.text:
• Checks inside the API server that run after authentication and authorization, before anything is saved to etcd
  • Inspect every create/update/delete request → modify it or approve/reject it
  • Final safety and policy layer → makes Kubernetes customizable and policy-driven without changing its code
  • Analogy → security guards at a building entrance

docs.title: The two kinds
docs.text:
• Mutating → the guard who fixes things → "you forgot your badge, I'll attach one" → changes the object
    • Examples → inject an Istio sidecar container, add default labels, set default values
  • Validating → the guard who says yes or no → "carrying a weapon, not allowed in" → can only allow or deny
    • Examples → block Pods running as root or privileged, only allow images from our registry, require resource limits, enforce naming rules
  • Order → mutating first, then validating → so validation checks the final version of the object

docs.title: Full request flow
docs.text:
1. API handler receives the request (raw YAML from kubectl or a controller)
  2. Authentication + authorization (RBAC)
  3. Mutating admission → built-in plugins and mutating webhooks change the object
  4. Object schema validation → correct apiVersion, fields, types
  5. Validating admission → built-in plugins and validating webhooks inspect the final object
  6. Approved → saved to etcd | denied → error returned, object never created

docs.title: Admission webhooks
docs.text:
• Built-in admission plugins are compiled into the API server → webhooks let me add my own logic as an external HTTP service
  • API server pauses the request → calls my webhook → "modify this?" or "allow this?" → continues based on the answer
  • Registered with MutatingWebhookConfiguration and ValidatingWebhookConfiguration objects
  • Tools built on this → Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper (policy), Istio (sidecar injection), cert-manager

docs.title: The classic gotcha
docs.text:
• Webhook server is down + failurePolicy: Fail → the API server can't admit anything that matches → e.g. no new Pods can be created anywhere it applies
  • Has broken real clusters, often during upgrades
  • Guard against it → narrow the webhook's scope (namespaceSelector, exclude kube-system), short timeoutSeconds, run the webhook with several replicas
  • Like a guard who must approve everyone, then goes missing → nobody enters

docs.title: CRDs (Custom Resource Definitions)
docs.text:
• Kubernetes ships with built-in types → Pod, Deployment, Service, ConfigMap
  • A CRD teaches Kubernetes a new object type → Database, Certificate, Backup
  • After that → kubectl get databases works exactly like kubectl get pods → stored in etcd, protected by RBAC, shown by kubectl
  • Analogy → Kubernetes is a form office that accepts only certain forms → CRD = registering a new form type ("also accept the Database form, with fields name, version, size") → Custom Resource (CR) = one filled-in copy of that form

docs.title: Step 1: register the type (CRD)
docs.text:
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: databases.example.com        # <plural>.<group>
spec:
  group: example.com
  names:
    kind: Database
    plural: databases
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            properties:
              version: { type: string }
              size: { type: string }

docs.title: Step 2: create one (Custom Resource)
docs.text:
apiVersion: example.com/v1
kind: Database
metadata:
  name: mydb
spec:
  version: "16"
  size: "10Gi"

kubectl get crds
kubectl apply -f crd.yaml
kubectl apply -f database.yaml
kubectl get databases
kubectl describe database mydb

docs.title: The catch
docs.text:
• A CRD alone does nothing → Kubernetes stores the Database object, but no database gets created
  • A filled form sitting in a drawer → no Pods, no volumes, nothing happens
  • To make it act → a controller

docs.title: Controllers and Operators
docs.text:
• Controller → a program that watches objects and reconciles real state towards them → same loop as the built-in Deployment and ReplicaSet controllers
  • CRD + custom controller = Operator → automates what a human operator would do (create, back up, upgrade, fail over)
  • Roles → CRD = the new form type | Custom Resource = a filled form | controller = the clerk who reads forms and does the work
Operator / tool Custom resource What its controller does cert-manager Certificate Gets and renews TLS certificates Prometheus Operator ServiceMonitor Configures what Prometheus scrapes Argo CD Application Syncs a Git repo into the cluster CloudNativePG Cluster Runs and manages Postgres Velero Backup, Restore Backs up and restores cluster resources
  • Written in Go with client-go / controller-runtime (Kubebuilder, Operator SDK)
  • This is the extensibility that makes Kubernetes different from its competitors → see Why Kubernetes

Quick revision

  • Webhook = "call this URL when X happens" (push, not poll)
  • Admission = mutating (change) then validating (allow/deny), after RBAC, before etcd
  • CRD = new object type | CR = one object of it | controller = acts on it | CRD + controller = operator

Interview points

  • What is a webhook? → an HTTP callback: a system pushes an event to a URL you registered instead of you polling it, like GitHub notifying Jenkins on a push
  • Webhook vs API? → with an API you pull data when you want it; with a webhook the other system pushes data when an event happens
  • What are admission controllers? → checks inside the API server, after authentication and authorization and before saving to etcd, that can modify or reject objects
  • Mutating vs validating admission? → mutating can change the object (e.g. inject a sidecar); validating can only allow or deny; mutating runs first
  • Why does order matter? → validation must check the final object, after all mutations
  • What happens if an admission webhook is down? → with failurePolicy Fail, matching requests are rejected, which can block Pod creation; scope webhooks narrowly and run them highly available
  • What is a CRD? → a way to extend the Kubernetes API with a new resource type, managed with kubectl like built-in objects
  • Does creating a custom resource do anything by itself? → no, it is only stored; a controller must watch and act on it
  • What is an operator? → a CRD plus a custom controller that automates running a piece of software, like cert-manager, Argo CD or Prometheus Operator
  • Tools built on admission webhooks? → Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper, Istio, cert-manager

docs.title: The problem with Docker alone
docs.text:
• Docker → great at packaging and running containers on one machine
  • Real apps → many containers, on many machines, running 24/7 → Docker alone can't manage that
  • What Docker alone does not give you:
Missing piece What it means Auto-scaling Add or remove containers automatically when traffic goes up or down Load balancing Spread traffic across many copies of the same app, on many machines Self-healing Container crashes or a machine dies → something brings the app back on its own Rolling updates / rollbacks Ship a new version with zero downtime, undo it if it breaks Scheduling Decide which machine has free CPU and RAM for a new container Service discovery Containers keep changing IPs → others still need a stable name to reach them
  • Analogy → Docker is one chef cooking one dish well | Kubernetes is the restaurant manager running 50 chefs in 5 kitchens, replacing anyone who calls in sick

docs.title: What Kubernetes is
docs.text:
• Kubernetes (K8s) → a container orchestrator → runs and manages containers across a group of machines called a cluster
  • K8s → 8 letters between K and s | Greek for "helmsman" (the person who steers a ship) | open-sourced by Google in 2014, now a CNCF project
  • It does not replace Docker images → it runs the same OCI images, just at scale
  • You describe what you want, Kubernetes works out how

docs.title: Desired state and reconciliation
docs.text:
• The core idea of Kubernetes → everything else is built on it
  • You never say "start a container on node 2" → you declare the desired state: "I want 3 copies of this image, 512Mi memory each, reachable on port 80"
  • That declaration is stored in the cluster's database (etcd)
  • Controllers keep comparing desired state with actual state → any difference gets fixed automatically
  • This loop is called reconciliation and it never stops
desired: 3 pods  →  actual: 2 pods  →  controller creates 1  →  actual: 3 pods  ✓
desired: 3 pods  →  actual: 4 pods  →  controller deletes 1  →  actual: 3 pods  ✓
  • Analogy → AC thermostat: you set 24°C (desired), it keeps measuring the room (actual) and switches the cooling on or off until they match
  • Declarative (say the end result) vs imperative (give step-by-step commands) → same idea as Terraform

docs.title: What Kubernetes gives you
docs.text:
• Scheduling → picks the right machine for each container based on free CPU/RAM and rules
  • Self-healing → container crashes → restarted | machine dies → its containers are recreated on another machine
  • Scaling → more or fewer copies of an app (HPA) | more or fewer machines (Cluster Autoscaler, Karpenter)
  • Service discovery + load balancing → Services give a stable name and IP in front of changing containers
  • Rolling updates + rollbacks → new version rolled out gradually, old version kept for instant undo
  • Config and secrets → ConfigMaps and Secrets, kept separate from the image
  • Storage → persistent volumes attached wherever the container lands
  • Extensibility → you can add your own object types to the API (CRDs + operators) → see Webhooks, CRDs & Operators

docs.title: Kubernetes vs Docker Swarm vs Docker Compose
docs.text: Kubernetes Docker Swarm Docker Compose What it is Full orchestrator for a cluster Docker's built-in simple orchestrator Tool to define multi-container apps Machines Many (multi-host cluster) Many (multi-host, smaller scale) One host only Complexity High Low Lowest Scaling Automatic + manual Manual, limited Manual Self-healing Strong (restarts, reschedules) Basic (restarts) None Load balancing Built-in, advanced Basic (routing mesh) Not built in Networking Advanced (Services, Ingress/Gateway, network policies) Overlay network Docker's default networking Stateful apps StatefulSets, Persistent Volumes Limited Volumes only Ecosystem Huge (Helm, Argo CD, Prometheus, Istio) Small, mostly stagnant Large, but for local dev Best for Production at any scale, microservices Small production setups Local development and testing

docs.title: Kubernetes vs the other options
docs.text: Kubernetes Nomad ECS Serverless (Lambda / Cloud Run) Complexity High Medium Low–Medium Lowest Portability Any cloud or on-prem Any AWS only Locked to the vendor Extensibility CRDs + operators extend the API itself Plugins None None Workloads Containers (VMs via KubeVirt) Containers, VMs, plain binaries Containers Functions / short-lived containers Hiring market Industry standard Niche Common in AWS shops Common

docs.title: Real advantages
docs.text:
• Extensibility → teach Kubernetes new object types (a Postgres cluster, a backup, a GPU job) and manage them exactly like built-in ones → no competitor has this
  • Portability → the same YAML runs on EKS, GKE, AKS, bare metal or kind on my laptop
  • Ecosystem → almost every infra tool supports Kubernetes first | AI infra (GPU scheduling, Kubeflow, KServe, Ray) is built on it

docs.title: Real downsides
docs.text:
• Operationally heavy → upgrades, CNI networking, RBAC, lots of YAML
  • Overkill for small apps → 3 services are often better on ECS or Cloud Run
  • Costs money when used badly → idle nodes, oversized resource requests
  • Steep learning curve → debugging needs Linux, networking and control-plane knowledge
  • Knowing when not to use Kubernetes is part of knowing Kubernetes

Quick revision

  • Kubernetes = container orchestrator for a cluster of machines
  • Core idea = desired state stored in etcd + controllers reconciling actual state towards it
  • Docker runs containers, Kubernetes runs them at scale with scheduling, healing, scaling and rollouts

Interview points

  • What is Kubernetes? → a declarative container orchestrator; controllers keep reconciling actual state towards the desired state stored in etcd, handling scheduling, self-healing, scaling, service discovery and rollouts
  • Why not just Docker? → Docker runs containers on one machine; it has no built-in auto-scaling, multi-host load balancing, self-healing or rolling updates across a cluster
  • Declarative vs imperative? → declarative = you describe the end state and the system works out the steps; imperative = you give each step yourself
  • What is reconciliation? → the never-ending loop where a controller compares desired and actual state and fixes the difference
  • Kubernetes vs Docker Swarm? → Swarm is simpler and built into Docker but has a small ecosystem and basic features; Kubernetes is more complex but is the industry standard with auto-scaling, strong self-healing and a huge ecosystem
  • Kubernetes vs ECS? → ECS is simpler and AWS-only; Kubernetes is portable and extensible through CRDs and operators
  • Biggest advantage of Kubernetes over competitors? → its extensible API (CRDs + operators), plus portability and the ecosystem
  • When would you not use Kubernetes? → small teams with a few services, where ECS or Cloud Run gives the same result with far less operational work

docs.title: Imperative vs declarative
docs.text:
• Imperative → tell the system how, step by step → kubectl run web --image=nginx
  • Declarative → describe what the end result should be, the system works out the steps → write pod.yaml → kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
  • Analogy → imperative = "copy file A to B, then run C" | declarative = "file A must exist at B with these permissions"
  • Kubernetes is built around declarative → I describe desired state, controllers keep reconciling towards it
Imperative Declarative Example kubectl run, create, scale, set image kubectl apply -f file.yaml Focus The commands The final state Run it twice create fails with "already exists" Same result every time (idempotent) Version control Nothing to commit YAML lives in Git → history, review, rollback Good for Quick tests, one-off fixes, exams Everything that must last
  • In real jobs → the YAML in Git is the source of truth → changes go through the file, not ad-hoc commands
  • Imperative commands are still useful → to generate YAML quickly (see Generate YAML instead of writing it)

docs.title: YAML basics
docs.text:
• YAML = YAML Ain't Markup Language → human-readable data serialization format
  • Data serialization → turning data structures (maps, lists, nested combinations) into text that humans can read and machines can parse
  • Used everywhere in DevOps → Kubernetes, Helm, Ansible, Docker Compose, GitHub Actions, Prometheus
  • Rules:
    • Indentation = structure → spaces only, never tabs → 2 spaces is the convention
    • key: value → the colon + space separates them
    • # → comment
    • Keys → lowercase, no spaces → first_name, my-app
  • Extensions → .yaml or .yml

docs.title: The three building blocks
docs.text:
1. Scalars → single values

first_name: Prakash     # string (quotes optional)
height: 5.9             # float
roll_number: 9          # integer
is_engineer: true       # boolean
pending_dues: null      # null

2. Dictionaries (maps) → key-value pairs, can nest

address:
  street: that_street
  contact:              # nested dictionary
    phone: "000111222"
    email: prakash@example.com

3. Lists → items starting with -

hobbies:
  - singing
  - traveling
args: ["sleep", "3600"]   # same thing, inline (flow) style

docs.title: Lists of dictionaries → the shape Kubernetes uses most
docs.text:
work_experience:
  - company: ABC Corp     # item 1 = a dictionary with 2 keys
    role: DevOps Engineer
  - company: XYZ Inc      # item 2
    role: DevOps Consultant
  • - starts a new item → keys under it at the same indent belong to that item
  • spec.containers is exactly this → a list where each item is one container's dictionary

docs.title: YAML gotchas
docs.text:
• Tab instead of spaces → parse error
  • Wrong indentation → a key silently lands under the wrong parent
  • Values that look like other types → quote them when a string is expected:
    • 1.20 → float 1.2 | "1.20" → string
    • yes, no, on, off → may become booleans
    • Annotation and env values must be strings → alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-interval-seconds: '15'
  • Validate → yamllint, the VS Code YAML extension, or kubectl apply --dry-run=server
YAML JSON XML Structure Indentation {} and [] <tag></tag> Comments Yes (#) No Yes (<!-- -->) Readability Best OK Verbose Typical use Config files APIs Legacy systems
  • JSON is valid YAML → Kubernetes accepts both → kubectl get pod x -o json / -o yaml

docs.title: What a Kubernetes object is
docs.text:
• An object = a record of something I want to exist in the cluster → a Pod, a Deployment, a Service
  • The YAML file on my laptop is not the object → it is the description
  • kubectl apply → API server validates it → saves it in etcd → now the object exists
  • Analogy → an AC remote: setting 24°C = the object (desired) | room at 30°C = actual | AC keeps cooling until they match
  • Every object has two halves:
    • spec → what I want → I write it
    • status → what is actually happening → Kubernetes writes it, I never do
  • Controllers keep comparing spec vs status and fixing the difference → reconciliation (see Why Kubernetes)
kubectl get pod web -o yaml     # my spec + a big status section I never wrote

docs.title: Anatomy of a manifest
docs.text:
• Every manifest has the same four top-level fields:
apiVersion: v1        # which API group + version
kind: Pod             # which type of object
metadata:             # identity → name, namespace, labels, annotations
  name: web
spec:                 # desired state → different for every kind
  containers: ...
  • Other names for manifests → config files, spec files, definition files, Kubernetes YAML → all the same thing

docs.title: apiVersion
docs.text:
• Format → group/version
  • API groups → related object types bundled together | analogy → departments in a government office
  • Core group → the original basic objects → has no name → written as just v1
  • Every other group → group/version
Object apiVersion Group Pod, Service, Namespace, ConfigMap, Secret, PVC v1 core Deployment, ReplicaSet, StatefulSet, DaemonSet apps/v1 apps Job, CronJob batch/v1 batch Ingress networking.k8s.io/v1 networking.k8s.io StorageClass storage.k8s.io/v1 storage.k8s.io ReplicationController (legacy) v1 core
  • Version stages → v1alpha1 (experimental, may vanish) → v1beta1 (mostly stable) → v1 (stable)
  • Old versions get removed → e.g. Ingress went extensions/v1beta1 → networking.k8s.io/v1beta1 → networking.k8s.io/v1 → old tutorials break on new clusters
  • What apiVersion + kind do → tell the API server which schema to validate the YAML against → unknown field = rejected
  • Wrong pair → apiVersion: v1 + kind: Deployment → error, Deployment is not in the core group

docs.title: apiVersion is not where objects are stored
docs.text:
• apiVersion is only a label on the form → it doesn't store anything
  • The API server checks the object and saves it in etcd under a path-like key:
/registry/pods/default/web
          │      │      │
        type  namespace name
  • Where apiVersion does show up → the API server's URL paths:
    • core group → /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/web
    • named group → /apis/apps/v1/namespaces/default/deployments/web
kubectl get pod web -v=6                            # shows the GET .../api/v1/... request kubectl sends
kubectl get --raw /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/web   # call the URL directly → JSON

docs.title: Looking things up instead of memorizing
docs.text:
kubectl api-resources                  # every type: NAME, SHORTNAMES, APIVERSION, NAMESPACED, KIND
kubectl api-versions                   # every group/version the cluster serves
kubectl explain deployment             # GROUP + VERSION + description
kubectl explain pod.spec.containers    # what a field means, drill down with dots
kubectl explain pod --recursive | less # the whole field tree
Kind Short name apiVersion Pod po v1 Service svc v1 ReplicationController rc v1 ReplicaSet rs apps/v1 Deployment deploy apps/v1 Namespace ns v1

docs.title: Example: a multi-container Pod
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: my-pod-2
  labels:                        # nested dictionary
    app: nginx
    environment: development
spec:
  containers:                    # list of dictionaries
    - name: nginx-container
      image: nginx               # no tag = nginx:latest → pin a version in real setups
      ports:
        - containerPort: 80      # documentation only, does not open or publish anything
    - name: sidecar-container
      image: busybox
      args: ["sleep", "3600"]    # keep busybox alive for 1 hour
  • One Pod, two containers → both share the Pod's network → same IP, reach each other on localhost
  • containerPort → informational → nginx listens on 80 either way → exposing it needs a Service
  • busybox has no long-running process → without sleep it exits instantly → CrashLoopBackOff
  • After 3600s sleep ends → container exits → restartPolicy: Always (default) restarts it → restart count goes up
  • Files are not shared → only through a declared volume (none here)
  • "sidecar" here is just a name → native sidecars (1.29+) are declared under initContainers with restartPolicy: Always → guaranteed to start before the main container
kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
kubectl get pods                                     # READY 2/2
kubectl exec -it my-pod-2 -c sidecar-container -- sh
wget -qO- localhost                                  # nginx page, from the busybox container
kubectl logs my-pod-2 -c nginx-container             # -c required with >1 container

docs.title: Generate YAML instead of writing it
docs.text:
• Nobody writes manifests from memory → let kubectl write the skeleton
kubectl run web --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > pod.yaml
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx --replicas=3 --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml
  • --dry-run=client → build the object locally, send nothing
  • --dry-run=server → send it to the API server for full validation, but don't save → catches typos before applying

docs.title: Reading validation errors
docs.text:
strict decoding error: unknown field "spec.template.metadata.label"
  • unknown field → a field name that isn't in the schema → almost always a typo
  • The path tells me where → here label should be labels
  • Other common ones → selector does not match template labels | Required value (missing field)

docs.title: kubectl apply and last-applied-configuration
docs.text:
• kubectl apply stores a copy of my file in the object → annotation kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration
  • Next apply → compares 3 things → my file now vs last-applied copy vs live object → works out what to change (three-way merge)
  • Imperative changes (set image, scale, rollout undo, edit) change the live object but not that copy → file, copy and cluster drift apart
  • That is the warning on kubectl rollout undo → "previously managed with kubectl apply…"
  • Fix → update the YAML to match what I want → kubectl apply -f again
  • create vs apply → create only creates (fails if it exists) | apply creates or updates

docs.title: kubectl command shape
docs.text:
• Most commands → kubectl <verb> <type> <name>
  • rollout, set, scale need the type → kubectl rollout status deploy/web or deploy web
  • Without it → the server doesn't have a resource type "web" → kubectl read the name as a type
  • Use the exact name → kubectl get <type> first and copy it → NotFound = wrong name or wrong namespace
  • Plural when listing, singular when acting on one → config get-contexts vs config use-context
